source_title: pandey_pandeymonium
question: In the Tata Cement story, what is the transferable observation, and how is it different from the lesson the author draws?
answer: The lesson he draws is that a creative person convinced they are right should stand by the work. The transferable observation is about REVIEW CONDITIONS, and he states it himself in passing: the strategy review board that rejected a month's work days before the pitch had not seen the work develop — 'If any of the board members had been involved from the outset, we wouldn't have been in this sorry state.' Reviewers who have not followed a work's development judge it without the context the team holds and cannot see the alternatives already discarded. The two are different because the review-conditions point is a property of a process that can be changed, while the conviction lesson is drawn from a single case in which the bet paid — and the author supplies the counterfactual himself, noting he could have been sacked and that being sacked at that seniority would have ended his career.
confounders: A creative director who refused equally firmly and lost the pitch would have written no book. This is the book's clearest instance of survivorship, and the author half-acknowledges it.
model_answer: The observation that transfers is that the people who actually decide a cement purchase are the mason and contractor on site, not the homeowner reading the ad. So the work has to speak in their language and about their concerns, strength and reliability, in a simple, earthy, local idiom. Pandey turns the episode into a lesson about gut feel, passion and 'thinking Indian'. That lesson is a personal credo. The transferable point is narrower: find the real influencer in the buying chain and brief to that person. [unsure]
missed: Review board uninvolved from outset; survivorship counterfactual of being sacked

source_title: dwyer_patel_cinema_india
question: This source describes darshan as a structure of looking. What is unusual about the direction of power in it, and how far does the author herself extend the claim?
answer: The look runs both ways and the power sits with the image rather than with the viewer: the beholder TAKES darshan (darshan lena) and the object GIVES darshan (darshan dena), and the image 'authorizes the look (rather than merely being its object), thereby benefiting the beholder'. That inverts the usual direction of power in accounts of spectatorship, where the gaze belongs to the one who looks. Dwyer reports its cinematic use — the star appears in tableau scenes that invite darshan, which hierarchises the look and lends the star the associations of kings and gods, the traditional granters of darshan. Her own extension is narrow and she draws the line herself: she reports this as Prasad's and Vasudevan's argument, says Vasudevan's contention about stasis and tableaux is one she finds persuasive, and then bounds it — while it may operate within the film to produce the star, she cannot otherwise see any culturally specific ways in which the star is produced.
confounders: The common summary is that Indian audiences 'worship' film stars. The source's claim is narrower and formal — about how a look is structured and where it is authorised from — and Dwyer explicitly declines the broader version.
model_answer: Darshan is a reciprocal looking: the devotee goes to see the deity, but more importantly the deity sees and blesses the devotee. Power runs from the image to the viewer rather than from the viewer who possesses the image (unlike the western voyeuristic gaze). The image looks back and grants something. The author borrows the idea (via Diana Eck and Ravi Vasudevan) as a helpful frame for frontal, iconic address in Hindi film posters and stills, but she hedges. She does not claim every cinematic look is religious darshan or that audiences literally worship stars. She treats it as a suggestive structure of frontality and exchange, not a universal law. [unsure]
missed: Dwyer bounds it: works within film to produce star, nothing more

source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
question: Sontag describes a reversal between the image and what it depicts. State it, give her example about the self, and give the boundary she puts on the claim.
answer: The reversal is that the copy becomes the measure: photographs, rather than the world, have become the standard of the beautiful, and instead of just recording reality photographs have become the norm for the way things appear to us — so it is reality which is scrutinised and evaluated for its fidelity to photographs. Her example about the self is exact: we learn to see ourselves photographically, so that to regard oneself as attractive is precisely to judge that one would look good in a photograph. She also reports the reversal in ordinary speech — people describing a violent event they were caught up in as having seemed like a movie, said not to diminish it but because other descriptions seem insufficient: it is how they explain how real it was. The boundary is hers and it matters: she says that in some non-industrialised countries people still felt apprehensive at being photographed, sensing a trespass, whereas people in industrialised countries seek to have their photographs taken and feel they are made real by them. The claim is scoped to the second case.
confounders: reading it as a claim that people confuse images with reality; her claim is about which is the reference
dropping the scope, which she states explicitly
model_answer: Sontag argues that reality has come to seem more like its images than the reverse: people describe a real disaster as being 'like a movie', and the image becomes the standard that experience is measured against. Her example about the self is that we learn to see ourselves photographically. To think yourself attractive is to judge that you would look good in a photograph. She limits the claim to modern, industrialised, camera-saturated societies, where images are everywhere. She does not offer it as a universal truth about human perception.

source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
question: Airey states an ordering between colour and form. What is the ordering, what working practice does he derive from it, and what does he say that practice does?
answer: The ordering is that colour is secondary to the form and the shape of the design. The practice he derives is to work only in black and white, and what he says it does is create more distinctive marks, because the contrast puts the emphasis on the shape or the idea. He offers this inside the distinctiveness section, as his answer to the question "how do you create a logo that is unique?" — so in his account working in black is not a presentation convention but a generation method. He restates the point negatively in tip 10: no amount of fancy gradients or colour options will rescue a badly designed mark.
confounders: reading this as the presentation argument from printed p. 111, which is a different claim about the client's attention
concluding that finished marks should be monochrome — his own examples on the facing pages are two-colour
treating it as a claim about colour psychology; it is a claim about which channel carries distinctiveness
model_answer: Airey puts form before colour: colour is secondary, and a logo's shape must work before any colour is added. His working practice is to design first in black and white (monochrome) and add colour only at the end. He says this keeps the focus on the concept and the shape, and it makes sure the mark still works in one colour, for example in single-colour print, faxes, stamps, embossing and newspaper reproduction, where colour cannot carry it.
missed: B&W working creates more distinctive marks; a uniqueness method, not reproduction check

source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
question: An organisation discovers two of its five reviewers are systematically harsher than the rest and equalises their averages through calibration training. It declares the consistency problem solved. What has it actually fixed, what has it not touched, and what design would have revealed the rest?
answer: It has fixed level noise — the differences in reviewers' across-the-board severity — which is genuinely worth fixing and which the book says organisations can sometimes see without an audit, provided cases are assigned roughly at random. What it has not touched is pattern noise: the variability in how each reviewer responds to particular items over and above their general severity. Two reviewers with identical averages can still rank the same set of items differently, because each has an idiosyncratic sensitivity to particular features and combinations of features. On the book's assembled evidence that is generally the larger component, which is why it says that "attaining only this objective would leave most of the problem of system noise without a solution." Equalising averages can even conceal the residual by making the summary statistics look healthy. The design that would have revealed the rest is a multi-case, multi-judge audit: several reviewers judging the SAME items, which is the only way an interaction between a reviewer and an item becomes recoverable, and which ordinary operations never arrange.
confounders: assuming equalised averages imply equalised judgements — the book's central point about the two components
importing a specific ratio of pattern to level noise, which the book declines to generalise
concluding that calibration training was worthless; the book says reducing level noise remains a worthwhile objective
model_answer: The calibration fixed level noise, the differences in each reviewer's average severity, for those two reviewers. It did not touch pattern noise, which is each judge's idiosyncratic response to particular cases (stable pattern noise), or occasion noise, which is the same judge varying with mood, time or order. System noise is level noise plus pattern noise, and in the book's audits pattern noise is usually the larger part. It also leaves shared bias alone. A noise audit would have revealed the rest: all five reviewers independently judge the same set of cases, with repeats where possible, and you measure the variability case by case, not only the averages.

source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
question: How does the source vary how directly the ad asks, across its four marketing objectives?
answer: Awareness: nothing objective-specific — "Apply core principles". Consideration: "Plant the seed of urgency", the softest of the asks. Action: "Present the ask after the context is set", which is an ordering instruction rather than a wording one. Full funnel: "Use CTAs throughout your ad, and be more direct as you go", the only instruction that both distributes the ask and escalates it. Those four cells are the entirety of the source's guidance on how directness should vary with objective; it offers no CTA taxonomy and no wording guidance beyond "say what you'd like viewers to do".
confounders: supplying a hierarchy of CTA verbs; the source gives none
assuming the action row asks for the most insistent CTA — its instruction is about ordering, and full funnel is the row that escalates
assuming awareness gets a soft CTA instruction; it gets none
model_answer: The Direct principle is scaled to the objective. For awareness, the ask is soft or absent: the aim is memorability and branding, so no hard call to action is needed. For consideration, the ask gets moderate: invite people to learn more, visit or search. For action/conversion (and for lead or sales objectives), the ask is explicit and repeated: a clear, specific call to action, often supported by on-screen text, voiceover and a CTA end card or overlay, sometimes shown early and again at the end. So directness increases from awareness to consideration to action rather than being one fixed rule. [unsure]
missed: Awareness gets no CTA instruction; action is ordering; full funnel escalates

source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
question: Berger distinguishes scarcity from exclusivity, which are usually run together. What is the distinction, and what does he insist about what can serve as the basis for exclusivity?
answer: Scarcity restricts HOW MUCH is offered — through high demand, limited production, or limits on the time or place something can be acquired. Exclusivity restricts WHO may have it, by criteria. His insistence is that the criterion need not be money or celebrity: exclusivity is also about knowledge — knowing certain information, or being connected to people who do. That is why a bar with no sign, reachable only through a phone booth inside a hot dog restaurant, is exclusive without being expensive, and why an invitation-only site is exclusive in a way money cannot purchase. Both raise perceived desirability, by two inferences he names: difficulty of acquisition is read as evidence of worth, and unavailability is read as evidence that many other people wanted it.
confounders: collapsing the two into 'limited availability', which loses the knowledge-based route to exclusivity that his best cases depend on
assuming exclusivity requires price or status; he explicitly rejects that
treating the Rue La La versus SmartBargains comparison as controlled; the two also differed in timing, brand and merchandising
model_answer: Scarcity concerns how much of something there is: limited quantity, limited time, supply restricted by production or distribution. Exclusivity concerns who can get it: access depends on a qualification such as membership, invitation or insider status, as with Rue La La's members-only sales or a hidden restaurant. Berger insists that exclusivity is not only about money or celebrity. It can rest on knowledge, connections or behaviour, such as being a loyal customer or knowing the secret menu. Ordinary products can therefore create insider status and the social currency that comes with it.

source_title: parameswaran_nawabs_nudes_noodles
question: An adhesive brand has no product demonstration budget and no headline. What does the reproduced Fevicol execution do instead, and what does the device require of its audience?
answer: It carries the whole argument in one photograph: an overcrowded Indian suburban train with dozens of men hanging off the side of a carriage, on which a 'FEVICOL — The Ultimate Adhesive' panel is mounted. There is no headline and no body copy; the adhesion claim is made by the juxtaposition alone, and the viewer infers it rather than being told. What the device requires is that the scene already be culturally familiar — it recruits an everyday sight the audience knows, so it does not travel to an audience that has not seen an Indian suburban train. That dependence is the extractor's observation from the plate, not something the source states; the book's caption asserts only that good creative work is possible for a humble category.
confounders: The source does not date this execution and gives no outcome data for it.
model_answer: The reproduced Fevicol execution has no demonstration and no headline. It relies on a single absurd, humorous visual metaphor of an unbreakable bond (the overloaded vehicle or egg style of joke), with the brand mark as the only text. It dramatises 'the strong bond' as a situation rather than proving it. The device needs a culturally literate audience that already knows Fevicol's long-running bond promise and its comic idiom, and that will close the gap and make the inference for itself. [unsure]
missed: Overcrowded suburban train scene; requires familiarity with that scene

source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
question: Give the five steps the authors say most retail category killers follow, in their order. Then identify the tension that steps 2 and 5 create with step 1 — a tension the book does not address.
answer: Narrow the focus; stock in depth; buy cheap; sell cheap; dominate the category. The authors chain them causally: narrowing permits depth, depth permits buying power, buying power permits low prices at maintained margin, and the result is domination, which they call the ultimate objective of any branding programme. The tension is that steps 2 and 5 are both expansions. Step 2 widens assortment inside the narrowed category — a Toys "R" Us store carrying ten thousand toys against a department store's three thousand — and step 5 enlarges the brand's share of it, with Microsoft at 95 per cent, Intel at 80 and Coca-Cola at 70 cited approvingly on the following page. So the brand contracts what it is about while expanding what it carries and how much of the category it takes, and the book never says where narrowing stops and depth begins. The domination figures also sit against the roughly 50 per cent ceiling the same authors state twice later.
confounders: resolving the tension by saying narrowing applies to category and depth to assortment — that is a plausible reading, but the authors do not make it and supply no boundary
assuming steps 3 and 4 are supported by figures; no retail economics of any kind appear in the chapter
treating the pattern as descriptive of all retail; the authors restrict it to 'most retail category killers'
model_answer: The five steps are: (1) narrow the focus, (2) stock in depth, (3) buy cheap, (4) sell cheap, (5) dominate the category. Step 1 is contraction, which the Law of Contraction praises. Step 2, however, means carrying a huge assortment within the category, so the brand's promise becomes breadth and selection. Step 5, domination, rewards growth, and a dominant retailer comes under pressure to widen the category it dominates. Both pull toward the expansion the book condemns elsewhere. The book never says where 'deep' becomes 'broad', or when domination turns into line extension.

source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
question: Compare a small bright highlight and a large dim one on the surface of a glass. What does the book say each does for the viewer, and what sets the difference in practice?
answer: They do opposite jobs. The tiny bright spots are distracting at the least and meaningless at best: they are too small and too bright to tell the viewer anything about surface detail or texture. A large highlight informs — it serves the constructive purpose of saying how the glass surface looks and feels. In practice the difference is set by how much of the relevant family of angles is filled with light, and, with a diffusion sheet, by the distance from the lamp head to the sheet: close in, only the centre of the sheet lights and the highlight is small and bright; pulled back, the whole sheet lights and reflects as a larger highlight. The authors add that the larger highlight should usually be kept dimmer, because a brightly lit whole sheet reflects as an obvious hard-edged rectangle that advertises a studio light and costs the scene its reality — and that strips of black tape on the sheet can make the reflection read as a window instead.
confounders: assuming brighter highlights read as more premium or more glossy
attributing the difference to the size of the source alone, ignoring the lamp-to-diffuser distance
missing that the source deliberately makes the large highlight dimmer, not brighter
model_answer: In the glassware chapter, highlights on glass define its surface and shape. A small, bright highlight (from a small source) reads as crisp and sparkling, signalling a hard, polished surface and adding brilliance, but it describes little of the form. A large, dimmer highlight (from a big source such as a large softbox or white card) describes the curvature and the extent of the surface, telling the viewer about shape and volume, while looking softer. What sets the difference in practice is the size of the light source and its distance, relative to the object: the reflection is essentially an image of the source, so source size and brightness determine highlight size and intensity. [unsure]
missed: Small highlights meaningless; lamp-to-diffuser distance; keep large highlight dimmer

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: Godin's music-teacher example: one teacher claims rigour and competition results, another claims the whole student and refuses competitions. What does he say this costs the first teacher, and what general rule is the example there to demonstrate?
answer: It costs him his freedom of action. Having claimed rigour, he now has to actually be more rigorous and professional than other teachers, has to make the difficult decision of expelling students who are not serious enough, and has to persevere until his students really do win competitions. The general rule is that a position is an obligation: once you claim a story you are on the hook to deliver, and Godin contrasts this with merely offering an alternative, which he calls the low-risk path — take it or leave it. He also adds two modern conditions on the claims themselves: they must be true and continually doubled down on in all your actions, and they must be generous, existing as a service to the customer. And he notes, without softening it, that this is not a teacher he would have wanted himself — which is the "it's not for you" principle applied to his own example.
confounders: reading positioning as a communications choice with no operational consequence
assuming Godin endorses the rigorous teacher; he explicitly says it is not for him
model_answer: By staking out the extreme of rigour and competition results, the first teacher gives up the families who want joy, balance and development of the whole child. They also commit to delivering winners. Those families are simply not their customers, and they must not try to win them back by blurring the promise. The general rule is Godin's positioning map: choose two axes that matter to the people you seek, find an empty extreme, and own it. Every choice of position deliberately excludes someone. Being for someone means not being for everyone.
missed: Position is an obligation; costs freedom of action (must be rigorous, expel students)

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: You are handed a brief that names a deliverable and a deadline. Applying Godin's method, what two things must be settled before anything is produced, and what are the two ways he says the second one gets answered badly?
answer: Who is it for, and what is it for — the second in its strong form, what change are you trying to make. He treats these as generative rather than descriptive: once you are clear who it is for, the answer shifts the product you make, the story you tell and where you tell it, so a brief that starts from a deliverable has already skipped the decisions. The two bad answers he names are specific. First, the grandiose one — a change that has never been done by anyone with your resources — which he says is both a heavy burden and a convenient excuse when things go badly. Second, the reverse-engineered one, constructed backwards from what you were already going to make and loaded with buzzwords. His three-sentence template forces the answers: my product is for people who believe ___; I will focus on people who want ___; I promise that engaging with what I make will help you get ___.
confounders: answering with the two questions and missing the two named failure modes
treating 'what's it for' as a statement of the deliverable rather than of the change sought
the modern default of starting from the channel or format
model_answer: Godin's method says two things must be settled first: 'Who's it for?' (the specific, smallest viable audience) and 'What's it for?' (the change you are trying to make in those people). The deliverable and the deadline are neither. He says the second question gets answered badly in two ways. One is to answer with the tactic or deliverable itself ('it's for the launch', 'it's an ad'). The other is to answer with a selfish goal for the marketer ('to make money', 'to get attention') instead of a change in the audience. [unsure]
missed: Bad answers: grandiose change, and reverse-engineered buzzword answer

source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
question: Airey gives a phrase for the boundary he sets on client feedback. What is the boundary, what does he say happens if it is not held, and what does he suggest saying to make it concrete?
answer: The boundary is that what he needs from the client group is strategic input and execution freedom. If it is not held — if the discussion collapses into them telling you which colours or typefaces to use — he says the identity will inevitably be weakened, because you are taking design decisions from too many non-designers. To make it concrete he scripts both halves for the client: saying you think a blue is too weak for an organisation trying to present strength, or that a typeface feels too old-fashioned, is exactly what he wants — expressing those impressions is critical to a project's success. Saying "make the blue darker" or "why not try a modern typeface" is what he asks them to stop at, with the reason given as trust: you have to trust that I can find the right design solution based on your feedback.
confounders: reading it as a rule against client feedback; he says expressing impressions is critical
treating it as a claim about client competence rather than about where the boundary sits
confusing it with the separate instruction to keep the presentation on the idea rather than the details
model_answer: Airey's line is that the client pays for your expertise, not for a pair of hands. Feedback should be judged against the brief and the business objectives, not personal taste, and the number of rounds should be limited. If the boundary is not held, the job turns into design by committee: endless revisions and a watered-down compromise mark nobody chose, and the designer ends up as a software operator. To make it concrete he advises writing the scope into the contract, for example a fixed number of concepts and revision rounds, with more charged extra. [unsure]
missed: Strategic input plus execution freedom; impressions welcome, prescriptions like 'darker blue' not

source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
question: Very large diversified companies are the obvious objection to the Law of Expansion. How do the authors handle that objection, and what does their handling of it cost them?
answer: They separate size from brand strength and say omnibus or mile-wide brands are weak, not strong: they look strong because they are well known and have been in business for decades, but where such a brand succeeds it is because its competitors are equally broad. Their formulation is that when two weak brands compete the winner is a weak brand that happens to be less weak than its rival, and their test of real strength is what happens when a broad brand meets a specialist — General Electric losing about $300 million in mainframes against IBM, and selling its appliance business to another omnibus brand. What it costs them is disconfirmability. This is the third use in the book of the same move: a counter-example is re-described as a case of weak competition rather than counted, and the book offers no way to establish independently that a set of competitors is weak, so no successful broad brand can ever count against the law.
confounders: accepting the two GE failures as a test; they are two cases chosen from a company with many businesses
assuming the authors deny the sales and profits of these companies; they concede them explicitly and relocate the disagreement to what 'strong' means
concluding that broad brands must therefore be strong — the passage establishes nothing either way, which is the point
model_answer: The Law of Expansion says the power of a brand is inversely proportional to its scope. The obvious objection is giants like GE, Mitsubishi, Yamaha or Samsung that put one name on everything. The authors reply that these firms succeed despite, not because of, line extension: their profit margins and returns are poor compared with focused competitors, and they win in markets lacking strong specialist brands (for example Asia). The cost is that the law becomes hard to falsify: success by a broad brand is redescribed as underperformance relative to a hypothetical focused alternative, or attributed to weak competition, so any counterexample is absorbed and the law's predictive content shrinks. [unsure]
missed: Test against specialists (GE vs IBM); weak-vs-weak framing

source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
question: Carroll allows telephoto lenses in some circumstances and warns about them in others. What is the condition that separates the two, and what does he say the lens does to the space in the picture?
answer: The condition is whether you could have got close. Telephoto lenses are essential where you are unable to get physically close — his examples are sports and wildlife — but when you are able to get close and choose not to, the images can start to feel predatory. So the fault is not in the lens but in a decision the picture records. To the space, the lens gives the illusion of compressing depth: everything seems flatter, a receding avenue reads as a flat vertical strip rather than leading into the distance, and buildings behave like layered cut-out shapes, which he says makes images look more graphic. He calls the compression an illusion and explains it no further.
confounders: treating the predatory reading as an absolute objection; Carroll concedes one photographer wanted it
explaining the compression optically; Carroll gives no mechanism and calls it an illusion
model_answer: The dividing line is whether you cannot get closer or are choosing not to. Telephoto is fine when physical access is impossible or would disturb the subject: wildlife, sport, candid moments you would destroy by approaching. Carroll warns against using it as a way to hang back and avoid engaging, because distance shows in the picture as detachment. Optically, a telephoto compresses space. It flattens perspective, so background and foreground appear closer together and elements stack into layers. Depth is squeezed rather than exaggerated, which you can use deliberately for graphic, flattened compositions.
missed: Close-by choice feels predatory; compression is an unexplained illusion

source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
question: A campaign is measured one week after launch, performs well, and is judged a success; a second campaign is measured over four months, looks flat, and is killed. On Berger's account, what might have gone wrong in each judgement, and what does he say determines which window is the right one?
answer: Both judgements may be reading the wrong window rather than the wrong campaign. Berger's own research history is the warning: he measured whether a property mattered without asking WHEN it mattered, found nothing, and only recovered a real finding by splitting the outcome into immediate and ongoing. A one-week measure will credit whatever is interesting, which his data say does not persist; a four-month pooled measure can bury a real immediate effect. What determines the right window, on his account, is the product's own economics rather than the campaign: films and new grocery items depend on immediate word of mouth, because theatre bookings and shelf space get reallocated fast, so an early read is the correct one. Anti-bullying campaigns and policy initiatives need people still talking months later, so an early read is meaningless for them. The window is a substantive decision, not a measurement detail.
confounders: assuming a longer measurement window is always better; it can bury a real immediate effect
treating the window as a matter of statistical power rather than of which outcome the product actually needs
attributing the general methodological principle to Berger; he demonstrates it and does not state it
model_answer: Berger separates immediate word of mouth from ongoing word of mouth. Interesting or surprising content creates a burst of immediate talk that fades. Triggers, meaning frequent environmental cues such as Cheerios or Friday, sustain ongoing talk. A one-week read can mistake a novelty spike for lasting success. A four-month read can miss a trigger-driven effect that builds slowly, or kill something whose value lies elsewhere. The right window depends on which kind of word of mouth the goal needs, immediate buzz or sustained ongoing discussion, and on how often triggers occur.
missed: Window set by product economics: films/grocery immediate, policy campaigns ongoing

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: SC 1.4.5 and SC 1.4.9 have nearly the same subject. Set out precisely what differs, including the condition one of them carries that the other does not.
answer: Three differences, all in the escape routes. First, SC 1.4.5 applies only "if the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation"; SC 1.4.9 carries no such condition. Second, SC 1.4.5 excepts images of text that can be visually customised to the user's requirements; SC 1.4.9 drops that exception entirely. Third, SC 1.4.9 admits pure decoration as a permitted use, which SC 1.4.5 does not need to name because it only governs text used to convey information. What is common: both except a particular presentation of text that is essential, and both carry a note declaring logotypes essential. The Understanding note adds a distinction stated nowhere in either criterion: SC 1.4.5 is met where an image of text is used in addition to the same information as text and both are presented to the user, whereas SC 1.4.9 applies to all images of text regardless of whether they duplicate text. SC 1.4.5 is Level AA; SC 1.4.9 is Level AAA.
confounders: assuming the only difference is the conformance level
assuming SC 1.4.9 forbids all images of text — it permits decoration and essential presentation
carrying SC 1.4.5's technology condition across to SC 1.4.9, where it does not exist
model_answer: SC 1.4.5 Images of Text (Level AA) applies only 'if the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation'. In that case text must be used instead of images of text, with two exceptions. Customizable: the image of text can be visually customized to the user's requirements. Essential: a particular presentation is essential, such as logotypes. SC 1.4.9 Images of Text (No Exception) (Level AAA) drops the technology condition and the customizable exception. Images of text are allowed only for pure decoration or where the particular presentation is essential, and logotypes still count as essential.

source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
question: Distinguish Samara's two narrative constructs, and say what he claims stays constant as a pictorialised layout runs across many pages.
answer: In narrative pictorialisation the layout is made to look like something discussed in the text — elements arranged to give the impression of objects swept up in a flood, or to construct a literal image of a car or other machine; in simplest terms the layout becomes a kind of illustration. In metaphorical allusion the layout structure and the visual language of its forms refer instead to a tangential idea that supports or manipulates perception of the meaning; his example is a film festival promotion splicing repeated images to refer to film editing. What stays constant across a pictorialised sequence is the governing logic: as the content progresses or takes a different direction from page to page or screen to screen, the subject the layout depicts changes while the logic that decides how to depict it does not.
confounders: collapsing the two into one 'conceptual layout' idea
assuming the depicted subject must stay the same across a sequence — he says it changes and the logic does not
confusing metaphorical allusion with vernacularism, which borrows a style rather than depicting an idea
model_answer: Samara distinguishes a sequential (linear, cinematic) narrative, where the layout unfolds page by page like a story with a beginning, middle and end and elements recur and progress, from a non-sequential or thematic narrative, where spreads are related by concept or variation rather than strict order. When a pictorial, image-driven layout runs over many pages, he claims what stays constant is the underlying structural logic: consistent proportional relationships, recurring alignments and a consistent visual vocabulary (typographic treatment, margins, rhythm), so that even as pictures change dramatically the reader perceives a unified system. [unsure]
missed: Constructs are narrative pictorialisation vs metaphorical allusion

source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
question: Sullivan repeats "write hot, edit cold" in two chapters. What is the mechanism he gives for the hot half, and what does he actually prescribe for the cold half?
answer: The mechanism for the hot half is mechanical and specific: if you try to edit too much in your head, your pen will stop moving. So generate without editing and let the words come out any way they want. The cold half is not merely "edit later" — he prescribes a cooling interval first, so the second pass is done with distance, and then a three-way sort: keep only the A-plus work, put the A-minus and B-plus in a separate pile to revisit, and either kill or shelve everything below. His strong form is that all first drafts are crap and all good copywriting is rewriting. What he does not supply is any criterion for what counts as A-plus; the grading is left entirely to the maker.
confounders: treating it as a preference for speed rather than as a claim about what simultaneous judgement does to production
omitting the cooling interval, which is what he says makes the cold pass cold
assuming everything below the top tier is discarded; two of the three tiers are retained
model_answer: The hot half works by switching off the internal critic. Judgement and generation interfere with each other: if you evaluate while you produce, you strangle ideas before they can lead anywhere. So you write fast and uncensored and aim for quantity, knowing most of it will be bad. For the cold half he prescribes distance. Put the work away, let time pass (overnight if possible), and come back to it as a detached, ruthless reader. Cut everything that does not earn its place and keep only what still holds up on sober rereading, often pinned up on the wall for testing.
missed: Pen stops moving; three-way A+/A-B+/kill sort, two tiers retained

source_title: jain_gods_in_the_bazaar
question: What does this source say changed after economic liberalisation, and why is this the object in the record most likely to be out of date?
answer: She describes a double movement: 'one set of processes creates identifiable symbols of cultural identity while another lays down the universal ground within which these markers of difference operate.' The mechanism she names in the trade is concrete — 'advertising agencies in India — the new Ravi Varmas, if you will — often use proprietary analytical models from their parent companies overseas, filling in the blanks with content specific to Indian market segments.' With it comes a narrowing of what 'culture' is taken to mean: circumscribed, globally portable signs of heterogeneity — language, dress, food, music, art, rituals, festivals — grafted onto the protocols of a putatively universal modernity, which relegates cultural difference to leisure and harnesses it to niche marketing. IT IS THE MOST DATED OBJECT IN THE RECORD because it is a characterisation of a media landscape observed to roughly 2004-06, drawn largely from one firm's transformation seen at two points, and it precedes the Indian smartphone, cheap mobile data, UPI and streaming entirely — any of which would change the picture materially.
confounders: The template-plus-local-content observation is sharp and quotable, which is precisely why its date and its narrow evidence base need to travel with it.
model_answer: Jain describes how the post-1991 liberalisation, together with satellite television and digital technology, changed the calendar and bazaar print industry. Hand-painted oleographic calendar art gave way to computer compositing and photographic and Photoshop imagery. New producers, markets and glossier globalised aesthetics came in, and the old artist-studio and printer networks changed. This is the object most likely to be out of date because it describes a then-current, fast-moving industrial and technological situation from fieldwork done up to the mid-2000s. It is a snapshot of a trend, not a stable historical claim. [unsure]
missed: Double movement; agencies fill global parent models with local content

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
question: Hopkins claims a guarantee's force comes from something other than its terms. What, and what second effect does he report that does not follow from the terms at all?
answer: It comes from who signs it. He observes that many an advertiser a thousand miles away offered to guarantee results, but the guarantors were strangers, so the promise carried no weight — redress from a stranger is not a real option to the buyer. His move was to have the neighbourhood druggist, to whom people actually paid their money, sign the guaranty. The second effect is the interesting one: the guarantee was written against a six-bottle, five-dollar purchase, few users ever bought that amount, and it nonetheless gave them confidence in every single-bottle purchase. That does not follow from the terms — it follows only if the guarantee is being read as a statement of the seller's confidence rather than as a contract. He reports the plan worked on a cough remedy and then on two further remedies and secured most of the trade, with no figure for this mechanism in isolation.
confounders: reading it as a rule about guarantee terms — coverage, duration, conditions — which is exactly what he says does not matter
treating it as third-party endorsement in the modern sense; his mechanism is that redress must be locally collectible
assuming the scope effect is a mistake by buyers; he reports it as the mechanism working
model_answer: Hopkins says a guarantee's power lies in the confidence it signals, the maker's visible willingness to take the risk himself, not in the legal or money-back terms, which few people ever invoke. The second effect he reports is on the advertiser's side. Claims under the guarantee turned out to be rare, and offering it made dealers and the maker's own organisation more confident, and more careful about the product. Neither effect follows from the wording of the terms. It is the psychology of the offer that sells. [unsure]
missed: Local druggist signs guarantee; confidence extends to single-bottle purchases

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
question: Your current campaign is working and you do not want to risk it, but you think a better approach exists. What arrangement does Hopkins describe, and what is wrong with the 75 per cent figure he attaches to it?
answer: Run the new methods as tests alongside the campaign rather than in place of it, so better methods can be sought constantly without interrupting plans already proved out. He reports doing this for one food advertiser over five years, trying more than fifty separate plans, finding an improvement every little while, and ending with a best plan that reduced the cost of selling by 75 per cent — four times more effective than the best plan used before. What is wrong with the figure is that it is the winner of fifty attempts reported as if it were the effect of the method: he gives no distribution of outcomes across the fifty, and a 75 per cent reduction accumulated over five years against a baseline that was itself the best of an earlier search cannot be attributed to the final plan alone. The advertiser, product, plans and absolute costs are all unnamed. The durable content is the structure — the proved plan keeps running while the candidate is tested beside it — not the number.
confounders: Quoting the 75 per cent as a demonstrated effect size for a testing programme.
That the improvement came from one change; he describes fifty attempts over five years.
Missing the champion/challenger structure, which is the part that does not depend on the figure.
model_answer: Hopkins says keep running the proven campaign in most of the field and test the new approach in a limited portion (a few towns or a fraction of the space) using keyed returns, so the established method continues earning while the challenger is measured against it. He adds that most new schemes fail, suggesting something like three out of four ventures prove wrong, hence the caution. The problem with the 75 per cent figure is that it is an unsupported rule-of-thumb assertion: he gives no data, sample or definition behind it, and it sits awkwardly in a book whose whole argument is that claims should rest on traced, measured results. [unsure]
missed: 75% is cost reduction, best of fifty plans, not a failure rate

source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
question: Pastel and muted are adjacent cases in Freeman's colour part and are easily confused. On his own colour solid, what is the difference?
answer: They move along different axes. Pastel is a move down the brightness axis to a lower, brighter, whiter level — he slides that section of the cylinder out to show the pale hues. He is explicit that the result is more about brighter than about less saturated: in his foggy Pennsylvania farm the grey wooden building is unsaturated, but the browns and greens still keep their colourfulness. Muted is the saturation move, inward from the rim, which he illustrates by drawing each main colour expanded back out to full saturation to show how much the soft grey light took away. He also gives a diagnostic for pastel: an overall pastel scene keeps its character by not containing black.
confounders: treating both as desaturation, which is exactly the collapse Freeman corrects
assuming pastel means pale colours of any brightness, when he ties it to a specific level of the solid
supposing the no-black rule is a compositional principle, when it is a processing caution about the black-point control
model_answer: Both pastel and muted colours sit toward the low-saturation core of Freeman's colour solid, which is organised by hue, saturation and brightness. They differ on the brightness (lightness) axis. Pastels are desaturated and high in brightness, near the upper, white end of the solid: pale, light, airy tints. Muted colours are desaturated at middle or lower brightness, pulled toward grey rather than white: subdued, dusky or greyed hues. So the two share low saturation and are separated by where they sit vertically, light versus mid-dark. [unsure]
missed: Pastel is a brightness move, muted a saturation move; not both desaturation

source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
question: A usability study on a new digital claims-filing flow is scheduled in a few weeks. Using this source's reverse planning method, derive what you should critique now and why — and state the three steps of the method in the order it gives them.
answer: Reverse planning runs: start from what actions you want to be able to take after the conversation; ask what questions must be answered in the critique to take them; and let those questions tell you which aspects of the design to present and focus on. Applied to the source's own worked case: because a usability study is coming, the action you want afterwards is to have the prototype be the best available reflection of the process and experience before it is tested. Since there is time to iterate before the study, a logical scope is the scenarios that use the new claims process. The goals the source derives are to identify the aspects that do not support the desired experience; to identify the aspects that most effectively produce it, so they can perhaps be expanded; and to identify where there is the most question or disagreement among the team, so the usability study can take those into account and perhaps build them into its plan. That third goal is the one usually missed: disagreement inside the team is treated as an input to the study's design.
confounders: planning forward from what is ready to show, which is what reverse planning replaces
scoping to the whole application because the study will cover the whole application
omitting the disagreement goal — treating internal disagreement as noise rather than as something a study can be pointed at
model_answer: Reverse planning starts from the future milestone and works backwards. The steps, in order: (1) identify the upcoming milestone or decision point (the usability study); (2) determine what must be true or ready for it (a testable claims-filing flow, the task scenarios, the key screens and the error and confirmation states); (3) work backwards to schedule critiques now of the things that must be settled first. So critique the core flow structure and task path, and whether they meet the filing objectives, now, before polishing any visual detail. [unsure]
missed: Steps: desired actions, questions to answer, aspects to present; disagreement goal

source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
question: The source gives a reason for keeping visuals bright and high-contrast. What is the reason, and what does the guidance not supply?
answer: The reason is device coverage: "Ensure visuals are optimized for all devices", and the source's own illustration reduces that to holding visual engagement on small screens. What it does not supply is any measurable target — no contrast ratio, no luminance figure, no reference screen and no viewing distance. The article instead points readers to a separate page for video specs and safe zones. So the guidance is a direction, not a specification, and any threshold used to check an ad against it is the implementer's rather than the source's.
confounders: supplying a WCAG-style contrast ratio, which this source neither gives nor references
reading the guidance as being about legibility of on-screen text; the source scopes it to visuals and devices, and states no legibility rationale for supers
assuming the specs page is part of this guidance; it is a separate linked article
model_answer: The reason given is attention: bright, high-contrast visuals stand out and hook viewers in a fast-scrolling feed, often on small mobile screens and sometimes with the sound off, so the ad registers in the first seconds. The guidance does not supply thresholds, meaning no contrast ratio, brightness or saturation value, and no definition of 'bright'. It also gives no causal evidence isolating this factor from the other ABCD elements, and no guidance on when brightness conflicts with brand palettes or mood. It is a heuristic, not a measurable specification.
missed: Reason is device optimisation/small screens, not feed attention hook

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: A team asks how to make an asset that people will share. Give Godin's two constraints, and say why they rule out most of what is usually attempted.
answer: First, the verdict is not yours. Whether something is remarkable is decided by the user: if they remark on it, it is remarkable — so remarkability can be observed but never claimed. Second, the motive belongs to the teller. People spread the word when it benefits them, because talking about your thing is a way of talking about themselves — look how good my taste is, look how good I am at spotting important ideas — and never because it matters to you, because you asked, or because you worked hard. Together these rule out the usual attempts: adding a share prompt, appealing to the importance of the cause, and the stunt, which Godin says comes from a place of selfishness and warns is not the same thing as remarkable. What is left is designing the reason to tell into the product or service itself, which is why he says effective marketers are also in charge of the customer's experience.
confounders: reaching for a share incentive or a call to action, which addresses neither constraint
assuming being talked about proves the mechanism worked; Godin notes criticism also spreads, as a signal to shun you
treating 'if they remark on it, it's remarkable' as a test rather than as the circular definition it is
model_answer: Godin's two constraints: people share things when sharing it makes them look good or advances their own status/goals (it helps the sharer), and when the thing works better the more people use it (network effects: sharing makes it more valuable to the sharer). Remarkability alone is not enough; the idea must spread because it benefits the person who spreads it. This rules out most attempted 'viral' content, because typical brand assets are made to benefit the marketer: asking people to share an ad gives the sharer nothing, costs them social capital, and the asset gains nothing from being used by more people. [unsure]
missed: Remarkability is decided by the user, not claimed; no network effects

source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
question: A pack promises "Made with real cheese" and a truck advertisement carries an asterisked monthly payment. Sullivan says both work against themselves. What is the shared inference, and what does he say created the audience that makes it?
answer: The shared inference is that the reassurance is evidence against the claim it defends: if the product were authentically cheese, it would not need to say so — his reductio is that nobody sells a phone by saying it is made with real phone — and an asterisk announces that a briefcase of qualifications is propping the number up, so the line can legitimately be read as saying "we're lying". Each is a defensive move that would be unnecessary if the claim were secure, so a reader who has learned the pattern treats the defence as a symptom. He grounds the learned pattern historically: the collapse of institutional authority, which he dates from a presidential resignation and traces through a chain of fallen public figures, produced what he calls a nation of eye-rollers and sceptics who no longer accept "because we said so". He places the same family: the exclamation point, the invented customer name, the stock photograph.
confounders: reading the objection as legal or ethical rather than as a claim about inference
assuming the remedy is to remove the qualifier, when his stated remedies are to have a claim that does not need one, or to embrace the weakness directly
treating the historical account as established; it is asserted
model_answer: In both cases the claim or disclaimer makes the reader ask what is not being said. 'Made with real cheese' implies that some of it, or the competition's, is not real. The asterisk signals a catch hidden in the small print. By trying to reassure or comply, the ad signals doubt and loses credibility. Sullivan blames the advertising industry itself for creating that suspicious audience: decades of hype, weasel words and fine-print tricks trained consumers to distrust ads and to decode every qualifier as evidence of deception.
missed: Collapse of institutional authority created the sceptics, not ad industry

source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
question: Berger rejects the influentials thesis in the body text and states something noticeably weaker in his endnote. What does each say, and why does the difference matter?
answer: The body text says conventional wisdom is wrong: some people are more persuasive and some have more friends, but in most cases that does not make them more influential in spreading things, and contagious content spreads regardless of whether the messenger has ten friends or ten thousand. The endnote says something different in kind — that right now there is little good empirical evidence that better-connected or more persuasive people have a bigger impact. That is an absence-of-evidence statement, not a demonstration that messengers do not matter. The difference matters because the body text's confident refutation is not what the endnote supports, and the book's whole shift of attention to the message rests on it. Berger does not deny that individuals supply an initial spark; his borrowed comparison, from Duncan Watts, is that big forest fires are not caused by big sparks.
confounders: reporting the body text alone, which overstates what the source establishes
reading the claim as 'messengers never matter'; he explicitly allows that individuals provide the spark
attributing the forest-fire argument to Berger; he credits Duncan Watts for it
model_answer: In the body text Berger rejects the Gladwell-style influentials or 'law of the few' thesis. He says it is the message, not the messenger, that makes things catch on, so marketers should not chase special influencers. In the endnote he concedes something weaker: influentials may matter somewhat, but the evidence is mixed and they are hard to identify and target cost-effectively. The difference matters because the body overclaims. The book cannot be cited as proof that influencers don't matter, only as proof that content features are a more practical lever.

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
question: A client wants to charge ten cents for the sample to filter out non-serious enquirers. What does Hopkins say it costs, and what is his reasoning about half-price offers?
answer: He says getting that dime may cost them from 40 cents to $1 — that is, it may add that much to the cost of each reply — and it also forfeits the word "Free" in the advertisement, which he holds generally more than pays for the samples on its own. Three in four will refuse to pay, he says, perhaps nine in ten. On half-price constructions — "You buy one package, we will buy the other", or a coupon good for part of the purchase price — his position is that any keyed returns will clearly prove such offers do not pay, because before a prospect is converted it is approximately as hard to get half price for the article as to get the full price. The barrier is the act of paying, not the amount: an unconverted prospect has no basis for valuing the article, so any price is a full-price decision to him.
confounders: The intuitive qualification argument — that a small charge filters for intent — which is what he is refuting.
That half price is a reasonable middle course; he places it in the same class as full price.
Confusing this with his separate chapter 6 point that the MAKER should buy the sample at retail rather than give away his own stock.
model_answer: Hopkins says charging for a sample, even ten cents, cuts replies sharply, by about three-quarters in his experience. Collecting and handling the coins can cost more than the samples saved, and the enquirers you lose include many good prospects, so the cost per real customer rises. His view is that it is better to give samples freely but only to people who have read the ad and asked for them. On half-price offers, a reduced-price offer does not create a true trial and cheapens the product in the buyer's mind. People who buy at half price act on a bargain, not on conviction about the product. [unsure]
missed: Dime costs 40c-$1 per reply, loses 'Free'; half price as hard as full

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: State Godin's mechanism for why narrowing the audience improves the work. The answer is not that a smaller audience is easier to reach — what is it?
answer: The mechanism runs through the artefact, not the audience. Pursuing mass means aiming at the centre of the curve, which requires you to offend no one and satisfy everyone, and those are constraints on the thing you make: they force compromises and generalisations, and produce work that is average. Narrowing removes the constraints. With a small, specific audience you can go to their extremes, take a position where you alone are the perfect answer, and overwhelm their wants with attention — producing a change profound enough that people cannot help but talk about it. So the size question is asked as a floor, not a target: what is the minimum number of people you would need to influence for the effort to be worth it.
confounders: the efficiency reading — that a small audience is cheaper to reach, which is not his argument
reading 'smallest viable market' as a starting size to be grown out of rather than as a constraint that improves the work
dropping the word 'viable'; Godin says no fair shipping junk
model_answer: Godin's mechanism is that choosing the smallest viable audience lets you understand their worldview, dreams and fears precisely, so you can make something specifically for them that they will find remarkable. Serving 'everyone' forces the work toward the average and bland; serving a specific group lets you make a change they care about, and the work becomes more generous and more useful. Those people then talk about it to others like them, so it spreads horizontally. The improvement comes from empathy and specificity, making the work matter to someone, not from lower reach cost.

source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
question: Carroll writes that "correct exposure" is just a matter of opinion. What is he actually claiming, and which later positions in the book depend on it?
answer: He is claiming that because shutter, aperture and ISO all act on the same quantity of light, several different balances satisfy any given scene, and the camera reports one of them rather than the right one. Which balance you want is a question about the picture — blur or freeze, shallow or deep — not about the light. Two later positions rest on this. His case against manual mode rests on the camera's exposure being a proposal that manual does not improve on, and his whole treatment of exposure compensation rests on it being legitimate to depart from that proposal on purpose. This is his stated position, not a finding.
confounders: reading it as saying exposure doesn't matter; he means several exposures are defensible, not that any is
attributing to him the idea that the meter is inaccurate — his claim is that it is answering a different question
model_answer: Carroll is claiming that the meter's 'correct' exposure is only a technical average. The camera tries to render the scene as mid-grey, and that is not necessarily the right picture. Exposure is a creative decision about mood and emphasis, so the photographer decides what should be bright or dark. Later positions rest on this: deliberately under- or over-exposing, using exposure compensation (for example, for snow or dark scenes), high-key and low-key images, silhouettes against bright backgrounds, exposing for the highlights, and generally overriding the meter instead of trusting auto modes.
missed: Several shutter/aperture/ISO balances valid; underpins case against manual mode

source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
question: Two layouts are equally chaotic on first impression; one is praised in this book and the other would not be. Reading the exhibit commentaries, what does Samara consistently credit for the difference — and what is the honest limit on that reading?
answer: He consistently credits a restricted substructure. In one commentary the designers attend to the parallel or divergent nature of axes and their junctures, distributing them along a limited selection of planar levels and directions, which he says ensures well-crafted, rhythmic cohesion instead of chaotic randomness. In another, spatial confusion and complicated interference between overlapping shapes and text are said to be underpinned by a rigorously controlled network of geometric axes in which the edges of every element line up with, or point to, those of other elements. In both cases the disorder is on the surface and something constrained survives underneath. The honest limit is that Samara says this about particular projects and never states it as a test; turning it into a diagnostic is a reader's generalisation, not his claim, and he offers no case anywhere in the chapter where apparent randomness turned out to be carelessness.
confounders: assuming the difference is the amount of visual disorder rather than what survives beneath it
attributing the generalisation to Samara; he describes projects and states no test
assuming a viewer can perceive the difference — the chapter asserts it and offers no reader evidence
model_answer: Samara consistently credits an underlying, intentional structure: hidden alignments, proportional relationships, a clear hierarchy and a controlled rhythm of contrast. He calls these the designer's deliberate control, which keeps a seemingly chaotic, deconstructed layout legible and coherent, while the other layout is simply disordered. The honest limit is that these are the author's post-hoc interpretive commentaries on selected exemplars. The 'hidden order' is asserted rather than demonstrated or tested with readers, so the reading risks circularity: praised work is credited with order because it is praised. [unsure]
missed: Restricted axes on limited planar levels; he states no general test

source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
question: A client mentions in passing that they promote themselves mainly through leaflets handed out at trade events. Airey treats that answer as changing the design, not just the media plan. What follows from it, and what should you have asked before designing?
answer: It changes the colour decision, and it changes it before any concept exists. He uses almost this exact case: if the company promotes itself through leaflets at trade events, you may need to remind the decision-maker that a multicoloured rainbow effect will cost more to produce than, say, a cool monotone grey design. The question you should have asked, and asked very early, is whether a print budget has been set — because colour usually costs more and can limit the scope of the design. He also warns not to assume: every printer's prices are unique, and with some the full-colour cost comes close to a one-colour job, though he says this is usually infrequent. He puts the duty on the designer: it is your job to inform the client about commercial print requirements and limitations at the start of the process. This is print economics of 2010, not a claim about any digital pipeline; the transferable part is the ordering — find out the constraint before you choose the palette.
confounders: treating the promotional-channel question as market research rather than as a production constraint
assuming full colour always costs substantially more; he explicitly allows the exception
delaying the question to the artwork-delivery stage, which is after the decision it should govern
model_answer: If the mark will live mainly on cheap printed leaflets handed out at events, it has to reproduce reliably: small, possibly in one or two colours, on low-grade paper and photocopies, and readable at a glance in a busy hall. So you need simple forms, no fine detail or gradients, and a version that works in black and white. Airey's point is that the brief comes first. Before designing, ask where and how the logo will be used, how the client currently promotes itself, and what the budget and reproduction methods are.
missed: Multicolour costs more to print; ask print budget early; designer informs client

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: Reconstruct the derivation W3C gives for 4.5:1 and 7:1. What is the baseline, what multiplies it, and what does the chain imply about what those numbers are measuring?
answer: The baseline is 3:1, described as the minimum level recommended by ISO 9241-3 and ANSI/HFES 100-1988 for standard text and normal vision. The multiplier is contrast sensitivity loss associated with acuity: the cited population finding is that 20/40 acuity carries a contrast sensitivity loss of roughly 1.5, so a reader at 20/40 needs 3 x 1.5 = 4.5:1 — the Level AA value. Following the same logic, a reader at 20/80 needs about 7:1, which is Level AAA. The note adds that 20/40 is commonly reported as typical visual acuity at roughly age 80, and that people with worse loss than 20/80 usually use assistive technology with contrast enhancement and magnification built in, which is why the ladder stops there. What the numbers measure is therefore compensation: how much extra luminance separation restores, for a reader with a specified acuity loss, the contrast experience a normally sighted reader gets at 3:1. There is no term in the chain for attention, appeal or communication effect, and the source claims none.
confounders: assuming 4.5:1 was chosen by testing reading speed at various ratios
assuming it is a threshold of general readability rather than a compensation factor for a stated acuity loss
treating the derivation as normative — it appears only in a Working Group Note
model_answer: The Understanding document starts from 3:1, the minimum contrast recommended by ISO-9241-3 / ANSI-HFES-100-1988 for observers with normal (20/20) vision. It then compensates for contrast sensitivity loss typical of vision around 20/40 (roughly age 80) by a factor of about 1.5, giving 4.5:1. For 7:1 it compensates for loss typical of about 20/80 vision, a factor of about 2.33 (3 x 2.33 = 7). The chain implies the ratios are not perceptual measures of legibility directly; they are the normal-vision baseline scaled by assumed contrast-sensitivity losses for low-vision users, i.e. a proxy for readability by people with reduced vision rather than an intrinsic property of the colours.

source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
question: Sontag's claim about images of suffering is that the medium works against the effect they were made to have. State it precisely, note the clause about intention, and say what it is not.
answer: Precisely: photographs can and do distress — protected inhabitants of the more affluent parts of the world learn about the world's horrors mainly through the camera — but the aestheticising tendency of photography is such that the medium which conveys distress ends by neutralising it. Two routes: cameras miniaturise experience and transform history into spectacle; and as much as photographs create sympathy they also cut sympathy and distance the emotions, producing a realism that is in the long run morally analgesic while remaining sensorially stimulating. The clause about intention is the part that bites: she says this of even the most well-intentioned and properly captioned work, so neither good intention nor accurate captioning exempts an image. What it is not: it is not advice. She does not say that images of difficulty should be composed differently, framed differently or avoided, and she recommends nothing at all here. Anything of that form would be an addition to what she wrote.
confounders: converting it into a rule about depicting difficult subjects, which is the characteristic way of misusing this source
assuming better intentions or accurate captions escape the tendency; she rules both out by name
model_answer: Sontag's claim is that photographs of suffering, made to arouse conscience, lose their force the more they are seen: 'Images transfix. Images anesthetize.' Repeated exposure makes horror familiar, less real and aesthetically consumable, and so erodes compassion. This happens regardless of the photographer's intention, because the dulling comes from the medium's reproducibility and its tendency to beautify, not from bad motives. The claim is not that such images never move anyone. A first encounter can be a revelation, like her own sight of the Belsen and Dachau photographs. Nor does she say photographs create a moral position. They can only reinforce one that already exists.
missed: Aestheticising neutralises distress; captions too; it is not advice

source_title: jain_gods_in_the_bazaar
question: What is the injunction against divine musculature, what reason do the practitioners give, and what breaks when they try to depict action?
answer: The injunction, attested from several independent practitioners, is that the divine body is not rendered with visible anatomy. Indra Sharma: 'Now the body is very strong, but we will not show the anatomy. For god's body, the description is of a gentle, beautiful (sukomal) body. . . . There won't be any muscles, we people avoid muscles.' Expressions must likewise be tranquil, almost meditative. The reason given is doctrinal: divine agency in the Vaishnava schema is a matter of lila, sacred play, not of labour — Ram Waeerkar, first illustrator of the Amar Chitra Katha comics, puts it as 'Bhagwan Krishna, Prabhu Ram . . . they have succeeded in fighting, but they are not fighters'. What breaks is action: attempting to depict bodily agency within these constraints 'render[s] irreconcilable the differences between narrative "realism" and sacred textual imperatives', which is a constraint conflict the artists themselves run into and name. Direct inspection of fig. 93 confirms it — Ram and Lakshman drawing bows in battle, with half-lidded eyes and unmuscled bodies.
confounders: This is the strongest-attested constraint in the source AND it was breached from the late 1980s — see qa_jgb_0016. Citing it without the breach misrepresents the source.
model_answer: Jain reports practitioners' rule that gods must not be shown with defined, straining muscles. Divine bodies should be smooth, soft, rounded and youthful. Their reason is that muscles signify human effort and labour, while deities act effortlessly: their power is not physical exertion, and their bodies are full of breath or grace. The trouble comes with depicting action such as battles, Hanuman lifting the mountain, or Krishna's feats. The frontal, static, iconic body cannot convey exertion, so the poses become stiff, awkward and implausible, and the naturalist logic of movement breaks down. [unsure]
missed: Lila not labour; conflict of narrative realism vs sacred textual imperatives

source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
question: A frame places a billboard model behind a tired commuter, implying a comment neither person intended. A colleague calls this dishonest. What is Freeman's position on the implied connection in a juxtaposition?
answer: He would not call it dishonest, and his position is unusually explicit. Setting one thing against another implies that together they equal something else — and he says that often, and maybe even usually, the two do not in reality have a connection, which does not prevent the photographer from making a point. He then says the technique is totally open to abuse, and calls that good, because the openness is what admits the whole range of ideas from silly to thoughtful and from clarifying a situation to complicating it. He also names who sees the connection: in his own case the participants are unaware, and only the photographer can see or suggest the link, through where they stand and the framing and the lens. A reader looking to this source for an ethical constraint on juxtaposition will not find one.
confounders: expecting a documentary-ethics position, which he does not take here — his ethics discussion is reserved for compositing in Part 10
assuming 'open to abuse' is a warning, when he explicitly calls it good
treating the false connection as an accident to be avoided rather than as the working material
model_answer: Freeman treats the implied connection as the whole point of juxtaposition. Two elements that have no real relationship are brought together by viewpoint and timing, and the viewer supplies the link. The meaning is created by the photographer and completed by the viewer, often as irony or wit. It is not a claim of fact that either person meant anything. For him it is a legitimate graphic and narrative device, the photographer's comment built from framing, and dishonesty is not the relevant category. The relationship is openly one of image construction. [unsure]
missed: 'Totally open to abuse' called good; only photographer sees link

source_title: dwyer_patel_cinema_india
question: Patel's account of why a poster opens with a face has two stages. Separate them, and say which one survives outside the culture.
answer: Stage one is pre-cultural and stage two is not, and she separates them explicitly. First, an image of a human face is 'instantly engaging because it is familiar to us all': of any mix of images the face is the one most likely to draw the glance, and this works WITHOUT recognition of the person. Second, and only within a specific cultural environment, the portrait is recognisable as a particular star, which arouses expectations built up over that star's career. Only the first survives outside the culture, and she states the boundary in the same breath — 'an Indian film star will be unknown to the wider Western audience where his or her films are not so popular and the poster will not evoke the same response'. The practical consequence is that a face still buys the glance anywhere; what the glance then delivers is entirely dependent on the viewer holding the star's history.
confounders: Collapsing the two stages produces the false generalisation that 'putting a face on it works' — which is true only of the attention effect, not of anything the face is supposed to mean.
