The concession is the strongest support he gives it — he had spent nearly thirty years in advertising and learned from hundreds of campaigns when he himself prepared a Pepsodent series he says would have wrecked the business in three months. The ratio he offers beside it, that perhaps one guess in fifty is right while fifty tests in fifty tell you what to do and avoid, is rhetoric: no derivation is given, and the second half is false as literally stated, since a test can also mislead. He also does not apply the rule uniformly — he repriced the Quaker puffed-grain line on conviction rather than test.
confounders: treating the fifty-in-fifty figure as an empirical result rather than a rhetorical flourish
reading it as a claim that experience is worthless; he claims experience does not transfer to a new problem, which is narrower
assuming he applied the rule consistently; the pricing decision at printed pp. 143-144 is his own counter-example
model_answer: The rule: do not rely on opinion or guesswork; test everything and let the public decide through traced returns, because the advertiser's judgment is usually wrong. His concession: he himself, even after long experience, is often wrong in guessing what will work; his instinct fails, so he tests. He offers a ratio such as being right perhaps only a minority of times, or new ventures failing in most cases. What is wrong with the ratio is that it is an unmeasured, anecdotal estimate: the author who insists on data offers a figure with no count or record behind it, so it is itself an untested guess. [unsure]
missed: Pepsodent series near-disaster; one guess in fifty vs fifty tests

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: In Godin's glasses case, the offer was reframed from a purchase to a decision about handing something back. What is his explanation for why that mattered, and what is the honest status of the result he reports?
answer: His explanation is about risk capacity, not about loss aversion in general. Shopping is a risk — you spend time and money on something that might be great — and it is enjoyable only to people for whom being wrong is not costly, because being wrong does not cost them dinner or a medical check-up. For an audience without that margin, the same offer reads as a threat rather than as fun. He draws the general rule that his own narrative about how to buy glasses is not better or worse, only his, and that insisting on it when it is not working is arrogance. The status of the result: he reports that removing the choice doubled the proportion who bought. That is an outcome claimed without controls — one afternoon, one village, one observer, no comparison group, no counts beyond "about a third" and "doubled" — and the risk-capacity explanation is his interpretation afterwards, not a tested hypothesis. It is not a rate and should not be used as one.
confounders: generalising it as 'loss aversion beats gain framing', which drops the risk-capacity condition that makes it his argument
citing the doubling as a measured effect size
assuming the finding transfers, when the point of the case is that the marketer's assumptions do not
model_answer: Godin's explanation is loss aversion and ownership. Once the glasses are in your hands, keeping them is the default and sending them back feels like giving something up. The decision flips from 'should I spend money?' to 'do I want to lose these?', and people hate losing what they already have (the endowment effect). The honest status of the result is anecdotal. It is a reported story with no controlled comparison, sample size or independent data, told to illustrate a principle rather than to prove it. [unsure]
missed: Risk capacity, not loss aversion; doubled result uncontrolled

source_title: parameswaran_nawabs_nudes_noodles
question: A brand must enter a category whose only mass public framing is a government health programme, and wants to be premium. What three requirements does this source report a name having had to satisfy at once, whose finding is it, and how was it arrived at?
answer: Maximum reach and intelligibility, an erotic connotation, and cultural legitimacy — satisfied simultaneously by naming the condom brand 'KamaSutra', positioned against the state's Nirodh family-planning framing as an enabler of better lovemaking and priced at a premium to both Nirodh and imported brands. The finding is the anthropologist William Mazzarella's, not the author's, and Mazzarella reached it by speaking with the campaign's creators after the fact — so it is a reconstruction of a naming decision rather than a record made at the time. The source presents the three requirements for this case and does not claim they generalise.
confounders: The campaign's outcome was contested — ASCI ordered modifications, a Rajya Sabha member sought a ban, Doordarshan withdrew its storyboard approval, and the company fell back to shop displays. Commercial success is not established.
model_answer: The case is KamaSutra condoms, entering a category defined by the government's Nirodh family-planning programme. The name had to satisfy three requirements at once. It had to shift condoms from contraception to pleasure and sex, be rooted in Indian culture so it would be legitimate rather than foreign or vulgar, and be premium and aspirational. The source reports this as the agency team's finding (Lintas, for JK Ansell), reached through consumer research and brainstorming during the brand's creation. [unsure]
missed: Reach/intelligibility requirement; Mazzarella's finding from post-hoc interviews with creators

source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
question: Sullivan bans the exclamation point. His objection is not that it is inelegant. What is the claim, and how does he demonstrate it?
answer: The claim is about a mismatch between intention and reception: the writer intends it to sound excited, and the reader receives a brand that sounds desperate. He calls it the used-car salesperson of advertising sentences, the jazz hands of punctuation, and kryptonite to authenticity — which ties it to his wider argument that a signal of enthusiasm supplied by the sender rather than earned by the content is read as a claim the content could not support. He demonstrates by making the point emphatically in the preceding sentence without using one, and then observing that he did.
confounders: treating it as a style preference rather than as a claim about how the mark is received
assuming it applies only to headlines; he states it for advertising copy generally
missing the link to his reassurance-signal family, which is what makes it more than a peeve
model_answer: Sullivan's claim is that an exclamation point is a confession: the writer is trying to add excitement with punctuation because the words lack it, and readers sense the forced enthusiasm and trust the line less. It is like laughing at your own joke. He demonstrates by showing that a line either carries excitement on its own or it doesn't. Take the exclamation point off a strong line and nothing is lost. Add it to a weak line and the line only sounds more like a pushy ad. [unsure]
missed: Demonstrates by making emphatic point without one; excited reads desperate

source_title: desai_mother_pious_lady
question: State the Imperfect Solution thesis, separate the part with general force from the part with none, and say why the separation matters.
answer: The thesis is that the Indian disposition to accept the almost-good-enough — usually deplored as *chalta hai* — encodes a defensible position about time: solutions are temporary equilibria, imperfection is a permanent condition conferred by time, and holding a solution perfect costs ever-increasing effort until it becomes unsustainable. The part with general force is the maintenance-cost mechanism: keeping any solution against a changing environment requires continuing effort that rises as the environment diverges from the one the solution was built for. The part with none is the cultural attribution — 'the Indian mind' versus 'Western analysis' — which is a pair of essayistic generalisations for which no evidence of any kind is offered. The separation matters because this is the object in the book most at risk of being universalised: it records that DESAI ARGUES this, and is not evidence that Indians or Westerners think in these ways.
confounders: The author anticipates the charge of arguing for passivity and answers it rhetorically rather than with evidence.
model_answer: Desai's Imperfect Solution thesis: Indian consumers often prefer a good-enough, affordable, adaptable product over a perfect expensive one; jugaad-like tolerance of imperfection, where what matters is fit to constraints. The general part: products designed for resource-constrained users should prioritise affordability and adaptability over completeness; that has force across markets. The parts that are asserted as uniquely Indian cultural character (a national temperament) have no general force and are anecdotal. The separation matters because a brand should adopt the design principle (affordability-led, flexible) based on constraint economics, not on cultural stereotypes that may not hold across segments or over time. [unsure]
missed: Thesis about time and maintenance cost of solutions, not affordability

source_title: parameswaran_nawabs_nudes_noodles
question: A paint company wants an outdoor execution containing no product, no pack and no person. What does the reproduced Jenson & Nicholson poster contain, and what kind of claim is it making?
answer: A white ground, one black headline — 'Whenever you see colour, think of us.' — a single large red cross-shaped block in the centre, and a footline reading 'Jenson & Nicholson [J&N monogram] The most trusted name in paints'. No product, no pack, no person and no body copy. The claim is about memory attribution rather than about any product property: the headline instructs the viewer to associate an entire perceptual category with the advertiser, and the single saturated symbol supplies the category's exemplar. The source's caption asserts only that this was 'an iconic first in corporate brand-building' and gives no date, market or outcome, so that characterisation is unsupported.
confounders: The red cross form closely resembles a protected humanitarian emblem; the source does not raise this and the extraction records it as an observation about the plate, not as a legal claim.
model_answer: The Jenson & Nicholson poster, built around the line 'Whenever you see colour, think of us', contains colour itself: a vivid, colourful scene or image with the brand name and slogan, with no can, no pack and no painter. It makes an associative, category-ownership claim rather than a product-performance claim. It tries to attach the brand to the idea of colour everywhere, so that any colourful sight in the world becomes a reminder of J&N. That is a brand-memory strategy, not a demonstration.
missed: White ground, black headline, single red cross block, no scene

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
question: An advertiser accepts that educating the market to a new habit is unaffordable as a campaign, so proposes devoting a quarter of each advertisement's space to it instead. What does Hopkins say?
answer: He calls it the same folly on a smaller scale and says it is not good business. His rule is that what cannot be done profitably on a large scale cannot be done on a small scale: the cost per convert does not fall with reduced commitment, only the number of converts does, so a fractional budget buys a fraction of an already unaffordable result. He notes there are many advertisers who know facts like these and concede them, would not think of devoting a whole campaign to such an object, and then devote a share of their space to it anyway. His own example of doing it right is the dentifrice maker who learned the convert cost by test and thereafter devoted not one line to the tooth-brush habit.
confounders: That a smaller commitment is a reasonable compromise — the intuitive answer and the one he names as the error.
That the objection is about focus or message clarity rather than about unit economics.
Confusing this with his separate point that co-operative advertising by many growers CAN build category demand.
model_answer: Hopkins would reject it. Educating people to a new habit is still education, and a quarter of the space is simply paying for it in instalments. The cost is out of all proportion to the returns. The benefit also goes to every maker in the category, competitors included, not just to you. Advertising should be devoted to selling to people already inclined to buy, with every line aimed at the sale, not at missionary work for the whole trade.
missed: Same folly smaller scale; unprofitable large means unprofitable small, cost per convert

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: WCAG gives a single-sentence operational test for whether *text* is purely decorative. State it, and say why it is stricter than it first appears.
answer: Text is only purely decorative if the words can be rearranged or substituted without changing their purpose. The general definition — serving only an aesthetic purpose, providing no information and having no functionality — is joined to that substitution test for text specifically. It is strict because it turns on the identity of the words, not on their visual treatment. Words chosen because they are those words are carrying something, so they are not decoration however faint, small or ornamental the setting. The source's illustration is a dictionary cover with random words in very light text in the background: any words would do, so they are decoration.
confounders: treating faintness or ornamental styling as evidence of decoration — the test is about substitutability, not appearance
assuming a tagline set as background texture is decorative; a tagline cannot be substituted without changing its purpose
confusing the decoration exemption with the incidental exemption for text inside a photograph
model_answer: WCAG's test is that text is purely decorative if the words can be rearranged or substituted without changing their purpose. It is stricter than it looks. Most text that seems ornamental still carries meaning: brand names, headings, labels, even decorative quotations whose particular words matter. If swapping or scrambling the words would change anything the user needs, it is not decorative. Very little real text qualifies, so the exemption is narrow, and images of text used 'for look' usually still need text equivalents and must follow 1.4.5 or 1.4.9.

source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
question: A key label in a dense, structureless poster is partly obscured. A colleague proposes repeating it in a clear area of the page. What does Samara say about that move, and what does he prefer?
answer: He allows it and then withdraws most of the allowance. Repeating partially obscured information in an open area may help, he says, but it may also confuse a viewer with its redundancy — better to give the information a little extra room where it appears in sequence. So his preference is to fix the element in place rather than duplicate it. He pairs this with a general fallback: when in doubt, simplify, because if the same visual effect can be achieved with fewer elements or less interference, the element will differentiate itself more efficiently from within a complicated field.
confounders: treating repetition as a straightforwardly safe redundancy strategy
assuming the fix is to increase the label's size, which is a different lever in his account
confusing this repetition with the repetition he recommends elsewhere, which marks which elements are alike in meaning
model_answer: Samara treats repeating the label elsewhere as a crutch that undermines the composition's integrity: it adds redundancy and breaks the visual logic without solving the hierarchy problem. He prefers fixing the relationships within the dense field: adjusting contrast, scale, weight or colour of the label, or shifting and clearing surrounding elements, so the information emerges from the texture while remaining integrated. [unsure]
missed: Prefers giving the element extra room in sequence; simplify

source_title: parameswaran_nawabs_nudes_noodles
question: What does the reproduced 'Thanda matlab Coca-Cola' plate show that the book's text does not say, and why does it matter?
answer: Two things. The line 'Thanda matlab' is set in DEVANAGARI beside the Latin Coca-Cola logotype, so the appropriation is of the Indian script as well as of the Hindi word — the text names the word and never mentions the script. And the setting is an ordinary unstyled small-town street: whitewashed wall, stacked red crates, a squatting child, a dog, a leaning pole, photographed without aspirational lighting. It matters because the mechanism is only visible in the image: appropriating a common noun makes the brand the default referent for a whole category of need, and setting it in the local script and an unstyled local place asserts that the claim already holds there rather than being addressed to it. A text-only pass would have recorded the word and missed both.
confounders: The plate is the outdoor execution and contains no celebrity, so the caption's claim about the television commercials is NOT settled by it. The footline small print is illegible.
model_answer: The plate appears to show details the text omits: the rural, small-town setting with Aamir Khan in character, the Hindi-language headline, and especially the low-price, small-pack offer (the Rs 5 'chhota' bottle). The text treats the line mainly as a linguistic coup, turning 'thanda', the generic word for a cold drink, into Coca-Cola. The visual shows that the campaign was equally about affordability and rural distribution. That matters because the campaign's success cannot be credited to the slogan alone. Price and pack were integral. [unsure]
missed: Devanagari script and unstyled local street; no celebrity in plate

source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
question: Ogilvy reports that the better the programme a direct-response commercial appears in, the fewer sales it makes. What is his explanation, and what does he conclude about buying media on audience size?
answer: His explanation is that a bored viewer will pick up the telephone and a riveted one will not: when viewers are bored by an old film they are more likely to order than when they are gripped by a popular drama. The act being asked for competes with the programme for the same moment, so attention to the programme is a cost rather than a benefit. His conclusion is blunt — there is no correlation between the size of your audience and the number of orders you receive — and his colleague buys time by counting the orders received each time a station broadcasts a commercial and eliminating the stations and dayparts that do not pay. Reach is the wrong currency where the response is an action taken during the exposure.
confounders: generalising the finding to brand advertising, where the response is not an act performed during the exposure
reading it as an argument for cheap inventory rather than for a different buying currency
carrying the specific dayparts and months forward as recommendations
model_answer: Ogilvy explains that viewers absorbed in a good programme won't break off to find a pencil, note the number or go to the phone, so involvement in the show suppresses response. Weaker, less engaging programming such as late-night shows and reruns leaves viewers free to act on the commercial. He concludes that you should not buy direct-response media on audience size or programme quality. Buy on measured results, meaning cost per response or order.

source_title: desai_mother_pious_lady
question: The book takes its title from a matrimonial phrase. What does the phrase mean, and why is it a good title for a book about reading culture from small things?
answer: The author glosses 'Mother pious lady' as connoting a mother-in-law 'concerned more with burning incense sticks than daughters-in-law' — that is, a signal to a prospective bride's family that she will not be interfered with. It is a good title for the book's project because it is three words that say a great deal to a reader who holds the convention and almost nothing to anyone else, which is precisely the claim the book makes about everyday material: that meaning sits in small, coded, unconsidered things, and that reading them requires belonging to the culture that shares the code.
confounders: The author himself marks the gloss as tentative — 'perhaps meant to connote'.
model_answer: 'Mother pious lady' is stock phrasing from Indian newspaper matrimonial ads, describing a prospective bride's or groom's mother as religious and virtuous. It signals the family's respectability, values and traditional grounding in a compressed, slightly odd Indian English. It suits Santosh Desai's book because the book reads middle-class Indian culture through small everyday artefacts and habits. One throwaway phrase carries a whole world of social codes: family, marriage, status and the blend of tradition and modernity. The small detail becomes a key to the larger culture.
missed: Phrase signals mother-in-law won't interfere; code legible only to insiders

source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
question: Sontag reports that when retouching became publicly known in the 1850s, the appetite for being photographed rose. What does she say people want from a portrait, and what inference rule does she attach?
answer: She reports that the news that the camera could lie made getting photographed much more popular. What people want, on her account, is the idealised image — a photograph of themselves looking their best — and they feel rebuked when the camera does not return an image of themselves as more attractive than they really are; few, she says, are lucky enough to look better in photographs than in life. The inference rule is a nice one: that photographs are often praised for their candour and honesty indicates that most photographs are not candid, since a property is remarked on where it is not the default. Note that the causal joining — that the appetite rose *because* people want flattery — is not something she states; she puts the two adjacent, and this bank records the connection as an interpretation rather than as her claim.
confounders: predicting the opposite effect, which a straightforward account of trust would give
treating the causal connection as Sontag's; she states the fact and the desire separately
model_answer: Sontag says people want the idealised image: to look their best, to be beautified, rather than to be shown truthfully. The news that the camera could lie made being photographed more popular. The inference rule: when a portrait is flattering, people take it as truthful; photography's value is in its claim to fidelity, but in practice people want a photograph that looks good and still accept it as evidence, so a photograph that shows them unflatteringly is deemed a bad photograph. [unsure]
missed: Praise for candour implies most photographs are not candid

source_title: pandey_pandeymonium
question: The author lists campaigns he says pre-testing would have killed. Why is this the weakest evidence in the book?
answer: Because it is counterfactual throughout. No pre-test was run on the Cadbury Dairy Milk dancing girl, the Fevicol work or the Vodafone Zoozoos, so what a pre-test WOULD have returned is not established — it is a confident assertion about a test that never happened. Three further problems compound it: the commercial success of the campaigns is asserted and never evidenced, since no sales, share or tracking figure appears anywhere in the book; the only concrete detail, the Fevicol objection that 'we did not show furniture', is a remembered objection rather than a recorded finding; and none of the work is reproduced in the book, so a reader cannot see what is being defended. It is also survivorship in the strict sense — campaigns that failed research AND would have failed in market are not counted, and neither are campaigns that passed research and succeeded.
confounders: It is the rhetorical centre of his argument and the least supported thing in the book; those are compatible.
model_answer: The claim is a counterfactual that cannot be tested. Those campaigns were not pre-tested, so we cannot know what a test would have shown. The list is chosen after the fact from the author's successes, so it suffers survivorship and selection bias, and it is self-serving. Campaigns that skipped testing and failed are absent. There is no data, no comparison and no independent check, only the author's assertion. So it illustrates his conviction and says little about whether pre-testing actually kills good work.

source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
question: Whose responsibility does Airey say brand style guides are, and what chain of consequences does he attach to consistency?
answer: The designer's — he states that many logos are accompanied by style guides and that creating them is your responsibility. Their function is to make sure anyone inside the client's company who uses the design does so consistently. The chain he attaches is two links and he states it compactly: consistency breeds trust, and trust wins customers. He makes the same claim in the earlier chapter, that the same visual identity seen over and over generates trust and trust makes customers come back for more, and his historical case is the Kellogg signature, used on the front of every packet since 1906. Neither link is evidenced; Kellogg is a survivorship case with a century of confounded marketing behind it.
confounders: assuming the client or their marketing team writes the guide
treating the trust-to-customers chain as an established finding rather than this author's assertion
confusing consistency with the template-per-application practice he praises at printed p. 15, which pulls the other way
model_answer: Airey says brand style guides are the designer's responsibility. The designer should create them and deliver them with the identity, so the mark is applied correctly by others. The chain he attaches: consistent application leads to recognition, recognition builds trust, and trust builds loyalty and brand value. Inconsistency dilutes the identity and erodes that chain.

source_title: jain_gods_in_the_bazaar
question: This source documents a production convention that outlived the constraint which produced it. Describe the convention, the original constraint, and what happened when the constraint lapsed.
answer: The convention is extensive MANUAL colour retouching of separated negatives at the pre-press stage — brushing on photo opaque and pink wash, scratching off emulsion, anything from two to twenty hours per separation — plus two blue and two red plates in addition to yellow and black, to reach maximum saturation, tonal contrast and strong highlights. The original constraint was technical: poor filters and insensitive film meant the separations did not reproduce the artwork faithfully without intervention. What happened when digital scanning removed that constraint is the finding: the practice did not lapse, it MIGRATED INTO SOFTWARE and continued. Jain states what it is doing now instead: 'retouching is not about faithful reproduction but primarily indexes the printers' perceptions of what they think their audience wants.' The practitioners describe the intended effect themselves — Indra Sharma on gaudy, distracting (chatkile bhatkile) colours, 'whether or not your gaze wants to go there it still goes'. Direct inspection of fig. 88, which photographs a print beside the original painting it was made from, confirms the print is visibly more saturated and higher in contrast.
confounders: The interesting fact is not that the colours are saturated but that the step survived the disappearance of its justification and acquired a new one. That is a general hazard, and this is a fully documented instance of it.
model_answer: In calendar and bazaar prints, a convention formed under early printing and commissioning limits. Images were composed for chromolithographic and early offset processes, with flat, saturated colour areas, frontal figures and a lower band or border left for the sponsoring firm's name, because the prints were given away as advertising calendars. When the constraint lapsed (better printing, and prints sold as devotional images with no sponsor), the conventions persisted. Artists and publishers kept the look because buyers now expected it as the proper look of a sacred image. The form carried on as style after its functional reason had gone. [unsure]
missed: Manual colour retouching of separations migrated into software after digital

source_title: desai_mother_pious_lady
question: The same household extracts value from every paisa and also spends ruinously on a wedding, sometimes into debt. Why does this source say that is not a contradiction?
answer: Because two different return currencies operate inside one budget. On a wedding the return sought is social rather than economic — 'the return on money is not economic but social' — and a social return is not commensurable with the savings made elsewhere, so the two budgets do not compete and no inconsistency is felt. The economising disposition applies only to the first currency. The author makes the same distinction in the other direction for a masala film, which he calls a paisa vasool film, so it is a real distinction in his account rather than an excuse constructed for one awkward case.
confounders: 'often ending up in debt' is asserted with no figure or source.
model_answer: Desai argues the Indian household runs on value-seeking in everyday consumption so that surplus can be saved and deployed for socially significant occasions. Thrift and extravagance serve the same logic: family status, obligations and social capital. Everyday frugality is a means; the wedding is an investment in family honour, networks and marriage prospects, a once-in-a-lifetime ritual expenditure that the whole community evaluates. So spending on the wedding is the goal that the frugality was saving for, not an inconsistency. [unsure]
missed: Two incommensurable return currencies: social vs economic

source_title: desai_mother_pious_lady
question: A team observes that the vocabulary of a long-running format has changed considerably over twenty years and concludes the practice has modernised. What does this source's measured finding say about that inference?
answer: That the inference does not follow. Across thirty years of matrimonial advertisements the surface changed considerably — appearance descriptors multiplied, individuals expressed needs with more specificity, the chaperoned ten-minute meeting stretched to two or three meetings with chaperoning becoming optional — while the underlying model did not move at all. Advertisements are still placed by parents, the parties are still called 'boy' and 'girl' whatever their age, personality is still barely mentioned, and the transaction is still between stations in life rather than between individuals. Caste mention, on the study's evidence, did not decline. Surface features respond to changing expression while the model that determines what the convention is FOR can persist unchanged underneath.
confounders: The study's method is entirely unreported, so the finding's strength rests on the author's authority alone. The book predates the migration of Indian matrimonial matching to websites.
model_answer: Desai's finding, in the matrimonial-advertisement analysis, is that vocabulary changes much faster than values. New words such as professional degrees, 'cosmopolitan' or 'broad-minded' replace old ones, but the underlying requirements (caste, community, fair complexion, family status, the demure homely bride) persist, often in updated terms. So lexical change is not evidence of modernisation. The format absorbs modern language to express continuity. The team is mistaking the surface for the structure, and would need to show that the underlying selection criteria changed. [unsure]

source_title: pandey_pandeymonium
question: Seven of this source's ten objects have no operational binding and none binds to Creative IR. Is that a gap?
answer: No. The book is about how people work together and how work is judged, not about what an artefact should be, so most of it is professional and organisational knowledge for which this project has no consumer — agency-client relationship practice, standing by one's work, retention of women in the industry, the structure of a multi-office national agency. The nearest Creative IR candidate, that a celebrity must not be the only memorable element, is stated as a requirement with no account of how to establish whether it has been met, so it fills no field without our inventing the test. Genuine knowledge with no current application is a legitimate state, and the alternative — manufacturing bindings for coverage — is the failure the mandatory-binding rule was retired to prevent.
confounders: A low binding count reads as a weak source and is not: the same audit records the strongest fit as two governance prohibitions that bear directly on live evaluator work.
model_answer: Not necessarily. Pandey's memoir is anecdotal, cultural and philosophical. Its objects mainly supply context, attitudes and illustrative campaign stories (Indian insight, emotion, local idiom) rather than testable production rules. Leaving them unbound is honest: forcing operational or Creative IR bindings would overclaim what the source supports. It is a gap only if a specific rule in it is actionable and has been missed. The default reading is correct scoping, not an omission. [unsure]
missed: Organisational knowledge lacks consumer; manufacturing bindings is the retired failure

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
question: Hopkins reports refusing most of the propositions brought to his agency. Give the ratio, the observation he attaches about who hesitates, and the reason he states for the agency's refusing posture — which is not the reason a reader expects.
answer: Of several hundred men with dubious prospects who came to the agency's standing advisory board of some sixteen experienced men, open without obligation, nineteen in twenty were advised not to proceed. His attached observation is that the men who hesitated over their own propositions were the large advertisers with most at stake, and that this is generally so. The reason he gives for the posture is frankly self-interested rather than protective: failures and disasters damage advertising as a whole and therefore damage the agency, while one conspicuous success encourages many new ventures. Two limits: nineteen in twenty is a ratio over a self-selected population — men with dubious prospects who walked in — and not a base rate for propositions generally; and nothing tells us how the refused propositions actually fared.
confounders: reading nineteen in twenty as a failure rate for advertising propositions in general
assuming the stated motive is client protection; he gives a reputational-externality argument for the agency
expecting the criteria to be in this passage; they are not, which is why the ratio alone teaches nothing
model_answer: Hopkins says his agency turned down the great majority of propositions, roughly nine in ten, after a short investigation or test showed they could not succeed. He observes that the people who hesitate and want proof are usually the sound advertisers, while those most eager to spend are usually the weakest prospects. The reason he gives for refusing is not ethics or protecting clients' money. It is protecting the agency: failures damage its reputation and its record, and success stories are what bring new business. [unsure]
missed: Nineteen in twenty; large advertisers hesitate; failures damage advertising as whole

source_title: desai_mother_pious_lady
question: A brand plans to lead on safety in a market where no competitor does. What observation and what explanation does this source offer, and how much weight does each carry?
answer: The observation is that in India at the time of writing, 'not a single brand of vehicle is sold on the basis of safety'. The explanation is that safety is a meaningful proposition only for a buyer who accepts a link between an action and its consequence, which he argues Indian traffic conditions do not train — a benefit claim requires the audience to hold the premise that makes the benefit meaningful. The two carry very different weight. The observation is a checkable claim about a category's advertising, though it is an absolute stated with no supporting survey and it is dated — the essays are late-2000s columns and this is exactly the kind of claim that changes. The explanation is the author's interpretation, offered without evidence and embedded in a sustained metaphorical essay whose metaphysics of time the extraction does not take.
confounders: It must never be used as a current market statement. The general shape — check whether the audience holds the enabling premise — is what survives.
model_answer: The observation: Indian consumers historically did not prioritise safety features (e.g. car airbags, helmets), and safety-led messaging rarely sold. The explanation offered is cultural: fatalism or a belief that fate, God or providence protects, and a tendency to value the family's immediate needs over hypothetical risk. The observation carries more weight since it reflects market behaviour; the cultural explanation is speculative and anecdotal, alternative explanations like price sensitivity and lack of regulation exist. A brand leading on safety should not assume it is futile, but should test. [unsure]
missed: Explanation: buyers lack action-consequence link, not fatalism

source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
question: Where does Freeman rank exact alignment among the things going on in a frame, and what changes that ranking?
answer: He ranks it low. Most of the time, he says, there are more important things going on in front of the camera than exact alignments — things like expression, action and gesture. What changes the ranking is a particular kind of subject rather than a decision by the photographer: his word is "inevitably". A gate in a wall with an identical gateway directly beyond it can only be shot from the exact centre line, because from an angle the gateway skews and from any head-on position that shows the second gateway even a slight misalignment reads as sloppy. Nested or repeated identical geometry gives the viewer a perfect reference, so the error becomes directly visible instead of merely felt.
confounders: the widespread assumption that careful alignment is generally a mark of good composition, which is the position Freeman contradicts for most photographs
reading the precision requirement as a preference of his, when he presents the subject as imposing it
confusing this with his four-square case, which is about a viewpoint and its meaning rather than about nested geometry
model_answer: Freeman ranks exact alignment low. Viewers attend first to content, then to the stronger graphic elements such as dominant shapes, lines, contrast and colour. Precise alignments of edges and points tend to be noticed only subliminally, if at all. The ranking changes when the image is sparse, graphic or minimal, with little subject content competing. Then alignment becomes prominent, and near-misses read as errors, so they must either be exact or clearly avoided. Deliberate framing in geometric and architectural subjects also raises its importance. [unsure]
missed: Nested identical geometry (gate within gate) forces exact alignment

source_title: jain_gods_in_the_bazaar
question: What does this source say is wrong with judging an image only as true-or-false or good-or-bad, and what does it propose instead?
answer: That the frame is juridical and forensic — treating an image either as evidence (true or false, real or fake) or as a perpetrator (good or bad, objectifying or empowering) — and that it is systematically blind to other forms of power an image has. Jain names the cost sharply and it cuts against her own political sympathies: 'the more explicitly politically invested the critical analysis of an image, the likelier it is to resort to the representational realism that has come to us epistemically and institutionally bundled with the modern discourse of justice ... As a result, the less likely it is to be able to engage — to apprehend or to counteract — the other forms of power available to the image.' Her alternative is to treat images 'as much objects as they are signs', attending to their efficacy as circulating things: as icons, commodities, gifts and items of ritual exchange. THE GENERAL SHAPE IS A CLAIM ABOUT FRAMES: a frame that asks only whether an image is adequate to a truth cannot see properties residing in how it moves and what it is used for.
confounders: This is an argued theoretical position, not a finding, and it is bound to nothing operational in the Canon record. It is retained because the frame-blindness point is general, not because the book demonstrates it.
model_answer: Jain argues that judging images only on representational truth (true or false) or on aesthetic quality (good or bad) imports a Western, disinterested and textual frame. That frame misses how bazaar images actually work. She proposes attending to what images do: their efficacy and their embodied, devotional and transactional engagement. She calls this 'corpothetics' as opposed to aesthetics, and it includes their power in ritual, commercial and political networks.
missed: Juridical/forensic frame blind to power; images as objects: icons, commodities, gifts

source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
question: What does Samara repeatedly report about how effortless-looking layouts were actually made, and why does that matter for judging a layout you did not watch being made?
answer: He repeatedly reports that the effortlessness is expensive. An exhibition catalogue whose apparent simplicity looks at a glance not really designed is said to depend on almost obsessive attention to the selection, ordering, cropping, colour transitions and colour-reversal logic of its images. A poster with no baselines, alignments or margins, letters floating as though scattered, is described as a carefully randomised layout with two spatial levels added for control, its forms placed precisely enough that legibility survives the overlap of red and black letterforms close in optical colour. A third project's playful structure is called accessible because each part of the information is decisively located and components are separated so the eye can reach them. Why it matters is also the difficulty: what he is describing is process, not an inspectable property. Removing the grid removes the mechanism that placed things correctly by default, and that work transfers to the designer element by element — but a reader who arrives only at the finished artefact is given no test that separates the two cases.
confounders: reading apparent randomness as evidence of low effort
assuming Samara supplies a test for the finished artefact; he describes how the work was made
assuming the exhibits are a fair sample — they are projects he selected and is commending, with no failure case shown
model_answer: Samara repeatedly reports that layouts which look spontaneous, intuitive or 'ungridded' were built on careful underlying structure, deliberate proportional systems and many rounds of sketching and refinement. The ease is manufactured. This matters because appearance is poor evidence of process. You cannot infer from a finished, loose-looking layout that it was made freely, nor that rules were abandoned. When judging or imitating work you did not see being made, look for the hidden structure and do not copy only the surface informality.
missed: No test exists for finished artefact; effort is process not inspectable

source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
question: Connor and Irizarry argue that the trouble with asking for feedback begins with the word itself, not with the people answering. What do they say "feedback" actually denotes, where do they take that sense from, and what do they say follows from it?
answer: They say feedback is nothing more than a reaction or response, and they take the sense directly from the interaction-design idea of a feedback loop, where feedback is the system's noticeable change of state after a user acts. Because the word covers every possible response, a request for feedback constrains nothing about what comes back, and the authors say what returns is an unpredictable mixture: a gut reaction, a list of instructions on what to change, or comments describing how the design differs from what the critic would have made. The consequence they draw is that the sorting work — deciding which of it is usable — falls entirely on the person who asked. Notably they do not prescribe abandoning the word, conceding that giving it up is "damned difficult" and that they use it throughout the book; the remedy is to know which of the three forms you want and shape the request accordingly.
confounders: reading the complaint as being about rude or unskilled feedback-givers, which is the opposite of the authors' point — their complaint is about the request
assuming they recommend banning the word 'feedback'; they explicitly decline to
confusing their 'feedback loop' derivation with the management-science sense of feedback as performance appraisal
model_answer: They say 'feedback' in its original sense comes from systems/engineering (cybernetics, electrical circuits): output fed back into a system as input, a signal of how the system responded. So feedback denotes any reaction, including gut reactions, not necessarily useful analysis. Asking for 'feedback' therefore invites any response: likes and dislikes, direction, or reactions. It follows that you must be specific about the kind of feedback wanted, distinguishing critique (analysis against objectives) from reaction and direction, and framing requests to get critique. [unsure]
missed: Sense from interaction-design feedback loop; sorting burden falls on asker

source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
question: A founder wants to imitate the market leader in her category and points out that the leader has just launched into three adjacent categories. Apply the authors' diagnostic from Chapter 2 to her reasoning, and state the correction they would make.
answer: They would say she is observing at the wrong point in the leader's history. Their diagnostic is that people look at currently successful companies, see them expanding, and infer that expansion causes success — inverting the order, since the expansion is a consequence of success and not its cause. Their analogy is personal wealth: buying an expensive house, a Rolls-Royce and a Rolex will not make you rich and is likely to make you poor, because those are things rich people do after becoming rich. The correction is to look at what the leader did before it led. Their cases are Domino's, Little Caesars and Papa John's, each of which sold a wider menu at the outset — Papa John's sold cheesesteaks, submarines, fried mushrooms, fried zucchini, salads and onion rings alongside pizza — and each of which narrowed. Note the analogy cuts against the book's own method too, since its evidence is overwhelmingly companies observed after success.
confounders: the competitive-benchmarking default of studying what leaders currently do, which is exactly the error the passage names
concluding that a leader's expansion is always a mistake; the chapter's claim here is only about what a follower should imitate
reading the wealth analogy as evidence; it is an analogy, and the chapter offers nothing else
model_answer: Chapter 2 is the Law of Contraction: a brand becomes stronger when you narrow its focus. The diagnostic asks what made the leader a leader. It was narrow focus on one category, not its line extensions. Its launch into three adjacent categories is a sign of the leader weakening itself, surviving on strength already built, not a recipe for success. The founder is copying the effect and ignoring the cause. The correction is not to imitate the leader but to be different and narrower: own a single word or category, ideally as the first brand in a new one.
missed: Wealth analogy; leaders narrowed early (Domino's, Papa John's wider menus)

source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
question: Ogilvy states that five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy, and then immediately draws a much stronger conclusion from it. What is that conclusion, and what step is hidden inside it?
answer: His conclusion is that unless the headline sells the product, ninety per cent of the money has been wasted. The hidden step is a move from a readership ratio to a spending ratio: the five-to- one figure is about how many people read two parts of an advertisement, and the ninety per cent is a claim about wasted expenditure, which requires the further assumption that readership of the headline is what the money buys. He also derives from the same ratio that the brand name must appear in the headline, since eighty per cent of readers never reach the body copy and would otherwise never learn what is being advertised.
confounders: reading the ninety per cent as a measured finding rather than as an inference from the readership ratio
assuming the claim is about attention span; it is about the fall-off between two elements of one advertisement
confusing this with the chapter-2 doctrine that advertising must sell rather than please — that is a different claim, about the criterion, not about where readership sits
model_answer: Ogilvy concludes that 'when you have written your headline, you have spent eighty cents out of your dollar', and that a headline that doesn't sell wastes 80% of the client's money. The hidden step is the assumption that value is proportional to readership, and that headline-only readers are worth as much as body-copy readers. The headline must therefore carry the selling message (brand and promise) by itself. The readership ratio alone doesn't establish that.
missed: Conclusion is ninety per cent wasted; readership-to-spending ratio step

source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
question: You are asked to build an automated check for the source's "Jump in" guideline. Why can it not be run on individual frames, and what does the source fail to give you?
answer: Because what "Jump in" describes is a property of a span, not of a still: how quickly the ad reaches the heart of its story, and whether the pacing and framing across the opening draw the viewer in. No single frame carries any of that, so the unit of observation has to be the opening sequence at least. What the source fails to give you is every number the check would need — no target time to the heart of the story, no definition of what the heart of the story is, and no reference point for "faster", which is comparative with nothing to compare to. The only figure anywhere nearby is a five-second mention in an illustrative caption about when one ad introduced its brand, which is a different guideline and is not stated as a rule. A check built from this can be directional; any threshold in it is the implementer's.
confounders: borrowing the five-second figure as a Jump in threshold; it belongs to a different guideline and to one example
treating tight framing as a per-frame property that makes the check frame-level — the guideline is about the opening's effect, not a single composition
assuming the source's video specs page supplies a timing rule; it covers specs and safe zones
model_answer: 'Jump in' means starting the story immediately, opening with action, product or people instead of a slow build-up. That is a property of time and narrative: how quickly something meaningful happens, pacing, motion and when the story begins across the first seconds. A single frame cannot show whether the action has started or whether the opening is a slow fade or logo card. It has to be judged on a sequence, with shot changes, motion and audio. The source does not give an operational definition: no time threshold, no measurable criteria for 'action', and no validation data for building a pass/fail rule.

source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
question: Berger runs an annual exercise with his own students that he presents as evidence of social influence. Describe the design, the result, and the alternative explanation he concedes.
answer: Every year he asks his second-year MBA students a question, splitting the class in half. One half is asked what they thought they wanted to do with their life when they STARTED the programme; the other is asked what they want to do NOW. Neither half sees the other's question and responses are anonymous. The result: the pre-programme answers are diverse — reforming health care, building a travel site, entertainment, politics, entrepreneurship, with a handful naming investment banking or consulting. The current answers are concentrated, with more than two-thirds naming banking or consulting. He describes the mechanism as snowballing: fewer than 20 percent were interested initially, but that was still larger than any other option, so a few switched, which made others more likely to switch. The alternative he concedes is that students genuinely learn about opportunities during the programme; he attributes only part of the convergence to social influence.
confounders: citing it as a study; it is a classroom exercise
ignoring the recall problem — the pre-programme half are remembering, not reporting at the time
reading the concession as decorative; it is the alternative explanation and he does not rule it out
model_answer: Berger has students in class rate or choose something, e.g. the size of a candy/food/intended donation or choosing among options, where some see others' choices. He describes his class exercise: students guess the length of a line or similar, after hearing others' answers. The result: students' answers converge toward what others said (conformity, similar to Asch). He concedes an alternative explanation: that people may be using others' answers as informative (information rather than normative pressure), or that students might simply rely on the answers because they lack knowledge. [unsure]
missed: MBA split-half career question; convergence to banking/consulting; learning alternative

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: A letterform carries an outline. WCAG says the same device can end up on either side of the contrast calculation. State the rule and the mechanism behind it.
answer: A border around a letter can add contrast and is used in calculating the contrast between the letter and its background. A narrow border is used as the letter — it joins the foreground. A wide border that fills in the inner details of the letters acts as a halo and is considered background. The mechanism is what the reader is actually distinguishing: once a border is heavy enough to fill the counters and interior detail of the letterform, the perceptual comparison is no longer letter against page but letter against halo, so the halo becomes the effective background. The note gives no numeric boundary between narrow and wide; the stated test is whether the border fills the inner details of the letters.
confounders: assuming an outline always helps, or always counts as foreground
looking for a stated pixel or point threshold separating narrow from wide — the source gives a functional test instead
assuming the underlying page colour remains the background once a heavy halo is present
model_answer: WCAG's understanding material for contrast says an outline around letters can be treated either as part of the text or as its background, depending on how it functions. A thick outline defines the visible letter shape, so its colour counts as the text colour and is measured against the surrounding background. A thin outline or halo acts as a separating edge, so the fill is the text and the outline serves as the background it is measured against. The mechanism is perceptual. What the eye takes as the letterform, and therefore what must contrast, depends on the outline's weight relative to the stroke. [unsure]
missed: Narrow border counts as letter; wide halo filling counters is background

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: Name the categories W3C gives for the Essential exception to SC 1.4.11, and state the underlying principle that unites them.
answer: The principle is destructive interference: the exception is intended to apply where there is no way of presenting the graphic with sufficient contrast without undermining the meaning. Since the remedy for low contrast is to change colours, the exception covers cases where changing colours destroys what the graphic exists to carry. The named categories are logos and logotypes, presented in a brand's specific colours; flags, which may not be identifiable if their colours are changed; sensory content — the source states there is no requirement to change pictures of real-life scenes such as photos of people or scenery; and things that cannot be represented any other way, for which it names screenshots demonstrating how a website appeared, medical diagrams using the colours found in biology, and colour gradients representing a measurement such as heat maps. As with the logo case, the exception is an exemption from a requirement, not a finding that these graphics are easily perceived.
confounders: assuming any photograph or brand asset is automatically exempt without the meaning-destruction reasoning
assuming the exception means the graphic is perceivable
conflating this with SC 1.4.3's Incidental exception, which is about text rather than graphics
model_answer: For the essential exception to SC 1.4.11 (non-text contrast), the W3C's Understanding document gives categories where the particular presentation is essential. These are logos and brand marks, flags, real-life representations such as photographs, screenshots and depictions of real objects, and data-driven graphics such as heat maps, where colour gradients encode the information. The principle uniting them is that changing the colours to meet the contrast requirement would change or invalidate the information or identity the graphic conveys: the presentation is itself the content.

source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
question: Someone cites 'immutable law' as a reason to weight a claim from this book heavily. Using three passages from inside the book itself, show what the authors actually claim about the status of their laws, and say what those concessions do and do not fix.
answer: Chapter 20 opens by saying that nothing in life and nothing in branding is ever absolute, that there are always exceptions to every rule, and that the Law of Change is the biggest exception to the laws of branding — one member of the set is described as an exception to the others. Chapter 21 opens by narrowing immutability to the laws themselves and excluding brands, which are born, grow up, mature and die. Chapter 15 opens by stating what the laws seem to suggest about concentrating on a single brand, agreeing it is true, and then licensing a second, third and fourth. So the authors themselves do not hold the twenty-two as independent universal axioms. What the concessions fix is the reading that every law applies always. What they do not fix is testability: no criterion is given anywhere for when an exception applies, so the concessions widen the laws rather than making them checkable, and they are never reconciled with the Introduction, which asserts the laws apply equally everywhere and assigns each named failure to the violation of a numbered law. The word "immutable" is a title, and it supplies no evidence.
confounders: concluding the laws are worthless; practitioner assertion is a real category of knowledge and this is an articulate instance of it — the point is only about how it should be weighted
assuming the concessions make the laws falsifiable; they name exceptions without giving any test for when one applies

treating the Introduction's universal framing as the authors' considered position and the concessions as slips, or the reverse; both appear in the book, unreconciled, and this lane did not choose between them
model_answer: Inside the book the 'laws' are qualified. (1) The Law of Change says brands can and sometimes should be changed, which contradicts immutability. (2) The authors admit exceptions and concede that brands breaking the laws sometimes succeed, attributing that to weak competition. (3) They present the laws as observations drawn from marketplace cases, a matter of perception and judgment, not as tested rules. These concessions reduce the overclaim in the title. They do not fix the method: the evidence is still selected anecdotes, hindsight explanation and survivorship, with no systematic testing, so 'immutable law' earns no extra weight. [unsure]
missed: Specific passages (ch.20,21,15); concessions give no exception criterion, not testable

source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
question: A centred layout that works on a desktop browser collapses on a phone. What does Samara say is lost, and what does he propose to recover some of it?
answer: What is lost is the contrast in lateral emphasis. He says maintaining a logic of contrasting form widths and margin spaces is easily accomplished in the generously wide format of a desktop browser but is more challenging within the narrow confines of a smartphone screen. His proposal is to force text elements to occupy a narrower-than-optimal width and to introduce punctuating graphical forms, which he says permits some of the contrast in lateral emphasis to translate into the smaller viewing area. Note the concession embedded in it: he accepts a sub-optimal measure in order to preserve a compositional contrast, and says only that some of the contrast survives.
confounders: assuming the fix is to keep the optimal measure and drop the contrast
assuming the contrast fully survives; he says only that some of it translates
confusing this with his general advice to exaggerate contrast, which addresses inertness rather than width
model_answer: Samara says a centred, symmetrical layout relies on the wide field around the central axis to create a sense of stasis, formality and breathing space; on a narrow phone screen the margins collapse and everything stacks in a single column, so the tension between content and space, and the hierarchy of scale, is lost. To recover some of it, he suggests adjusting proportions and spacing in the responsive grid: preserving generous vertical intervals, contrast in scale and type size, and inset margins so the centred axis still reads, i.e. translating horizontal space into vertical rhythm. [unsure]
missed: Lost contrast in lateral emphasis; narrower-than-optimal text plus punctuating forms

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
question: What is Hopkins's position on prevention as an appeal, and what evidence does he give?
answer: His position is that prevention is not a popular subject however much it should be: people will do much to cure a trouble and little to prevent one. He applies it to a tooth paste that both prevents decay and beautifies the teeth, saying tests will probably show the beauty appeal many times as strong, and reports that the most successful tooth paste advertiser never features tooth troubles in his headlines because tests have proved them unappealing. His evidence is: "This has been proved by many disappointments", naming no disappointment, and "Tests have proved them unappealing", reporting no test, no advertiser and no margin. Measurement is asserted and the result is withheld in both places.
confounders: Treating the claim as demonstrated because he uses the word 'proved' twice.
That the prevention weakness is about credibility rather than about motive to act now.
Naming the tooth paste advertiser; Hopkins does not.
model_answer: Hopkins holds that prevention is a weak appeal. People will do little to prevent troubles but will pay to cure them or to gain a positive benefit, so ads should promise gains such as beauty, health or pleasure rather than warn of ills. His evidence is traced results from keyed tests. Positive, happy appeals consistently outperformed negative, fear-based ones. His Pepsodent example sold whiter, film-free teeth, a beauty benefit, rather than decay prevention, and it succeeded where preventive toothpaste appeals had failed.
missed: Evidence is asserted 'proved', no test reported; advertiser unnamed

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: Why does Godin use dog food rather than a human product to make his point about performance and appeal, and what is the general claim it is there to support?
answer: Because it separates the two parties cleanly and unarguably: he has never seen a dog buy dog food. The premium ingredients and rising prices are for the owners — for how buying it makes them feel, the satisfaction of caring for an animal, the status of a luxury purchase — and we have no idea whether dogs enjoy the expensive kind, because we are not dogs. The general claim is that there is almost always a disconnect between performance and appeal, and that the engineer's choice of the best price-performance combination is rarely the market's choice. So a marketer trying to sell more dog food by making food that tastes better has taken on the wrong problem; the formula is food that owners want to buy.
confounders: reading it as a claim about pet marketing rather than as an argument about buyer and user coming apart
assuming the point is that customers are irrational; his point is that the valuer is not the one you assumed
model_answer: Godin uses dog food because dogs don't buy it; their owners do. Performance for the end user (the dog's taste or nutrition) matters less than how the purchase makes the buyer feel: a good, caring owner. Feature-and-performance thinking misses that. The general claim is that people buy stories, feelings and status rather than specs. Marketing serves the wants and worldview of the person making the decision, not the objective merits of the product.

source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
question: Ideas are arriving easily in the first hour of a session and the team feels it is going well. What does Sullivan say this means, and what does he instruct?
answer: He says to distrust it. Early ideas that come quickly are easy, and his objection is availability rather than quality: pretty much everybody else working the same problem will see the same easy solutions. The instruction is not to discard them but to write down every too-easy idea and move on, because one may later be convertible into something new. He then names what comes next and says there is no shortcut through it — the stretch where nothing usable arrives, which he maps onto the incubation step of James Webb Young's five-step model and treats as an expected stage rather than as failure. His summary of the ordering is that the breakthrough arrives only after the slog.
confounders: treating ease as a sign of a strong idea, which is the intuition the passage is written against
discarding the easy ideas rather than recording them; he says to write them down
confusing the barren stretch with a failure of the assignment, which is exactly what he says it is not
model_answer: Sullivan says early easy ideas are a warning sign, not success. The first ideas to arrive are the obvious ones, the same ones any other team, and the client, would think of: clichés and category conventions. His instruction is to write them all down to get them out of your system, not fall in love with them, and keep going well past that point. The original ideas come after the easy ones run out, when the work gets hard.

source_title: bijapurkar_we_are_like_that_only
question: State the demand-structure claim this book rests on, and give the worked case that shows why it changes which segment matters.
answer: The claim: 'Consumer demand in the emerging economies is made up of lots and lots of people consuming a little bit each, adding up to a lot' — so total demand can sit overwhelmingly in a segment with low per-head consumption, simply because the segment is very large. The worked case is rural two-wheelers, and its arithmetic was checked directly against Figure 4.1 in this pass: penetration runs 42 / 25 / 10 / 2.7 per cent across four income groups, household counts 7 / 18 / 63 / 66 million, and two-wheeler numbers 3.8 / 4.5 / 6.4 / 1.8 million. The lower-middle group has about one-fourth the penetration of the high-income group and about nine times the households, and ends up with about 1.6 times the sales — 6.4 divided by 3.8 is 1.68, which matches the text. What it changes is which segment a firm should care about: a penetration-led reading picks the top group, and the volume sits below it. Source line on the figure: Indian Readership Survey, 2008 — third-party data, correctly attributed by the author, and dated.
confounders: The arithmetic is sound and the inputs are a 2008 survey. The structural point survives the date; the specific numbers do not, and no figure here should be quoted as current.
model_answer: Bijapurkar's claim is that Indian demand is pyramid-shaped: most households are at the bottom and middle, and the numbers of consumers are large but per-capita consumption is small; aggregate demand is dominated by the large base of lower-income households. The worked case: a product category where the top 'rich' segment has high penetration but small absolute numbers; the bulk of volume actually comes from the middle/lower segments, so growth depends on the 'consuming class' not the elite. So the segment that matters for market size is the large, lower-income mass, not the premium top. [unsure]
missed: Worked case: rural two-wheelers, lower-middle group 1.6x sales

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: Godin's empathy principle has a clause at the end that changes what it demands. State the principle with that clause, and give his strongest formulation of the consequence.
answer: The principle is that the people you seek to serve do not believe what you believe, do not know what you know and do not want what you want — and the clause is: they probably never will. That turns empathy from a stage on the way to persuasion into a standing constraint. You are not modelling them in order to bring them round; you are modelling them because they are not coming round. His strongest consequence inverts the usual ethics: if you are unwilling to have empathy for the narrative of the person you seek to serve, you are stealing — withholding a valuable option from someone who would have benefited. His supporting case is a fundraiser who cannot ask for a large donation because she cannot imagine making one, when the donation was never for her.
confounders: reading empathy as a step toward eventually converting them, which the 'never will' clause rules out
reading 'you're stealing' as the claim rather than as the rhetoric on top of it
model_answer: Godin's empathy principle is that other people don't know what you know, don't want what you want and don't believe what you believe, and that's okay. The closing clause means you may not treat them as wrong, ignorant or in need of correction. The demand shifts from persuading them to adopt your view to understanding and serving theirs. His strongest formulation of the consequence is that it is never the customer's fault. If your offer doesn't resonate, you chose the wrong people or the wrong story. The market is right about what it wants, and your job is to change, not to scold. [unsure]
missed: Clause 'they probably never will'; unwilling empathy is stealing

source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
question: Sontag separates three forms of photographic acquisition. Name them, and say which she calls the most inclusive and why.
answer: First, in its simplest form, surrogate possession of a cherished person or thing — which she says gives photographs some of the character of unique objects. Second, a consumer's relation to events, both those that are part of our experience and those that are not, a distinction she says habit-forming consumership blurs. Third, and the one she calls the most inclusive: acquiring something as information rather than as experience, through image-making and image-duplicating machines. It is the most inclusive because the others follow from it — the importance of photographic images as the medium through which events enter our experience is, she says, only a by-product of their effectiveness in furnishing knowledge dissociated from and independent of experience. Through being photographed, something is fitted into schemes of classification and storage, and reality is redefined as an item for exhibition, a record for scrutiny and a target for surveillance.
confounders: collapsing the three into 'photographs are possessions'
assuming the first is the most important; she says the third is the most inclusive
model_answer: In 'The Image-World' Sontag names three forms of acquisition through photography. The first is surrogate possession of a cherished person or thing. The second is possession as a consumer of events, both those in our lives and those that aren't. The third is acquiring something as information rather than experience. She treats the third as the most inclusive, because through photographs anything and everything can be turned into information, classified, stored and possessed, reaching far beyond what one could own or experience. [unsure]

source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
question: Sontag's documentary example: photographers took dozens of frontal pictures of one subject until satisfied. What is the point of the example, and what does she say about photographers who work without discrimination?
answer: The point is that a standard is imposed on the subject by a decision that leaves no visible trace. They shot until they had the precise expression that supported their own notions about poverty, light, dignity, texture, exploitation and geometry — so the surviving frame agrees with a prior idea, and the agreement was produced by selection. Her general form is that in deciding how a picture should look, and in preferring one exposure to another, photographers are always imposing standards on their subjects, and that even those most concerned with mirroring reality are haunted by tacit imperatives of taste and conscience. About undiscriminating work she closes the escape: occasions when picture-taking is relatively promiscuous or self-effacing do not lessen the didacticism of the enterprise, because the passivity and ubiquity of the photographic record is itself photography's message and its aggression. Note that the reading of what the photographers were satisfied by is entirely hers, offered with no account of how she knows.
confounders: reading it as a criticism of those photographers rather than as a claim about all selection
assuming neutral or artless shooting escapes the argument; she closes that route explicitly
model_answer: The example is the Farm Security Administration photographers of the 1930s, who took dozens of frontal pictures of a sharecropper until they had the expression they wanted, one that matched their idea of poverty, dignity and so on. The point is that documentary photography is not neutral recording. It is selection and construction guided by the photographer's taste and ideology. On indiscriminate photographers, Sontag argues that photography's leveling tendency, treating everything as worth photographing, is itself a stance. It turns the world into a collection of equally interesting items and aestheticises it. Even indiscriminate shooting imposes a point of view. [unsure]

source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
question: You have a campaign that includes a roadside board and a subway poster. Sullivan treats these differently. What is the differentiating variable, what does he permit for each, and what two tests does he give?
answer: The variable is how long the audience dwells with the medium. For roadside boards he reports the received limit of about seven words, notes the logo adds two or three, calls ten pushing it, and says eleven can work with the right execution — helped by having no visual. For subway postings and bus stops he says concepts can risk a slightly longer fuse, because the audience dwells. The two tests: show it to someone for two seconds, take it away and ask what it said; and view the layout from ten feet away as a legibility check. His craft advice follows the same logic — when a campaign includes outdoor, start there and pretend there is no photography budget, because being forced to carry the idea in words boils the thinking down.
confounders: applying the same word limit to both placements, which is exactly the distinction he draws
treating seven words as a measured threshold
missing that his section is also a polemic — he quotes Gossage's argument that a billboard is not a medium at all, and notes cities that have banned them
model_answer: The variable is viewing time and context: a roadside board is seen at speed for a couple of seconds, while a subway poster is seen by a captive audience waiting on a platform.
