question: A quality process routes every item flagged as failing to a second reviewer for confirmation, and the second reviewer is shown the first reviewer's verdict and reasoning. Management treats agreement between the two as strong evidence. Diagnose this using the book, and state the minimal change.
answer: The second review is not an independent observation, so the agreement carries almost none of the weight management is putting on it. This is precisely the flaw the book identifies in the ACE-V verification step in fingerprint work: because the verifier knows the first examiner concluded an identification, "the verification step therefore does not provide the benefit normally expected from the aggregation of independent judgments, because verifications are not, in fact, independent." The book's Mayfield case shows how far it can run — three FBI experts concurred on an erroneous identification, the later investigation found that once the first examiner erred "the subsequent examinations were tainted", and even an independent expert appointed for the defence agreed. Two further defects here. Only failures are double-checked, so the process is structurally incapable of catching a wrongly-passed item. And routing on the flag itself supplies the biasing context. The minimal change is the book's: the second reviewer should not be aware of the first judgement. Withholding the verdict and the reasoning costs nothing and restores the independence the aggregation assumes.
confounders: assuming a second opinion is valuable regardless of what the reviewer was told
proposing to instruct the second reviewer to ignore the first verdict; the book's finding that context changes what is perceived makes instruction an unreliable remedy
treating this as a problem of reviewer independence in the organisational sense — seniority, reporting lines — rather than of informational independence
model_answer: Showing the second reviewer the first verdict and reasoning destroys independence. It creates an anchoring or informational cascade, so agreement is largely an echo rather than corroboration. The error gets confirmed, not caught, and noise and bias are amplified while looking like consensus. Because only flagged items are routed, the check also never tests false passes. The minimal change is to have the second reviewer judge blind and independently, without seeing the first verdict or reasoning, and to reconcile afterwards. That is the book's 'aggregate independent judgments'.

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
question: Dealers in a category buy hand-to-mouth and will not hold stock. Hopkins solved this on Goodyear with a device that used no salesmen and no discount. What was it, what was the qualifying condition, and what does he say makes it compound?
answer: He ran a large local newspaper campaign and offered to name, in every advertisement, every dealer who stocked. The qualifying condition was a minimum stock — he states $250 — so the dealer had to buy in before he could appear. He reports inducing some 30,000 dealers to stock Goodyear tires on that basis within a few months, and says the campaign did much to change the whole complexion of the tire business. The compounding mechanism he gives is peer visibility rather than economics: no dealer likes to see his rivals named in a big campaign with his own name omitted, so the more dealers who join, the easier it becomes to get the rest. He claims to have secured almost universal distribution on new products this way more than once, and calls the plan an almost irresistible inducement to stock. No cost-per-dealer or sell-through figure is given.
confounders: reading it as co-operative advertising, in which the dealer pays a share; here the manufacturer pays and the dealer's price of entry is holding stock
the modern retailer-locator or store-finder analogy, which is a service to the shopper rather than a lever on the dealer
confusing it with the pre-announced coupon plan at pp. 103-105, which works through consumer demand the grocer cannot afford to miss
assuming a margin concession is involved; the whole point at pp. 129-130 is that he refuses to pay the trade
model_answer: For Goodyear, Hopkins used the advertising itself to create dealer demand. Ads listed local dealers, or directed readers to named dealers, so consumers asked for the product at specific shops. Dealers qualified for a listing by stocking the product, carrying an agreed supply. It compounds because each listing sends customers into listed shops, which raises their turnover and draws more dealers wanting listings, which puts more stock on hand and makes the brand more available. No salesmen or discounts were needed. [unsure]
missed: $250 minimum stock; compounds via peer visibility of rivals named

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
question: You interview a manufacturer and he says a detail of his process is too ordinary to mention because every competent maker does it. Separately, he volunteers at length the thing he is proudest of. On Hopkins's account, what should you conclude about each, and why?
answer: His diagnostic runs in both directions. The fact the maker dismisses as commonplace is the cue that it may be the campaign, because his dismissal is caused by familiarity and familiarity is exactly what the buyer lacks — he is too close to his product, sees only the ordinary in his own methods, and does not realise the world at large might marvel at them. The thing he volunteers is what he takes pride in, and Hopkins's repeated finding is that this is usually of no interest to the buyer: makers talk construction because construction is what interests them. The Goodyear case is the paired example — the company promoted a construction name while the two results it produced went unmentioned. Two limits Hopkins does not supply: a fact being unfamiliar does not make it interesting, and he offers no test for which commonplace facts are worth telling short of running the campaign. The discipline that keeps the cue from licensing any process fact at all is his own procedure elsewhere — find out what buyers say they want first, then get figures on those things.
confounders: inverting the cue and treating the maker's enthusiasm as the signal, which is what he says produces bad copy
assuming any dismissed fact will do; unfamiliar is not the same as interesting, and he gives no filter
reading it as a research method; it is a cue observed during an interview, and the actual method he prescribes is buyer interviews first
model_answer: Hopkins: what the maker thinks too ordinary is often the best selling point, because the public does not know it: the first to tell it gets credit for it (Schlitz steam-cleaned bottles, pure water from deep wells). So you should use the ordinary detail. The thing he is proudest of may matter to him but not to customers; it may be uninteresting to buyers or not unique. You should judge by what the consumer would find impressive, not by the maker's pride. [unsure]

source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
question: Describe the test-light procedure for locating the family of angles, and state the inversion the book says will make hot spots easy to find afterwards.
answer: Hang a white target where you think the family will be — larger than you think you need, and the less sure you are, the larger. Put a narrow-beam test light exactly at the lens position, removing the camera if necessary. Aim it at the point on the metal nearest the camera; where the reflected beam lands on the target is the near limit of the family, and you mark it with removable tape. Aim it at the farthest point for the far limit, and mark as many additional points as the subject's shape requires. The procedure works because light paths are reversible: a beam sent from the camera's position and reflected by the subject traces exactly the path a source would need to occupy. The inversion to remember is that the point reflecting in the metal edge at the BOTTOM of the image corresponds to the limit marked at the TOP of the test surface, and vice versa.
confounders: putting the test light where the main light will go, rather than at the camera
forgetting the top/bottom inversion, which is what makes the marked area interpretable
assuming the marked family must be filled exactly; the source says a source or gobo that exactly fits is almost never needed
model_answer: Place a small test light, or a point source, near the lens and move it around the subject while watching from the camera position. Note each position where the light reflects directly in the surface and each where it stops. The boundary positions mark the edges of the family of angles, which you can mark with tape or stands. The inversion is to swap light and viewpoint: put the light where the camera is and look from the subject's side, or think of the camera as the light source. Because light paths are reversible, hot spots then become easy to see. [unsure]
missed: Test light at lens aimed at near/far points; bottom-top inversion

source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
question: What does Freeman say distinguishes the Chinese "mountain-water" scroll from the European painting tradition, and what method does he report for building one?
answer: He names two differences. Long and vertical is not part of the European painting canon. And the Chinese approach is to express the essence of the landscape rather than an image of what can be seen. The method he reports is to combine elements from the landscape in general and stack them vertically, almost always leading to an upper peak. Attempting it photographically in the Nujiang gorge, he began with a shot of a footbridge and built upward from images taken within an hour or two's drive up and down the gorge, including a large rock window high above the valley. He accepts that the combined view is impossible and claims that, like a mountain-water painting, it shows more of the essence of the gorge than a single image could.
confounders: treating his account as art history rather than as a practitioner's working summary
assuming vertical panoramas in Western photography are the same idea, when his stated point is the difference in aim — essence rather than view
reading the impossibility of the view as a defect, when he presents it as the form's whole premise
model_answer: Freeman says the Chinese mountain-water (shanshui) scroll rejects the European single fixed viewpoint and linear perspective. It uses a shifting, multiple viewpoint that the eye travels through, with a vertical, layered arrangement of near, middle and far distances instead of one unified space. The method he reports for building one photographically is to shoot separate frames at different distances and viewpoints and assemble them vertically as a composite, stacking the distances in the manner of the traditional 'three distances'. [unsure]
missed: Vertical format not European canon; essence rather than seen view; upper peak

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: Godin's retail failure case: an incoming chief executive ended a chain's constant discounting because he could not imagine a quality store behaving that way. What does Godin say the customers were actually buying, and how strong is this as evidence?
answer: They were not enduring the discounts, they were playing a game that made them feel like they were winning — so removing the discounts removed the product. The executive's decision was made from his own worldview as a luxury buyer, and it abandoned the store's true fans: people who loved the sport of bargain hunting. Godin reports sales falling by more than fifty per cent. As evidence it is weak and should be labelled: a single retrospective case, no controls, a figure reported without a source, a causal attribution to worldview mismatch in a decision with many other moving parts, and a US department-store episode of the early 2010s in a retail environment that no longer exists in that form.
confounders: treating the fifty-per-cent figure as evidence for the mechanism rather than as a reported outcome
reading the lesson as 'don't remove discounts' rather than 'don't decide from your own worldview'
model_answer: This is J.C. Penney under Ron Johnson, who scrapped coupons and sales for everyday fair pricing. Godin says customers were not buying low prices but the experience of the deal: the thrill of the hunt, the feeling of being a smart shopper, and the story they told themselves about winning. Removing the game removed what they valued, and sales collapsed. As evidence it is one well-known case explained in hindsight and confounded by other changes Johnson made at the same time (store redesign, brand mix, alienating core shoppers). It illustrates the point but does not isolate the cause.

source_title: bijapurkar_we_are_like_that_only
question: What is the 'analogy school', and what is the objection to it?
answer: The practice of predicting a market's evolution by studying a more developed market assumed to be analogous — plotting per-capita GDP against per-capita consumption of a category in the comparator, locating the target market on that curve, and reading its future off the curve. The objection is that the method assumes the two markets differ only in WHERE THEY ARE ON A SHARED PATH, when they may differ in the path itself: the comparator's trajectory was produced by its own particular cost structures, infrastructure, credit availability, household structure and business models, none of which the target market need share. A market that develops a business model the comparator never had will not follow the curve, and the method has no way of representing that. The argument is made by exhibiting the assumption rather than by testing the method against outcomes — no forecast made this way is scored against what happened — so what the source establishes is that the assumption is doing unacknowledged work, not that analogy forecasts have failed at any measured rate.
confounders: The objection is not that comparators are useless; it is that the comparator's path is an assumption about the target and is rarely stated as one.
model_answer: The analogy school predicts India's future consumption by comparing it with where other countries (China, South Korea, Southeast Asia) were at similar income levels, assuming India will follow the same path. The objection: India is different, its demand structure, income distribution, culture, and slow growth path mean that analogies mislead; India's consumers behave in their own way, and the country has multiple markets coexisting. Using analogies leads to wrong forecasts and to strategies designed for another country. [unsure]
missed: Comparator's path itself may differ, not just position on shared path

source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
question: How do the authors tell a market leader to think about its advertising budget, and what do they say the budget actually buys? Quote the analogy they use.
answer: They tell leaders not to think of advertising as an investment that will pay dividends but as insurance protecting against losses caused by competitive attack. Their analogy is a national defence budget: "your advertising budget is like a country's defense budget" — the tanks, planes and missiles buy nothing, they only keep the country from being overrun. What the money buys, on their account, is a raised price of admission: heavy spending forces any challenger to spend heavily too, which they say many competitors cannot afford and those who can will not bother, settling instead for crumbs. They go further and concede that advertising may not pay for itself, adding that if you are the leader it will at least make your competitor pay through the nose for the privilege of competing with you.
confounders: the effectiveness tradition's treatment of advertising as an investment with a measurable return and an optimal share of voice — this passage is the direct opposite of that position, and the book supplies no measurement on either side
assuming they recommend cutting advertising; they recommend massive spending, but for deterrence rather than return
reading it as advice for challengers; it is explicitly advice for leaders, and the chapter says advertising will not build a fledgling brand
model_answer: The authors say publicity builds brands and advertising maintains them. A leader should see its advertising budget as defensive: it maintains and protects a position already won through publicity, rather than creating it. The budget buys insurance, protection against competitors attacking the leadership position. They use an insurance analogy, treating advertising as the premium the leader pays to keep its brand on top. I cannot quote the exact wording with confidence. [unsure]
missed: Defense-budget analogy; raises challengers' price of admission

source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
question: Samara suggests deconstruction "might even improve readability." What does he mean by readability there, and how confident is the claim?
answer: He redefines the word. Readability in that sentence means the quality of, and the degree to which, the type engages its readers with the content — not the ease of decoding it. The claim is hedged: "might even", and it arrives immediately after his statement that these qualities should be made visual not merely as a tool for clarifying hierarchy and not just as intriguing eye candy, but to lay bare an author's methods and intent. It carries no reader evidence of any kind. Read as a claim about decoding ease it would flatly contradict his own admission that fragmenting text interferes with reading; read as a claim about engagement it does not.
confounders: reading 'readability' in the standard legibility sense, which makes the sentence contradict the same section
treating a hedged aside as one of the chapter's supported claims
confusing it with the accessibility sense of readability, which this book does not discuss
model_answer: Samara means readability in the sense of engaging readers and pulling them in: arousing interest and activity so the content is actually read and remembered. He does not mean legibility or reading speed. The claim is hedged ('might even') and is speculative. It is offered as a possibility from designers' intentions and argument, with no research evidence behind it, so it has low confidence.

source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
question: A brand in a category with rigid customer expectations wants remarkability and has no unusual product feature to point at. What two constructive routes does Berger offer, and what does each exploit?
answer: First, break an expected pattern. Remarkability is relative to an expectation, so the expectation itself is the raw material — which means a category with a firm norm is an advantage rather than an obstacle. His cases are a low-cost airline supplying a comfortable seat, varied snacks and seat-back television against no-frills expectations, and a hundred-dollar cheesesteak against what a cheesesteak is. Second, unresolved mystery or controversy, which works by a different mechanism: an open question that undermines a settled belief gives people a reason to ask others to help settle it, and the disagreement itself generates more discussion. His case is the 1999 film whose viewers could not tell whether the footage was real. He insists remarkability can be found in anything, and offers black toilet paper at a party as his cheapest demonstration.
confounders: reaching for a striking execution rather than for the category expectation the audience actually holds
treating mystery as the same mechanism as pattern-breaking; his mystery route works by prompting people to consult each other, not by surprising them
assuming a strong category norm is a constraint; on his account it is the material
model_answer: Berger's routes are these. First, find inner remarkability by breaking a pattern and violating expectations. Something surprising in an ordinary category, like Snapple's cap facts or a hidden bar behind a hot-dog shop, exploits the attention and talk that surprise generates. Second, use game mechanics and insider status through scarcity and exclusivity, which exploit people's desire to look good, achieve status and be in the know. Both create social currency without a novel product feature. [unsure]
missed: Second route is unresolved mystery/controversy prompting consultation

source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
question: A raking light reveals the texture of a light-blue sponge beautifully and destroys the texture of a black leather notebook. Explain the mechanism, and give the book's remedy for the leather.
answer: Texture is read as a tonal difference between two faces of each texture particle. Raking light creates that difference by shadowing one face and relying on diffuse reflection to light the other. The sponge is light-toned and strongly diffuse, so both halves are present. The leather is black, and a black subject by definition produces little diffuse reflection, so the shadow side survives and the diffuse highlight side does not — there is no difference left to read. The authors are explicit that the failure is caused by the subject, not by the technique. Their remedy is to switch the surface to the reflection channel it actually has: a large source above the subject, big enough to fill the whole family of angles, so the leather is rendered by direct reflection instead. They note this is the exact opposite arrangement on both variables — direction and size — and say the earlier theory taken alone would call it the worst possible way to light the leather. The texture highlight moves from near black to middle grey with the same light falling on the subject and no exposure increase.
confounders: answering 'increase the exposure', which the source explicitly refuses on two stated grounds
assuming the leather needs an even harder or more raking light — more of the failing treatment
attributing the difference to colour rather than to the diffuse-reflection channel that colour implies
model_answer: Raking light shows texture by creating tiny highlights and shadows on the surface. For the light sponge, the diffuse surface reflects so highlights and shadows contrast. For black leather, the surface is dark with low diffuse reflection and is somewhat glossy: the texture is visible mainly through direct reflections; raking light from the side produces little diffuse contrast and its direct reflections go away from the camera, so the texture disappears. The remedy: light from a position that produces direct reflection (within the family of angles) using a large, not too diffuse source, so the texture shows as highlights. [unsure]

source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
question: A company is deciding whether to pay customers a hundred dollars per successful referral. Berger's objection is not that it is expensive. What is it, and what does he propose instead?
answer: His objection is substitution. People already talk about products they like, for free and unprompted, and as soon as you pay them for doing it you crowd out the intrinsic motivation. The consequence is that sharing decisions stop tracking how good the product is: the quality and quantity of buzz becomes proportional to the money received rather than to the customer's opinion, so the referral stops carrying the signal that made it valuable. He grants that paying works in the narrow sense — lots of people will refer for a hundred dollars — and that it scales in cost rather than in quality. His alternative is social incentives: harness the desire to look good, which is what makes people publicise airline status and check-ins without being paid, and which he says is more effective in the long term.
confounders: objecting on cost grounds, which is not his argument
assuming a smaller payment avoids the problem; he states the effect without any threshold, though he also offers no evidence for that absoluteness
confusing crowding out with the separate claim that paid endorsements lack credibility
model_answer: Berger's objection is that money crowds out the real motive for sharing. People share because it makes them look good (social currency) and helps others. Paying them turns a social act into a commercial one: it makes referrers look like shills, undermines the intrinsic motivation, and sharing stops once the payment does. Instead he proposes leveraging social currency: make people feel like insiders, give them something remarkable to talk about, use game mechanics and status, and create exclusivity. Customers then share because it enhances their self-image.
missed: Buzz tracks money not product quality; not a shill-credibility point

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: White type is set over a photograph that runs from bright sky to dark foliage. What does WCAG actually give you for measuring this, and what does it not give you?
answer: It gives you a failure and a partial method, not a measurement procedure. The failure is F83: failure of SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.6 due to using background images that do not provide sufficient contrast with foreground text or images of text. The measurement rule assumes a specified background — Note 3 says contrast is measured with respect to the specified background over which the text is rendered in normal usage, with white assumed if none is specified — and a photograph is not a specified colour. The nearest thing to a method is in the non-normative note on graphical objects: where there are multiple colours or a gradient, test the least-contrasting area, and if that area falls below the ratio, assume it is invisible and ask whether the object is still understandable. That transfers naturally to worst-case testing of text over an image, but the source frames it for graphical objects, not for text over photographs. What the source does not give you is a defined value for the whole setting, a rule for averaging, or a threshold for how much of a glyph may fall below the ratio. It does supply one relevant device: Note 5 on letter borders, under which a narrow outline joins the letter and a wide halo becomes the effective background — which is why scrims and outlines can change the answer rather than merely improve the appearance.
confounders: computing an average background colour and reporting a single ratio as though the standard defined one
assuming the white-background default of Note 3 applies — it applies when no background is specified, not when the background is an image
assuming the graphical-object gradient method is the standard's stated method for text
model_answer: WCAG gives the contrast ratio formula based on relative luminance and the thresholds of SC 1.4.3: 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, with 7:1 and 4.5:1 for AAA. The Understanding notes say text over images needs sufficient contrast against the background behind the characters. It doesn't give a normative method for varied or gradient backgrounds: which pixels to sample, whether to use the worst case or an average, or how to handle anti-aliasing. That measurement protocol is left to testers, who in practice check the worst-case area.
missed: F83 failure; Note 3 specified background; least-contrast area note; letter borders

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: A caption is set in a hairline geometric sans at 11pt, in a grey computing to 4.6:1 against white. A reviewer says WCAG has nothing to say about it because it passes. What does the source actually say about this case, and what does it stop short of saying?
answer: It passes SC 1.4.3 as computed — 4.6:1 exceeds 4.5:1, and computed values are not rounded, so it is a real pass rather than a marginal one. But the source raises two related concerns and states both as concerns rather than requirements. Note 1 to the definition of large scale says fonts with extraordinarily thin strokes or unusual features that reduce the familiarity of their letterforms are harder to read, especially at lower contrast levels. And the Understanding note explains why the number can flatter this setting: because the contrast ratio may be evaluated with anti-aliasing turned off, and because evaluation refers to the colours in the markup rather than the text as presented, a thin face rendered by a user agent with anti-aliasing may appear much fainter than its declared colour — producing text that nominally passes while having much lower contrast in practice. The note's response is best practice, not obligation: choose a font with stronger, thicker lines, or aim for a combination that exceeds the normative requirement. What the source stops short of saying is that this caption fails anything. It has no test for stroke weight, no requirement to exceed a threshold, and no claim about whether the caption reads well.
confounders: reporting a failure on the strength of the thin-stroke note, which creates no requirement
reporting nothing at all, which discards the source's own stated concern
assuming the 4.6:1 figure describes what the reader perceives
model_answer: The caption is normal-size text (11pt is below 18pt/14pt bold), so SC 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1, and 4.6:1 passes on the numbers. The Understanding documents note that very thin or decorative fonts are harder to read and that stroke width affects legibility. They advise authors to use higher contrast for thin fonts, but the contrast calculation does not account for font weight. So the source acknowledges the problem and encourages more contrast, but stops short of making it a failure. Technically the caption conforms.
missed: Anti-aliasing and markup colour make nominal ratio flatter thin fonts

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
question: Hopkins built risk transfer into successively stronger forms. Trace the escalation, state his general finding about people who are trusted, and name his own counter-case.
answer: The escalation runs: a druggist-signed money-back warrant on a remedy; then a warrant covering a five-dollar lot of six bottles, so that a single-bottle purchase was underwritten by it; then paying outright for the buyer's first fifty-cent bottle and warranting the six that followed. His formulation is that asking a person to take a chance on you means a fight, while offering to take a chance on him makes the way easy, and that he analysed his propositions until he was sure the buyer had the best end of the bargain. His general finding is that very few people cheat a seller who offers a square deal — try to hedge or protect yourself and human nature likes to circumvent you — and that he has been robbed often but at roughly a tenth of what enforcing a safe proposition would have cost. His own counter-case is the Racine Club shoe scheme, where he guaranteed a fit and the returns absorbed most of the profit. So the cost of risk transfer depends on how often the product actually disappoints.
confounders: generalising the sub-2-per-cent claim rate; it is one product in one year on a remedy whose efficacy a buyer could not judge
assuming a guarantee is a contract the buyer intends to use; his account is that it functions as a statement of the seller's confidence
separating the mechanism from its evidence too cleanly; the evidence comes from campaigns he repudiates as a class
model_answer: Hopkins escalated risk transfer from the advertiser: free samples, then money-back guarantees, then letting customers try the product first and pay later, or buying a product at the dealer's risk (e.g. the coupon that pays the dealer for a free package). His general finding: people who are trusted are honest; very few abuse a guarantee or free trial. His counter-case: some offer where people did abuse it or where free sampling was wasteful, e.g. giving to people who would not buy. [unsure]
missed: Escalation of warrants; Racine shoe scheme counter-case

source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
question: A team proposes fixing rater disagreement by expanding its review form from six questions to thirty-two, and adding more raters. Using the book, give three reasons this may make things worse.
answer: First, halo. The book says the proliferation of dimensions is pernicious as well as useless, because "the halo effect implies that supposedly separate dimensions will in fact not be treated separately. A strong positive or negative rating on one of the first questions will tend to pull answers to subsequent questions in the same direction." Its cited horror case is a system with forty-six ratings on eleven dimensions per rater and ratee. Second, rater capacity. "It would take a superhuman rater to recall and process accurate, relevant facts about numerous people being evaluated on so many dimensions," and the explosion in demands on time-constrained raters "cannot be expected to improve the quality of the information they supply." Third, cost against benefit. The book puts this case directly in the noise-reduction-costs frame: "In this case, the reduction of noise may not be worth the cost." Its example of where that lands is a firm calculating it spent two million hours a year on evaluations. What the book would do instead is not more questions but better scales: make the dimensions few and specific, anchor them in concrete reference cases, train raters to use the scale consistently, and score each dimension separately — the length of the form is not the lever.
confounders: assuming more dimensions means more structure — the book's structuring principle requires independent SCORING, not more questions
assuming more raters always helps; the book records diminishing returns and a real cost
treating the problem as insufficient detail rather than as ambiguous scales and contaminated dimensions
model_answer: First, more questions don't produce independent assessments. The halo effect bleeds an overall impression across items, and long forms invite fatigue and inconsistency (occasion noise). Second, unless each item is anchored on a shared scale with a common frame of reference, more items add more room for level noise and pattern noise. The book favours a small set of well-defined mediating assessments, about five or six, rated on relative scales. Third, extra raters reduce noise only if their judgements are independent and aggregated. If they discuss first, cascades and group polarisation can amplify error rather than cancel it.
missed: Rater capacity overload and cost-not-worth-benefit reasons

source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
question: A committee runs the mediating assessments protocol and the resulting profile is uneven — some assessments strongly positive, others weak. A member argues the analysis must be flawed because a good option should look good on everything. How does the book answer this?
answer: The unevenness is the expected result of doing it correctly, not evidence of a flaw. The book has its CEO character notice exactly this on reading the report: because the assessments were kept independent of one another, they did not paint a simple, all-systems-go picture. "When excessive coherence is kept in check, reality is not as coherent as most board presentations make it seem." A conventional report looks uniform because each section is written in the light of the conclusion the team is already reaching — which is the contamination the protocol exists to prevent. The book then treats the discrepancies as the point: "These discrepancies between assessments will raise questions and trigger discussions. That's just what we need to have a good debate… The diverse results will not make the decision easier, for sure—but they will make it better." The instruction to the analysts reinforces it: include all relevant factual information in each chapter, and "if there is information that seems inconsistent or even contradictory with the main rating, don't sweep anything under the rug."
confounders: treating a coherent, uniformly favourable analysis as a sign of quality — the book treats it as a symptom of contamination
resolving the unevenness by averaging the assessment ratings, which the book's protocol explicitly declines to do at the final step
assuming the protocol is meant to make decisions easier or faster; the book claims better, not easier
model_answer: The book answers that an uneven profile is expected and informative, not a sign of error. The point of mediating assessments is to evaluate each dimension independently and fact-based, so as to avoid the halo effect, where one impression colours everything. Real options usually have strengths and weaknesses. A profile where everything looks good would more likely indicate halo or excessive coherence. The committee should weigh the uneven profile holistically at the end rather than smooth it away.

source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
question: What is Freeman doing with the abalone shell behind the quartz crystal, and what is the general permission he draws from it?
answer: He is using defocus to strip an object of its identity and keep only its hue. The crystal is colourless but refracts, so he placed a polished abalone shell several inches behind it and shot at a fairly wide aperture — just enough to keep most of the crystal sharp. At that distance and blur the shell is made completely abstract and unrecognisable for what it was, present only as iridescent blue and green which the crystal's facets then refract. The general permission he states is that there are times when colour will enliven an image and times when it matters less what those colours actually represent in real life.
confounders: reading this as a bokeh or background-quality question, which is about the character of blur rather than about recruiting an object as pure colour
assuming the shell needed to be recognisable or thematically related, when he says the colours had nothing to do with the crystal
supposing this is a lighting technique; the colour comes from an object placed in the scene, not from a light
model_answer: Freeman uses an abalone shell as a background behind a quartz crystal, chosen for its iridescent colour and texture rather than for any contextual connection. The shell complements and sets off the crystal's clarity and form. The general permission is that in still life and constructed images the photographer may choose backgrounds and props purely for their graphic and aesthetic contribution, such as colour, tone and contrast, without needing a logical or natural relationship to the subject. [unsure]
missed: Defocus strips shell's identity leaving only hue refracted by crystal

source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
question: Most people presenting work for critique try to explain every decision up front. This source says to do the opposite. Give both reasons it offers, and the rule it gives for choosing what to say instead.
answer: The first reason is that pre-empting every question overwhelms participants and eats the meeting's time; the authors read the over-explanation as an attempt to foreclose questioning at all — "it's as if we're trying to avoid the potential for questions." The second is the more interesting one: when the details arrive in answer to questions, they are more closely tied to the participants' own insights and questions, so the explanation lands where someone actually needed it. The rule for what to say instead is to focus on what is not obvious or cannot easily be seen — participants do not need to be told that the navigation is at the top of the page — and the authors' usual way of doing that is to present the design from a user's perspective. Give enough for the team to understand how the design is intended to work, no more, and if you feel the pace ran fast, say so and invite questions.
confounders: assuming the aim is to save time; the authors give the tying-to-questions reason as the more important one
reading it as a licence to present badly or vaguely — the requirement is that the team understand how the design is intended to work
conflating it with the constraints caution, which is a specific case with its own reasoning
model_answer: The book advises not to explain every decision up front: first, explaining everything takes time and leaves less for critique; second, it biases the critics and preempts their fresh reactions, and they will not see the design as a user would. The rule: give just the context necessary: the objectives, the problem, the constraints, and what you want feedback on, and leave other decisions to be discovered and discussed. [unsure]
missed: Details tied to questions; focus on what is not obvious

source_title: pandey_pandeymonium
question: This author is known for rejecting research. What exactly does he reject, what does he keep, and what does he put in its place?
answer: He rejects the PROCEDURES he has seen, not research as such — 'I reject the procedures that I have seen, but I don't undervalue homework and thoroughness', and he notes he has attended more research sessions than most creative people. What he keeps is homework and thoroughness, and his own preferred practice of chatting with people without an agenda. What he puts in place of self-report is direct behavioural observation: he describes throwing away the headphones behind a one-way mirror and watching body language instead, on the criterion that a respondent chatting and not looking at the commercial after five seconds is lost.
confounders: The usual summary — 'Piyush Pandey thinks research is useless' — is not what the source says, and the distinction he insists on is load-bearing.
model_answer: Pandey rejects research as the judge of creative work: pre-testing ads, focus-group verdicts and scoring that decide whether an idea lives. He keeps research as input for understanding consumers and markets. He puts in its place deep immersion in real Indian life, including observation, conversation, travel and everyday language, plus the gut instinct and experienced judgement of creative people and clients willing to trust ideas that feel true to how people actually live.
missed: Rejects procedures seen; body-language observation behind one-way mirror

source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
question: In the Yosemite Falls picture Freeman accepts a specific loss to buy a specific gain. What is the exchange, and why did the composition force it?
answer: He needed the silhouetted branches in the foreground and the distant falls to be equally sharp, because the effect depends on the branches reading as a flat overlay on the scene beyond rather than as a separate near object. That meant plenty of depth of field, so he stopped down to ƒ/32, which in that light gave 1/5 second — and he says plainly that he accepted some softness in the falling water as the price. The only moving thing in the frame is the thing that paid. He states the trade as a fact of the picture he made, not as a general exposure rule, and he does not claim the softness was desirable.
confounders: treating this as a generic depth-of-field lesson, when the requirement comes from a compositional decision about an overlay
assuming he wanted silky water, which is a common reason for a slow shutter on a waterfall and is the opposite of what he says
supposing a tripod or higher ISO would have resolved it; he reports the trade as taken, not as avoidable
model_answer: In the Yosemite Falls picture Freeman accepts cutting part of the scene, the top of the falls or the surrounding context and sky, to gain the full vertical sweep and scale of the falling water together with a foreground anchor. The tall, narrow subject in the frame format and the fixed viewpoint meant he couldn't include everything, so he had to choose between completeness and the stronger vertical dynamic and scale. [unsure]
missed: Stopped to f/32 for sharp overlay branches, accepting soft water at 1/5s

source_title: dwyer_patel_cinema_india
question: A studio is designing the poster for a sequel to a fifteen-year-old film that has since acquired a following the original release never had. What does this source's re-release material say to do, what does it not settle, and what would you have to know that the source cannot tell you?
answer: What it says to do: design for retrieval, not for information. The re-release finding is that where the audience already knows the film, publicity's job is 'to create an image that would most effectively trigger people's memories', and the designs accordingly targeted whichever scenes and images had OVER TIME become the key signifiers — which is why Aan's poster acquired a sword fight that was not on the original. So the operative question is not what the original was sold on but what the audience now retains, and those can differ. What it does not settle: a sequel is not a re-release. The re-release cases carry no new film to sell, whereas a sequel must both retrieve the old and introduce the new, and the source documents no case of that mixture. Nor does it establish any effect — no attendance, sales or recognition figure is reported for any redesign, so the finding is about intent and craft, not outcome. What you would have to know independently: WHAT THE AUDIENCE ACTUALLY RETAINS, which the source cannot supply for a film it never studied and which cannot be inferred from the original campaign. Patel's designers evidently knew it for their titles; how they knew it is not documented, and that gap is the whole problem in the sequel case.
confounders: It is easy to take the Mother India reduction — the whole film to Radha pulling the plough — as a rule that less is more. The rule is that the retained image wins, and finding out what is retained is the part the source does not teach.
model_answer: The re-release material shows posters being redesigned for new circulation. Distributors update imagery to the later status of stars and to current graphic fashion, and emphasise what has since become famous about the film rather than reproducing the original. That suggests leaning on the elements the later following cherishes. It does not settle whether to preserve the original visual identity for nostalgia or modernise it. What you would need to know, and the source cannot tell you, is who the following is, what they value (iconic scenes, stars, the original poster art), and how the new audience's expectations differ. That requires current audience research. [unsure]
missed: Sequel is not re-release; design for retained memory; no outcome data

source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
question: "Random errors cancel out, so noise doesn't matter." Reconstruct the book's answer, and be precise about the condition under which cancellation actually would occur.
answer: Cancellation requires averaging multiple judgements OF THE SAME CASE. That is exactly what an operating system does not do. A noisy system makes single judgements of different cases: one underwriter prices one policy, one adjuster handles one claim, one judge sentences one defendant. So one overpriced contract and one underpriced contract are not an average that comes out right — they are two costly errors, one losing business and the other losing money. The book's sentence is "In noisy systems, errors do not cancel out. They add up." It concedes the cancellation property itself is real and says it is precisely what noise-reduction strategies exploit: averaging several independent judgements of the same case does reduce noise, which is why aggregation is one of its recommended remedies. The error in the objection is applying a property of repeated measurement to a process that never repeats a measurement.
confounders: conceding the point for evaluative judgements because there is no true value — the book's fairness argument applies there too: two felons who both deserve five years getting three and seven is not justice on average
confusing the wisdom of crowds, which averages many judgements of one case, with a system, which makes one judgement of many cases
assuming the objection is simply wrong; the book's position is that the property is real but misapplied
model_answer: The book says noise does not cancel out in real systems because each judgment affects a specific person or case: a too-harsh sentence and a too-lenient sentence do not cancel, they are two errors. In mean squared error, bias and noise contribute independently; errors add up as squares. Cancellation only happens when judgments are aggregated, e.g. averaging multiple independent judgments of the same case (the wisdom of crowds), where the average has less noise. Single decisions do not benefit.

source_title: desai_mother_pious_lady
question: A reviewer asks why this source's visual pass has a null result and whether that is a gap. What is the answer?
answer: It is a result, not a gap. Thirty of the thirty-three images are 700–1,840-byte decorative ornaments recurring at essay openings, and the other three are the cover and two front-matter marks; both non-ornament images were opened. The book argues about objects — a scooter, a thali, a matrimonial column — entirely in prose and never reproduces or points at an image of any of them, and no sentence in the book directs the reader to look at anything. So a text-only representation loses nothing of the argument. The Audit Gate vocabulary separates exactly this case: inspection_state is inspected_figure_level (we looked) and visual_argument_role is no_visual_argument (there was nothing to see), which is a different state from not having looked.
confounders: The two-axis vocabulary exists because a single 'visual completeness' field cannot distinguish these, which is what CANON-003 got wrong.
model_answer: The visual pass has a null result because this source contains no images to analyse. Desai's book is a collection of text essays about Indian middle-class culture, with no reproduced advertisements, photographs or plates. It is not a gap in the analysis. It is a property of the source. The consequence is that any visual claims about the ads or objects he discusses cannot be supported from this book and must be checked against other sources that reproduce the material.
missed: Images exist (ornaments) and were inspected; no visual argument

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
question: What is Hopkins's verdict on colour, what exception does he state, and what makes the exception work?
answer: His verdict is that colour does not generally pay better than black and white, "according to the evidence we have gathered to date" — one of the few explicit provisionality hedges in the book. His exception is lines whose appeal is the appearance of the product itself: certain food dishes look far better in colours, and tests on lines like oranges and desserts are said to show colour paying. What makes it work is that colour "comes close to placing the products on actual exhibition" — it does selling work no other treatment can do. Colour used to amuse or to gain attention falls back under his general rule: it may attract many times as many people yet secure a hearing from no more of the people wanted. The verdict is a judgement on a 1923 colour-printing premium he never states, so it is a cost finding rather than a claim about colour perception.
confounders: Reading the verdict as a claim about colour and attention rather than about a price premium.
That the exception is 'food' as a category; his stated principle is exhibition of appearance, which is why oranges and desserts qualify.
Dropping the hedge 'to date', which is the source scoping its own finding.
model_answer: Hopkins's verdict is that colour usually isn't worth its cost. It adds expense without proportionately increasing sales, and 'fine' pictures don't sell. The exception is when colour is essential to showing the product, for example foods, fabrics or products whose appeal is their appearance. The exception works because there the colour itself carries the sales argument. It demonstrates the product truthfully and attractively, so it pays for itself in traced results.

source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
question: Sullivan gives two signs that an idea has reached platform size. Name both, and say which one you should distrust most and why.
answer: First, it fits on a sticky note: a big idea can be summed up in a sentence, and needing more than a sentence or two to set it up means it is probably not there yet. Second, once spoken aloud its rules start talking and the platform unpacks itself — other people in the room begin generating executions unprompted. The second is the one to distrust, because it is a social measurement: it is confounded by who is in the room and by the enthusiasm of whoever is presenting, and Sullivan does not address this. He also hedges the first himself, calling it "kind of weird" and framing the whole formula around it as a tool rather than a rule.
confounders: reporting the sticky-note sign as a length limit for a tagline; it is a test of whether the idea has one centre
treating spontaneous generation in a room as evidence about audiences rather than about colleagues
assuming these are tests of quality; they test for size and legibility of the rule set
model_answer: One sign of a platform-sized idea is that executions come easily. Many different ads and media extensions suggest themselves, and it can run for years. The other is that other people, colleagues and clients, start adding their own executions and building on it. Distrust the first most, because ease of generating executions can come from a format or formula (a template or gimmick) rather than a genuine idea. Many executions can simply be repetition. The test is whether the idea stays fresh and meaningful across executions. [unsure]
missed: Sticky-note test; distrust the social 'rules start talking' sign

source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
question: Sontag's attrition argument has two parts, and only the second makes it a mechanism. Give both, and give her comparative example.
answer: First: photographs shock insofar as they show something novel, and the shock of photographed atrocity wears off with repeated viewing — she places it beside pornography, where the surprise of the first encounter also wears off after a few more. Second, and this is what makes it a mechanism rather than an observation: the ante keeps getting raised, partly through the very proliferation of such images. The supply of images draws down the stock of novelty on which any response depends, so the level required to produce a response rises with the number of images produced. Her example is two famine reportages a generation apart, the later having less impact for some viewers because such images had become banal, and a further set that she says must have seemed to many like an unbearable replay of a now familiar atrocity exhibition. Her conclusion is that concerned photography has, in recent decades, done at least as much to deaden conscience as to arouse it.
confounders: giving only the wearing-off half, which is an observation and not a mechanism
reading it as advice about frequency or variation; she recommends nothing
assuming the effect is about the viewer's callousness rather than about the supply of images
model_answer: The attrition argument: part one, repeated exposure to images of suffering dulls our response; shock fades. Part two, which is the mechanism, is that photographs make events seem real at first, but with repetition they make them less real: the image becomes familiar, a spectacle, and the viewer's capacity for feeling is used up. Her example contrasts the first time she saw Holocaust photographs (Bergen-Belsen, Dachau) at twelve, producing a lasting negative epiphany, with later images of the Vietnam war, which viewers are anaesthetised to. [unsure]
missed: Proliferation raises the ante; famine reportages example

source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
question: A review board of six people has signed off unanimously on every one of the last forty submissions, with high stated confidence. A manager reads this as evidence that the review criteria are clear and well applied. Using this book's material only, give the two readings the manager has not considered and say what would distinguish them.
answer: First reading: contagion rather than agreement. If the six express views in sequence and can see each other, an informational or social-pressure cascade will produce unanimity regardless of what the members privately think, and the book stresses that observers systematically underestimate how much of an apparent consensus is people following predecessors. Group polarisation compounds it, since discussion also produces greater confidence and unity. Second reading: the illusion of agreement. If the board's records simply never contained a mechanism capable of surfacing disagreement, the absence of recorded disagreement is not evidence of its absence — the book's insurance underwriters worked alongside one another for years without discovering that they differed by a median of 55%. What distinguishes them from real agreement is the same thing in both cases: collect each member's judgement independently and before any discussion, on the same submissions. If the pre-discussion spread is small, the manager's reading survives. If it is large, the unanimity was manufactured. The book adds that unanimity should be treated with more suspicion than a split, not less.
confounders: treating high stated confidence as corroboration; the book's whole argument on the internal signal is that confidence is not evidence of accuracy
proposing to interview the board members about whether they really agreed — a self-report that the illusion of agreement predicts will be reassuring and wrong
concluding the board should be disbanded; the book's move is to measure first, and it says nothing about whether this board is accurate
model_answer: First, unanimity may reflect a lack of independence rather than clarity. If members hear each other before judging, informational and social cascades, deference to a senior member and group polarisation produce false consensus and inflated confidence. Second, the board may share a common bias: they agree with each other, low noise, but are systematically wrong. Agreement measures noise, not accuracy, and confidence is not validity. To distinguish them, collect independent private ratings before discussion (a noise audit) to see whether agreement survives, and compare decisions against later outcomes to detect bias.
missed: Illusion of agreement: no mechanism to surface disagreement

source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
question: Berger uses the word "viral" constantly. In his own footnote he narrows it. What does he say it does and does not mean, and what does that narrowing do to the rest of the book's promises?
answer: He says that when he claims something will make an idea more viral, he means only that it will be more likely to spread from one person to another — and expressly not that one person will generate a long chain that infects a population. He says the disease analogy holds only up to a point, that the key difference is expected chain length, and that long chains may be less common with products and ideas than the analogy implies. The effect on the book is substantial: every promise to make something contagious means raising the probability of a single pass-on, not producing an epidemic. He hedges the empirical half — long chains "may be" less common — and cites Goel, Watts and Goldstein for it.
confounders: assuming 'viral' in this book means what it means in ordinary usage, namely explosive population-wide spread
missing the placement: the book's most important self-limitation is in a footnote, and the body text never repeats it
treating the short-chain claim as Berger's finding rather than as a hedged citation
model_answer: In his footnote Berger narrows 'viral'. He doesn't mean true epidemic spread, where each person infects more than one other and cascades grow exponentially from one seed, which almost never happens. He uses the word loosely to mean spreading from person to person through word of mouth and social transmission. That narrowing reduces the book's promises: the STEPPS principles increase the likelihood and amount of sharing, but they can't guarantee blockbuster viral cascades.

source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
question: You are processing a facade shot in which the vertical planking should dominate, and your instinct is to even out the tonal range. What did Freeman do instead, and what else did he remove?
answer: The opposite. He says he was far from wanting to balance tones and actively wanted strong contrast so that the vertical lines would dominate, and he processed for contrast accordingly. The reason is that contrast is what separates a line from its surroundings sufficiently for the eye to read it as a line rather than as a boundary between two similar tones. He then removed everything competing: he cropped to eliminate anything that would distract from the verticals — naming a window at the left and lit grass below — and shaved the frame at top and bottom. He also offers, conditionally rather than as a recommendation, a further step: if you do not mind altering the geometry in post-production, straightening the roof ridge from diagonal to horizontal would allow an even tighter crop. Note that the picture did not begin as an image about verticals; he was photographing the architecture and redirected when the low sun caught the planking.
confounders: the default of protecting highlights and opening shadows, which is the instinct he reverses here
assuming this is a general rule about contrast; it is a reversal stated for a picture that is about its lines
treating the geometry correction as recommended, when he prefaces it with a condition
model_answer: Instead of evening out tones, Freeman increased contrast and pushed the tonal separation so that the vertical lines of the planking became the dominant graphic feature. He went for a strong, almost abstract rhythm of lines, not a balanced full-range rendering. He also removed colour, converting to black and white or strongly desaturating, and cropped out distracting elements, so nothing competed with the linear pattern. [unsure]
missed: Did not remove colour; cropped window and lit grass; conditional ridge straightening

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: Under SC 1.4.11, when does a logo *lose* its exemption from the contrast requirement? Give the source's stated condition and its worked case.
answer: The exemption rests on the assumption that logos must comply with stricter colour choices mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines — that is, on a constraint the author cannot alter. The source states the consequence directly: where a logo is presented with insufficient contrast but that presentation was an author choice rather than mandated by brand guidelines, the low-contrast presentation is not "essential", and the logo is not exempt. The worked case is an author who displays partner or company logos at low contrast by default and raises the contrast only on hover; being logos does not rescue that, because the initial low-contrast presentation was chosen, not mandated. The source separately flags that the exemption is problematic when a logo acts as a user interface component such as a link, and recommends as best practice a higher-contrast logo variant where brand guidelines allow, or an equivalent control that meets the requirements. Caution on authority: this narrowing is non-normative, and it sits alongside SC 1.4.3's normative clause that exempts logotype text with no condition attached.
confounders: assuming 'it is a logo' is always sufficient — the source ties the exemption to a brand mandate
presenting the narrowing as a normative requirement when it appears in a Working Group Note
assuming a hover state that restores contrast cures the default presentation
model_answer: SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast does not apply to logos or brand names that are part of a logo; but a logo loses its exemption when it is used as a control (e.g. a link to the home page) or conveys information as part of UI component. Actually the source says logotypes are exempt, but if graphics in the logo are required to understand content, they need contrast. Worked case: a logo used as a home link where the logo itself is the control indicator must have contrast; or a logo that includes an icon required to understand. [unsure]
missed: Loses exemption when low contrast is author choice, not brand mandate

source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
question: The book's error equation says bias and noise contribute equally to overall error. Give the exact class of judgements it applies to, and the counter-cases the book uses to mark the boundary.
answer: It applies to purely predictive judgements — forecasts and estimates that aim to approach a true value — scored by mean squared error. MSE is the two-hundred-year-old standard for scientific measurement; it yields the sample mean as the best estimate, treats positive and negative errors equally, and penalises large errors disproportionately. The book states the boundary itself: "The error equation does not apply to evaluative judgments." Its counter-cases show why. A lift's maximum load: underestimating is costly, overestimating is catastrophic, and squared error is beside the point. When to leave for a train: being one minute late and five minutes late cost you the same thing, the train. Insurance pricing, where the costs of the two directions of error are different in kind. In all of these the error costs are asymmetric and there is no reason to think they are proportional to the square of the deviation. The book also concedes that MSE conflicts with common intuition — people care about near-misses and are insensitive to the difference between two large errors, which it calls "almost the mirror image of what they should be".
confounders: applying the equal-contribution result to acceptance or grading decisions, which are evaluative
reading MSE as a description of what error actually costs; the book says it does not reflect the real, often asymmetric costs of judgement errors
assuming that because MSE is standard it is uncontroversial — the book records its clash with intuition
model_answer: The error equation (mean squared error = bias² + noise²) makes bias and noise equal contributors only for predictive or verifiable judgements with a true value, where errors in either direction are equally costly and error is scored by squared deviation. The book marks the boundary with asymmetric-cost cases, where overshooting and undershooting cost very different amounts. Its example is getting to the airport, where arriving late is far worse than arriving early. In such cases a deliberate bias can be sensible. Evaluative judgements with no true value also fall outside it.
missed: Book's counter-cases: lift load, train departure, insurance pricing

source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
question: Berger defines "remarkable" and insists on a particular emphasis in the word. What is the definition, what is the emphasis, and what does he report about how remarkability relates to being discussed?
answer: Remarkable things are unusual, extraordinary, or worthy of notice or attention — novel, surprising, extreme, or just plain interesting. His emphasis is on the second half of the word: the most important aspect is that they are worthy of REMARK, worthy of mention. The test is whether a thing is worth saying out loud, not whether it is impressive. He reports his own analysis, with Raghu Iyengar, of 6,500 products and brands scored for perceived remarkability against how frequently each was discussed online: more remarkable brands were talked about almost twice as often as less remarkable ones. The mechanism he gives is transfer — telling someone a remarkable thing makes the teller seem remarkable.
confounders: reading remarkability as impressiveness or quality; his test is mentionability
treating the 'almost twice as often' result as causal; the design is correlational and the source's narration does not mark that
missing that this finding sits in unreconciled tension with the BzzAgent null in the next chapter, where interest, novelty and surprise showed no relationship with word of mouth
model_answer: Berger defines remarkable things as unusual, extraordinary or novel: things worthy of notice. He insists on the emphasis 'worthy of remark', meaning literally worth mentioning or talking about. He reports that remarkable products and content get talked about more (from his and others' studies of word-of-mouth data), because sharing remarkable things gives the sharer social currency and makes them seem interesting.
missed: 6,500 brands study: remarkable ones discussed almost twice as often

source_title: dwyer_patel_cinema_india
question: The source names a form it calls the most distinctive of its medium and then does not study it. Which form, why not, and what does that do to every claim in the book about the medium as a whole?
answer: Hoardings. Patel identifies them in the Introduction as 'the most distinct feature of film advertising', with their large-scale vibrant images and bright colours, and also as the most ephemeral, destroyed once a film finishes its run: 'since there is little surviving evidence of the type of imagery depicted on early hoardings, this study is based primarily upon handbills, posters and booklets, which, despite their fragility, have survived'. WHAT THAT DOES IS MAKE THE EVIDENCE BASE A SURVIVAL SAMPLE, AND NOT A RANDOM ONE: the form that survived is the small, printed, collectable one, and the form that did not is the large, painted, public one. So any statement here about what Indian film advertising looked like is a statement about what its durable printed forms looked like. The source states the gap plainly, which is why it is a bound on the evidence rather than a hidden defect — and it is the medium's gap, not a digitisation loss, since a reader of the 2002 print edition was in exactly the same position.
confounders: One hoarding IS reproduced (illus. 105, Balkrishna Arts, 2000) and it is a late one, which can create the impression the form is covered.
model_answer: The form is the song-and-dance sequence (film music and song picturisation), which the authors call the most distinctive element of Hindi cinema but do not study in depth. The book is about visual culture: sets, costumes, posters and publicity. Songs are a musical and performative form outside that scope and would need a separate study. As a result, every claim about Hindi cinema as a whole is partial. The book describes the medium with its defining component largely left out, so its generalisations apply to the visual and material culture of the films, not to the medium entire. [unsure]
missed: Hoardings; unsurvived so evidence is survival sample of printed forms

source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
question: "Black magic" in this book is not a figure of speech. What is it, and how is its hardness controlled?
answer: Black magic is anything added to a lighting set-up solely to place a black reflection in a metal surface. Its uses are practical: a black reflection in an edge helps differentiate that edge from the background, and reflected across the centre of a slightly irregular surface it adds dimension. It usually means a gobo, and its hardness is set by which side of the diffusion sheet the gobo sits on. Between the diffusion sheet and the subject, it makes a hard black reflection. Behind the sheet, away from the subject, it makes a softly graduated one, and the farther back it goes the softer it becomes. Where the source is an opaque reflector rather than a diffusion sheet a gobo cannot graduate, and the authors substitute a soft-edged stripe of black spray paint across the reflector.
confounders: assuming black magic means removing light, when its purpose is to place a specific dark shape
reversing the gobo rule — near the subject is hard, not soft
confusing it with a black card used as negative fill on a diffuse subject, which works by subtraction rather than by reflection
model_answer: 'Black magic' is the technique of using black cards or flags (black surfaces) positioned near the subject to create dark reflections on glossy surfaces or dark edges on glass, a subtractive lighting technique. On metal and glass, reflections of black cards produce dark lines that define shape. Its hardness (sharpness of the edge) is controlled by distance: the closer the black card is to the subject, or the further from focus, the softer or sharper the edge; a black card further from the subject gives a harder edge, near gives soft. [unsure]
missed: Gobo between diffuser and subject hard, behind diffuser soft

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
question: A designer proposes a striking, unexpected image on the ground that it will make the advertisement impossible to ignore. Give Hopkins's two separate objections.
answer: First, an attention objection: a picture that is eccentric or unique takes attention from the subject, and since the main appeal lies in the headline, overshadowing the headline kills it — "Don't, to gain general and useless attention, sacrifice the attention that you want." Second, a respect objection: treating the subject lightly or attempting frivolity lowers regard for the advertiser and the article, because people do not patronise a clown; his figures are the man who gains attention by wearing a fool's cap and the salesman in conspicuous clothes, whom the sane and thrifty majority despise. He supplies no comparison of an eccentric and a plain treatment for either objection, and this is squarely a period position at odds with much later practice that buys attention deliberately.
confounders: Collapsing the two objections into one; the attention argument and the respect argument are separable and only one concerns the headline.
That he objects to distinctiveness as such — chapter 17 says the opposite about manner and tone.
The modern default that attention is the scarce resource and worth buying with surprise.
model_answer: Hopkins makes two objections. First, striking or unusual images attract the wrong people: the merely curious, not prospective buyers. An advertisement should single out and appeal only to those interested in what you sell, so attention for its own sake is waste. Second, pictures take expensive space and must earn it by selling. Art that is merely decorative or eccentric distracts from the salesmanship and lends frivolity to a serious appeal. Use pictures only when they help sell, and test them.
missed: Eccentric picture overshadows headline; frivolity lowers respect (clown)

source_title: jain_gods_in_the_bazaar
question: In this account, is iconographic correctness a criterion that makes an image better, or something else? Give the distinction and the trade behaviour that follows from it.
answer: Something else, and the distinction is the useful part. Jain reports Richard Davis's 'aesthetics of presence' — the idea, informing most icon worship in South Asia since the medieval period, that the icon is a privileged housing for the divine essence, an embodiment as much as a signifier — and states the operational consequence: 'if an icon is not produced in accordance with iconographic prescriptions it will not "work" (that is, it will not accrue efficacy, value, and power) — or worse, it will have the opposite effect, becoming inauspicious and bringing bad fortune.' So correctness is an ENABLING CONDITION, not a grading criterion: an incorrect icon is held not to be a worse image but a vacant one, and the failure mode is not disappointment but inauspiciousness. The trade behaviour follows: artists report iconographic accuracy as the main thing changed before a design goes to press, and a printer's reasoning runs the same way — South Indians prefer seated Lakshmis because 'if she sits down, wherever you keep the calendar, the god or goddess will stay in that place'. Jain draws out the triangulation implied: before the deity can look at the worshipper through an image, it must first recognise itself in it and decide to inhabit it. What is established is the TRADE's behaviour; that buyers reject incorrect images is imputed to consumers by printers, at one remove.
confounders: Most quality vocabulary assumes grading — better and worse on a scale. This is a threshold of function, and the two behave differently: you cannot trade a little correctness for a little more beauty.
model_answer: In Jain's account iconographic correctness is a threshold condition, not a merit: an image must get a deity's attributes, colours, weapons and mounts right to be acceptable or efficacious. Correctness doesn't make it better, and it cannot make one image more saleable than another. Artists and publishers therefore check and correct iconography as a must-pass requirement. Buyers reject incorrect images whatever their beauty, while competing on other qualities such as style, expressiveness, glossiness and appeal. [unsure]
missed: Incorrect icon is vacant/inauspicious; buyer rejection only imputed by printers

source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
question: Sullivan calls comprehension speed the "Speed of the Get" and likens it to a fuse. Most advice about clarity treats slowness as the only failure. What is the second failure he names, and why does he say it is a failure at all?
answer: The fuse can be too short.
