Even if prediction accuracy is limited by objective ignorance, reducing noise gives small improvements (e.g. correlation gains) that, applied across many decisions, yield meaningful benefits; small increases in accuracy are valuable across large numbers of cases.
missed: Lottery 59% vs 65%; internal signal of intuitive judgement

source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
question: What conclusion does Samara draw from the history in this chapter, and why is that conclusion, rather than the history itself, the part worth keeping?
answer: The conclusion is that rational structure — the grid — is one of many possible systems for organising visual material, and that context is an important factor in determining which system is best for a specific project. He closes the survey by saying that intuitive and idiosyncratic approaches now participate on equal terms with rational, grid-based ones, and that the designer's set of tools includes several methods from which the most appropriate for a given project can be chosen. That conclusion is the reusable part because the rest of the section is chronology — names, schools, dates — which carries no mechanism. The claim also does the load-bearing work for the chapter: it converts a historical narrative into the premise that selection, not habit, governs.
confounders: treating the historical narrative as the source's argument rather than as its setting
reading 'equal terms' as a claim that the approaches are interchangeable; his point is that selection is required
assuming the equality claim is about quality; it is about which system may legitimately be chosen
model_answer: From the history of modernist Swiss grid systems and the reactions against them (postmodern, deconstructivist and intuitive layout), Samara concludes that the grid and its breaking are not opposing ideologies. They are complementary tools. The choice between them should follow the content, the audience and the communication goal, not style or dogma. That conclusion is worth keeping because it is a working principle you can apply to any layout decision today. The history on its own only describes past movements, while the conclusion tells you how to decide.

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: What reason does W3C give for preferring real text to images of text? Name the specific capabilities that are lost.
answer: The reason is user adjustability, not fidelity. The intent stated for SC 1.4.5 is to let people who require a particular visual presentation of text adjust it as needed — the note lists font size, foreground and background colour, font family, line spacing and alignment. An image of text takes all of those out of the reader's hands. The Understanding notes for SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.4 add two consequences: images of text do not scale as well as text because they tend to pixelate, and it is harder to change foreground and background contrast and colour combinations for images of text, which some users need. This is why SC 1.4.4 excepts images of text from the 200 percent resize requirement — not as a concession, but because they cannot satisfy it. The stated beneficiaries are people with low vision, people with visual tracking difficulties who need to change line spacing or alignment, and people with cognitive disabilities affecting reading who need to restyle text.
confounders: assuming the objection is that images of text cannot be read by screen readers — that is SC 1.1.1's concern, and images of text may carry text alternatives
assuming the objection is image quality or file size
assuming SC 1.4.4's exception for images of text is a permission rather than an acknowledgement that they cannot comply
model_answer: W3C (SC 1.4.5, images of text) prefers real text because users can adapt it to their needs, while images of text fix the presentation. What is lost includes resizing without pixelation, changing font family, size, colour and background (foreground/background contrast), adjusting line, letter and word spacing, and reflow or wrapping. Other losses: user style sheets, magnification without blur, and ready interpretation by assistive technology such as screen readers, text-to-speech and translation.
missed: Screen-reader loss is not the reason; user adjustability only

source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
question: Ogilvy admires an advertiser's consistency at length and then names it as their weakness. Explain the double reading, and say what it qualifies in his own earlier doctrine.
answer: He reports strategies unchanged for thirty years with executions continually retested, campaigns running ten years or more, and never changing a successful strategy — and then says their Achilles heel is their consistency: they are always predictable, and it helps to win battles when you can anticipate the enemy's strategy. Consistency is what allows a strategy to be validated and re-used, and the same property makes the next move inferable by a competitor; the advantage and the vulnerability are one fact seen from two sides. This qualifies his chapter-2 doctrine that advertising should project the same image year after year, which names only the internal forces that erode consistency and no external cost of holding it. It is the same author adding a cost to his own earlier claim.
confounders: reading the Achilles heel remark as a general argument against consistency
treating this as a disagreement with chapter 2 rather than as Ogilvy adding a cost to his own rule
assuming the predictability cost falls on the advertiser's audience; it falls to a competitor who can anticipate them
model_answer: Ogilvy praises Procter & Gamble's disciplined consistency: sticking with proven formulas, the same positioning for decades, rigorous testing and never chopping and changing. Then he names that same consistency as its weakness. The formula-bound ads became predictable and dull, and it was hard to break into fresh creative territory. The double reading qualifies his own doctrine that you should stick with a campaign and build a consistent brand image. Consistency of positioning is a virtue, but consistency of formula and execution can harden into stale sameness. [unsure]
missed: Predictability lets competitors anticipate strategy, not dullness

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: A campaign is widened to a general audience and the work gets progressively blander over three rounds of feedback. What does Godin say happened, and where does he say the mechanism operates?
answer: Seeking the largest possible audience guarantees mass rejection — the chorus of no becomes deafening, and the feedback arrives direct, personal and specific. Under that pressure the natural response is to sand off the edges and fit in, and to fit in more than anyone else. His point about location matters: the mechanism operates through the maker, not the audience. Nothing about the audience changed; the maker averaged the work in response to rejection from people it was never for. Since the edges were what made it fit its intended audience, more reach destroyed the thing that was working. His instruction is to resist, on the ground that the rejection carries no information: it is not for them.
confounders: attributing the blandness to committee process or client timidity rather than to the reach decision
concluding all negative response should be ignored; Godin separately distinguishes feedback from advice
assuming the audience changed; his mechanism is that the maker did
model_answer: Godin says trying to please everyone leads to mediocrity: widening to the mass audience makes the work average because each round of feedback comes from people who aren't the audience and each objection sands off what made it remarkable. The mechanism operates inside the team or organisation: feedback and approvals push toward safe, bland outcomes, before it reaches the market. [unsure]
missed: Maker averages work reacting to rejection from wrong audience

source_title: jain_gods_in_the_bazaar
question: What are the regional iconographic codes described here, and what role do they play in whether an image is accepted?
answer: They are a well-defined regional iconography — reported consistently by artists, printers, distributors and clients — operating not only at the level of which deities are favoured but at the level of their attributes and formal treatment. Jain's enumerated examples: Lakshmi and Shiva preferred standing in the north and seated in the south; the eyes of Shiva and Hanuman wide open in the south and often half-closed in the north; Ganesh's ears and trunk longer in the north, his face paler in Bengal; Lakshmi accompanied by an owl in Bengal and nowhere else; Radha often portrayed with her garments askew in the north, while in Bengal all goddesses are covered to the point that even their ears are hidden. Their role is that they are THE MAIN GROUND OF REJECTION: artists develop a thorough knowledge of the codes because accuracy in following them is a particularly stringent requirement, and getting one wrong is what gets a design turned back. Note the direction of the reported evidence, which the source is clear about: the codes are reported by the trade as things it must satisfy, and the acceptance behaviour is the trade's.
confounders: The enumerated list looks like a code that could be turned into a checkable specification. Jain reports illustrative examples from informants, not a complete or dated code, and reports no survey of prints against it.
model_answer: Regional iconographic codes are the local conventions for how a deity or figure should look in different regions of India: attributes, dress, ornaments, colours, facial types, postures and associated symbols, such as distinctly South Indian versus Bengali or North Indian forms. They act as gatekeepers of acceptance. An image that departs from the local code is not recognised as the right or efficacious form and will not sell or be worshipped, so publishers and artists produce regional variants that match each market's expectations. [unsure]
missed: Specific examples; codes are the main ground of rejection

source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
question: A new entrant in a category where the leader owns the category's natural colour asks which colour to take. Apply the authors' rule, and state the trade they say you should accept.
answer: Take the colour opposite the major competitor's, not the one symbolic of the category — the leader has first choice, and the leader normally takes the symbolic colour. Their own worked case is a Brazilian tractor brand they named Maxion. John Deere, the leading tractor brand, had green, the colour of grass and agriculture; the second brand had red; so they made Maxion blue. The trade they say to accept is stated plainly: is blue a good colour for a farm tractor? No — but it is more important to create a separate brand identity than to use the right symbolic colour. They run the same logic through car rental (Hertz yellow, so Avis red, National green) and hold up Pepsi as the counter-case, having taken red and blue together and so struggled for decades against a world that seems awash in Coca-Cola red. They add that whatever colour is chosen must be held consistently over years, which is their reading of the Tiffany box.
confounders: choosing the category-symbolic colour for recognisability, which is the move the passage explicitly rejects for a non-leader
assuming the leader's rule and the follower's rule are the same; the chapter separates them, and only the leader is told to take the symbolic colour
reading the red/blue physiology as established; it is asserted, and the emotional readings drawn from it are conventions rather than consequences of optics
model_answer: The Law of Color says a brand should use a colour that is the opposite of its major competitor's, to create a distinct identity. The leader naturally takes the category's most representative colour, so the new entrant should take a contrasting colour, as Pepsi took blue against Coke's red. The trade they say to accept is giving up the category's natural colour association in exchange for differentiation and ownership of a distinct identity.
missed: Maxion blue tractor case; Pepsi is counter-case of red and blue

source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
question: The book raises seven objections to noise reduction against itself. List them, and state the single structural reply it gives to nearly all of them.
answer: One: reducing noise can be expensive and might not be worth the trouble, or even be feasible. Two: the strategies used can introduce errors of their own, including systematic bias. Three: dignity — people want an individualised hearing and a real person with the power to act, and noise may be its price. Four: noise leaves room for moral and political values to evolve, where a noise-free system might freeze existing values. Five: clear rules that remove noise create clear edges that people can game, so a little vagueness may prevent wrongdoing. Six: unpredictable penalties may deter better than certain ones. Seven: people do not want to be treated as cogs, and some strategies squelch creativity and morale. The structural reply is that these are objections to particular INSTRUMENTS — nearly always firm rules — and not to noise reduction as such: "whether an objection is convincing depends on the particular noise-reduction strategy to which it is meant to apply. You might, for example, object to rigid guidelines while also agreeing that aggregation of independent judgments is a good idea." Hence the reply to a crude instrument is a better instrument, not tolerated noise. The book states it presents the objections as sympathetically as it can and by no means endorses them as reasons to reject the goal.
confounders: reading the catalogue as concessions the book accepts
assuming an objection that defeats one strategy defeats the programme
missing that the book concedes real force to some of them, particularly cost and demoralisation
model_answer: The objections are: (1) noise reduction is costly; (2) rules and algorithms can introduce their own errors and bias; (3) mechanical rules deny dignity, since people want to be judged as individuals and heard; (4) rigid rules freeze values that should evolve; (5) clear rules invite gaming; (6) some unpredictability deters wrongdoing; (7) rules demoralise judges and stifle creativity. The structural reply is that these objections target particular crude methods, not noise reduction itself. The costs of noise must be weighed against the costs of reducing it, and the right mix of decision hygiene, rules and standards can usually keep most of the benefit while answering the objection. [unsure]

source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
question: Ogilvy holds that photographs beat drawings on readership, believability and memory, and then names a condition under which he found the reverse. What is the condition, what case does he give, and what does the reversal tell you about why photographs win in the first place?
answer: The condition is reproduction quality: photographs reproduce so badly in some newspapers that a line drawing gives a more lifelike picture. His case is that scratch-board drawings sold more shoes for one retail client than photographs did. The reversal tells you the advantage of a photograph is realism rather than the medium itself, so the advantage survives only as far as the printing preserves it — where reproduction destroys the realism, a drawing that keeps its form wins. This is one of the few boundary conditions in the book that names a physical circumstance and reports a case where the general rule flipped.
confounders: treating the exception as a preference for illustration style; it is a claim about the printing process
reading the tripled tourism as evidence for the photograph rule; only the readership figure is a measurement
assuming the rule concerns aesthetic realism rather than believability under degraded reproduction
model_answer: Ogilvy found drawings do better for some products, e.g. when a photograph would look unappetising or when the subject cannot be photographed well; the case he gives is a Guinness or food ad, or illustrations in ads for Rolls-Royce? The reversal: when the photograph fails to be more realistic or believable. It shows photographs win because they are perceived as real and believable, not because of any intrinsic appeal. [unsure]
missed: Poor newspaper reproduction; scratch-board shoe drawings outsold photos

source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
question: A set of dark-field glass frames comes back looking flat and slightly milky, with no visible streak or fogged corner anywhere. Is flare a plausible cause on this book's account, and what would you do?
answer: Yes, and the absence of visible streaking is not evidence against it. The book calls the basic dark-field arrangement probably the worst flare-producing arrangement one could encounter, because the very thing that makes it work — a large source surrounding a small dark background — puts non-imaging light just outside the field of view on all four sides at once. It states that even where the flare is not bad enough to produce visible fogging or streaking, the general degradation from all sides accumulates, and at best produces a picture with low contrast. The same invisible-uniform failure is named again in the extremes chapter for large white backgrounds. The remedy is a gobo that blocks non-imaging light from all four sides of the field of view — four cardboard blades, or a single board with a rectangular hole, clamped to a stand in front of the camera — positioned by the book's own trick of looking into the front of the lens and moving the card until the offending source is no longer reflected there, then pulling back slightly.
confounders: ruling out flare because nothing is visibly streaked, which is the specific error the source warns against
raising contrast in post, which treats the symptom
gobo-ing only the top, which is standard practice and inadequate here
model_answer: Yes, flare is plausible. The book notes that flare in dark-field setups often shows up not as streaks or fogged corners but as overall veiling: lower contrast, a milky or flat look, and greyed blacks. Stray light from the bright background area outside the picture enters the lens and scatters. The remedy is to mask the background light so that it is no larger than needed, with black cards or flags cutting it to just outside the frame edges, and to use a lens shade. Then compare test frames for restored contrast.

source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
question: Airey's only direct instruction about typeface selection is one line. What is it, and what does a designer on the facing side of the same book actually do?
answer: Tip 14: show a level of unity across your design — for example, if you show a playful mark, try matching it with a playful typeface. That is the whole of it: one example, one direction, no mechanism, and no treatment of the deliberate mismatch a designer might use for tension. What the designer of the French Property Exhibition mark actually says he did is different in kind: with three lines of text he chose regular, evenly weighted Avenir caps in order to keep the type flush with the lines of the mark. That is a proportion and alignment argument, not a register-matching one. Both are in the book and only the weaker of the two is elevated into a tip. The practical reading is that "match the type to the mark" underdetermines almost every real decision, and Airey's other constraint on lettering — tip 12's immediate-legibility gate — does more work.
confounders: elaborating tip 14 into a theory of type pairing; the book contains one sentence
assuming register-matching is his general position on type; the worked case reasons about alignment
confusing it with tip 12, which is a legibility gate rather than a matching rule
model_answer: Airey's direct instruction on type is roughly to choose a typeface that suits the client and the brand's character, since fonts carry personality. The designer featured on the facing page doesn't stop at picking a font. They customise or hand-draw the letterforms, modifying an existing typeface into bespoke lettering so the mark is distinctive and ownable. [unsure]
missed: Tip 14 match playful mark with playful type; Avenir chosen for alignment

source_title: bijapurkar_we_are_like_that_only
question: What is the molting/morphing distinction, what detection problem does it create, and what evidence supports it?
answer: MOLTING change sheds the old for the new like a snake's skin; MORPHING change is slow and from within, 'like an amoeba which, with every tiny particle it ingests, infinitesimally changes shape'. She argues Indian change is of the second kind and gives a physics analogy for why it still matters: since Force = Mass x Acceleration, 'a small acceleration (small changes over long periods of time) can also unleash a large force of change, if the mass that is changing is very large'. The detection problem follows directly: morphing change 'is not visible through the usual run of the mill "usage and attitude" type surveys that most companies ritualistically engage in', because each annual reading falls inside the noise — hence the executive who watches annually, finds nothing worth mentioning, and five years later finds the market distinctly different and asks 'when did we blink and not see this happening?'. Her proposed unit of observation is the CHANGE CONFLUENCE: a collection of individually insignificant shifts that together cross a threshold. THE EVIDENCE IS THE WEAK PART AND MUST BE SAID: the framework is illustrated by consulting cases with no client name, no date, no sample size and no outcome, plus a reported executive experience. The mechanism is clear; nothing measures it.
confounders: The Force = Mass x Acceleration line is an analogy, not a model; nothing in the book quantifies either term.
model_answer: Bijapurkar distinguishes molting, where a consumer sheds an old skin and replaces old behaviours with new ones, from morphing, where the consumer gradually transforms, keeping the old and adding the new so the underlying identity persists. Indian consumer change is mostly morphing. The detection problem is that surveys and trackers keep finding continuity in the old behaviours and miss that people are becoming something different, or they mistake additions for replacement. The evidence is mostly her consulting observations and illustrative examples, plus some macro consumption data, not systematic longitudinal studies. [unsure]
missed: Morphing is slow internal change; annual U&A surveys miss; change confluence

source_title: dwyer_patel_cinema_india
question: A team is building an image-generation system and proposes a 'star portrait' control that reproduces a named performer's recognition features. Using only what this source establishes, what can be justified and what cannot?
answer: Justified: that recognition of a performer runs on a SMALL SET OF STABLE FEATURES rather than on overall likeness, and that those features are identifiable by survey of the existing images — the source does exactly that survey and names Bachchan's heavy-hooded eyes and enhanced full lips as the recognition carriers. Also justified: that the target is the constructed identity rather than the person, since identity here is 'cumulatively constructed by the star, the artist and the public'. NOT justified, and the source blocks each directly: that any particular feature set transfers to a different performer, since the features are found per star by inspection and no general rule is offered; that recognition works outside the culture that built it, since Patel states an Indian star 'will be unknown to the wider Western audience'; and that reproducing the features produces the response, since the response depends on expectations built up over a career, which no image supplies. A further constraint comes from outside this passage: reproducing a living performer's likeness is a rights and consent question this source says nothing whatever about, and its silence is not permission.
confounders: The temptation is to read the Bachchan feature list as a recipe. It is a finding about one star produced by looking at his posters, and the method — survey the corpus — is the transferable part, not the features.
model_answer: The source establishes that star images in Indian film publicity rely on recognisable facial features, frontal address and iconography, and that star identity is central to publicity. It can justify that recognition features (face, style, costume) drive posters. It cannot justify reproducing a real performer's likeness: the source does not address rights, consent, or legitimacy; its historical analysis is descriptive, so any control reproducing a named performer would lack permission basis. [unsure]
missed: Features found per star; no transfer across stars or cultures

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: A team wants to change its campaign because everyone internally is sick of it. What does Godin say is happening, what is his memory claim, and what stopping rule does he actually supply?
answer: They are inside the dip — the gap between when the maker gets bored and when the audience gets the message — and changing now forfeits the trust that frequency was building. His memory claim is that people do not remember what they read, hear or see; they remember what they rehearse, the things seen again and again, and the market has been trained to associate frequency with trust, because the familiar is normal and the normal is trusted. The stopping rule he supplies is a quoted maxim: do not change your ads when you are tired of them, or when your employees are, or when your friends are — change them when your accountant is tired of them. That is a heuristic with no criterion in it, and it cannot distinguish persistence from stubbornness. He generalises the point well beyond advertising: people give a talk a few times and move on, or raise money and spend it fast, hitting the wall just before the good part.
confounders: treating internal boredom as evidence of audience wear-out
reading the accountant maxim as an actual decision criterion
confusing this with a claim about creative quality; his claim is about repetition and trust
model_answer: Godin says the team is bored because it lives with the campaign every day. The market has barely noticed it. Internal fatigue is not audience fatigue. His memory claim is that people forget quickly and need many repeated exposures before a message even registers. Consistency and repetition build trust and recognition, so abandoning a campaign early throws that away. The stopping rule he actually supplies is to change when it stops working with the people you seek, not when you are tired of it. He gives no precise metric or threshold. [unsure]
missed: Accountant maxim; heuristic with no criterion

source_title: dwyer_patel_cinema_india
question: What changed in the 1990s in who makes Indian film posters, and how does the source handle the disagreement about whether the change was a loss?
answer: From the early 1990s photographic stills fed into a computer could be manipulated on screen, 'allowing for the smooth superimposition, juxtaposition, reduction, enlargement and colour contrasting of images and text with relative ease', and the overpainted montage of the previous two decades gave way to images 'defined by simplicity and elegance'. The personnel consequence is stated plainly: 'the role of the traditional artist has been displaced by the computer specialist', and she names the firms — H.R. Enterprises, run by two publicity designers who are not trained artists but have extensive computer knowledge, and Yash Raj Films' in-house Design Cell under Fayyaz Badruddin, also a computer specialist. The disagreement is handled by RECORDING BOTH SIDES AS PRACTITIONER VIEWS rather than adjudicating: Yash Chopra prefers painted work, others prefer the new. Nothing in the source measures which performed better, and the record does not supply a verdict the source does not give.
confounders: Practitioner preference on either side is testimony about taste and craft, not evidence about effectiveness, and no effectiveness evidence appears anywhere in this book.
model_answer: In the 1990s poster-making moved from hand-painted work by specialist studio artists and painters to digitally composed, photographic designs by graphic designers, advertising agencies and publicity firms using computers and still photography. The source handles the disagreement by presenting both views. Some see a loss of the painted craft and its vivid, idiosyncratic aesthetic. Others see professionalisation and new possibilities. The authors report and contextualise the positions rather than adjudicating them. [unsure]

source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
question: Airey slips in a test a designer can run on their own prose rather than on the artwork. What is it, what does he claim, and in which direction does the claim actually run?
answer: Having described a mark in a single clause — an "open newspaper" symbol in the form of the letter A — he draws attention to how easy the description was and asserts a rule: distinctive marks are almost always simple enough to be described easily. The claim as stated runs only one way, from distinctiveness to describability. The useful diagnostic runs the other way — if you cannot describe your mark in a short phrase, it is probably carrying more than one idea — and that inversion is a reader's inference, not his claim. Two further limits are worth keeping: he hedges with "almost always", and the single demonstration is the author describing a mark whose intended meaning he had just been told, which is the opposite of the blind condition that would make the test informative.
confounders: attributing the reverse entailment to Airey; he states only that distinctive marks are describable
dropping his 'almost always' hedge
treating one self-administered description as evidence
model_answer: Airey suggests that if you cannot explain your design rationale clearly and simply in words, the design may not be resolved. Writing the rationale tests the concept. The claim is that a clear idea can be put in clear prose. The implication only runs one way. Muddled writing may indicate a muddled design, but an articulate rationale does not prove the logo is good, since plausible stories can be written for weak marks after the fact. The test catches some failures and certifies none. [unsure]
missed: Describability test: distinctive marks easily described; one direction only

source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
question: A magazine spread is proposed with a full-bleed photograph, a sans-serif headline reversed out of it, one column of copy running the full page width and no captions. Working only from what Ogilvy states in the layout and typography sections, list what he would change and give his reason for each.
answer: Five changes, each with its own stated reason. Move the headline off the illustration and beneath it: readers look first at the illustration, then the headline, then the copy, and he reports headlines below the illustration read by ten per cent more people. Set the headline in lower case rather than reversed out: reverse is almost impossible to read and capitals retard reading because they lack ascenders and descenders. Set the copy in a serif face: readers are accustomed to serifs in books, magazines and newspapers, and the eye is a creature of habit. Break the single full-width column into columns of roughly thirty-five to forty-five characters: people are used to about forty characters in newspapers, and a measure too wide is illegible. Add a caption under the photograph carrying the brand name and the promise: more people read captions than read body copy, so an uncaptioned illustration wastes the best-read position on the page. Every reason turns on what readers of his period had been trained by editorial print to expect.
confounders: justifying any of the changes on aesthetic grounds; every reason he gives is about a trained reading habit
keeping the reversed headline on the argument that it is more striking, which he answers with a fund-raising comparison
treating the caption as optional decoration rather than as the second-best-read element
model_answer: Ogilvy would change: reverse type (white on dark) reduces readership, so use black type on white; sans-serif is harder to read, use serif; full-page-width column is too wide, use narrower columns; headline should be below the photograph; add captions because captions are read more than body copy. Reasons: all based on readership research.

source_title: pandey_pandeymonium
question: Ten sentences in this copy appear twice. What caused it, how was it found, and why does it matter beyond being untidy?
answer: The printed book's pull-quotes have been flattened into the body text, so each appears once inside its paragraph and once standing alone. It was found mechanically: a scan for sentences over 90 characters occurring more than once returned exactly 10, each occurring exactly twice. It matters for two specific reasons rather than as untidiness. A naive extraction pass could read the standalone pull-quote as a second, separate claim and double-count it — which would inflate an object count and manufacture emphasis the author did not place. And any word-frequency or emphasis analysis over this copy is corrupted, because ten sentences carry double weight.
confounders: Each duplicated sentence is genuinely the author's; the defect is the duplication, not the content.
model_answer: The duplicates most likely come from the book's layout: pull quotes or callouts that repeat sentences from the body text were captured as ordinary text when the copy was digitised or extracted. They were found by a duplicate-sentence check during processing of the text. This matters beyond tidiness because duplicated sentences inflate apparent emphasis and frequency, can be double-counted as separate evidence in retrieval or quotation, and can misplace a quote's context. Analyses and citations need to deduplicate and trace each passage to its original location. [unsure]

source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
question: Godin's phrase is "people like us do things like this". What is the loop he describes, what does he say the marketer's first job is, and what does he say is the wrong way to do it?
answer: The loop is: normalisation creates culture, culture drives our choices, and those choices lead to more normalisation — with the individual choice made in answer to one question, do people like me do things like this. He adds that even outliers are aligning, with the behaviour of outliers. The marketer's first job is simple and he states it as such: define "us". The more specific, the more connected and the tighter the "us", the better. The wrong way is to define it by outcome — "the people who give are people like us" — which he says is backwards. And the scope claim matters: we cannot change "the culture", only "a culture", our little pocket of the world, which is why he treats the smallest viable market as the unit that maximises the chance of changing anything at all.
confounders: treating it as a slogan about social proof rather than as a self-reinforcing loop with a defining step
defining the group by who already buys, which is the backwards definition he rejects
model_answer: Godin's loop is culture. People take their cues from their group, so behaviour spreads as norms: when people like us do something, others in the group adopt it, which reinforces the norm. The marketer's first job is to define and understand the 'us', the specific group whose culture you're joining or shaping, and then create tension that moves them to change together. The wrong way is to try to change everyone, the mass, at once, or to fight the culture head-on instead of working through a smaller group whose norms spread.
missed: Wrong way is defining 'us' by outcome, e.g. who already gives

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
question: A brand aimed at buyers of limited means proposes to lead on how much money the product saves them. State Hopkins's objection, his substitute, and the character of the evidence he offers.
answer: His objection is that the reason for a purchase is rarely economy, and that where economy is a necessity most people like to defy it: suggest a thing because it is economical and you arouse opposition, you hurt their pride. A price appeal classifies the buyer, and buyers who must economise experience that classification as an injury. His substitute is to direct the appeal to those who do not consider cost, so that the buyer who must economise can include herself without accepting the classification — she demands what the best people use. His evidence is his own observation of the gardeners, their families and the village folk near his country home, whom he presents as typifying the ninety-five per cent who are his customers; and a cosmetics experience in which a low price on perfume did not appeal to the girl who should have economised. That is a convenience sample chosen and interpreted by him and presented as authoritative. The passage is heavily bounded by 1920s American assumptions about class, pride and gender, and is recorded as his framing, not as a finding about buyers.
confounders: reading it as a rule against price mechanics; he used coupons, free bottles and a published margin extensively
treating the country-place observations as research
generalising it beyond the socially visible goods and the 1920s American context he draws it from
model_answer: Hopkins objects that people of limited means do not want reminders of their poverty. Economy and saving appeals point to what they lack and carry the stigma of cheapness. He substitutes positive appeals to pleasure, aspiration, quality, health or beauty, offering what they want to become rather than what they save. His evidence is anecdotal and experiential: campaigns he ran or tested where the aspirational appeal outsold the economy appeal. These are keyed-return comparisons within his own practice, not controlled studies, and are reported from memory. [unsure]
missed: Appeal to those who ignore cost; evidence is village convenience sample

source_title: desai_mother_pious_lady
question: This source says the scooter carried an aura of safety its engineering does not merit. What is the engineering point, what produced the perception, and how well supported is each?
answer: The engineering point is that the scooter's smaller wheel size makes it LESS stable than the motorcycle it was felt to be safer than. The perception, he argues, came from the images surrounding it: the stepney, the space to squeeze in a whole family, the dickey for the household's sundries — an attribute term attaches to whatever most visibly stands for it, so 'safe' attached to a vehicle visibly enabling responsible family life, and the physical property the term names went unconsulted. Neither half is well supported: the stability claim is asserted with no engineering authority cited, and the perception is asserted from the author's memory of the object's standing with no measurement at all.
confounders: Both halves are asserted; the object is valuable as a shape of failure, not as an established fact about scooters.
model_answer: The engineering point: a scooter (e.g. Bajaj Chetak) with small wheels and a side-offset engine is less stable than a motorcycle. The perception came from its design, a covered body protecting feet and the family image (family riding), feeling safe. The engineering claim is plausible but not rigorously supported; the perception is argued with anecdote and advertising, so weaker support. [unsure]

source_title: parameswaran_nawabs_nudes_noodles
question: A regulator forbids the single word a product category depends on. What does this source record an advertiser doing, what is the mechanism, and why is this not the same as a word wearing out through overuse?
answer: Doordarshan forbade *gori* ('fair') in fairness-cream advertising. The advertiser substituted *nikhri*, whose dictionary sense is 'improved' or 'better', and sustained use loaded the permitted word with the forbidden meaning until, the author says, nikhri came to mean 'fairer' to the lay public. The prohibition changed the word and not the proposition. The mechanism is that a lexical ban acts on a token, not on the meaning an audience assigns: if one advertiser uses a permitted token consistently in the banned token's slot, the audience learns the mapping. It is the opposite of a word wearing out — here a word ACQUIRES a meaning it did not have, under an external prohibition, driven by one advertiser's sustained investment, whereas inflation is a word LOSING force through universal adoption by many writers with no prohibition involved.
confounders: The claim that nikhri now means 'fairer' to the lay public is the author's assertion; no survey supports it. Nothing here endorses the category's proposition.
model_answer: The source records an advertiser answering the ban by substitution. For example, in surrogate advertising (liquor or tobacco brands advertising soda, music or other extensions), or by replacing a forbidden claim word with an image, coined term or euphemism, the brand keeps communicating the category. The mechanism is transfer: audiences already know the code, so the substitute inherits the forbidden word's meaning and the prohibition itself makes the allusion legible. This differs from a word wearing out, where meaning drains away through overuse. Here the meaning is preserved intact and simply rerouted around the ban. [unsure]
missed: Gori banned, nikhri substituted and acquired meaning 'fairer'

source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
question: A client wants a demonstration commercial that names the competing brand and shows it losing. What does Ogilvy report about that, and what does he say the risk actually is?
answer: He reports that his agency's studies found commercials naming competing brands less believable and more confusing than commercials that do not, and names a specific risk: viewers tend to come away with the impression that the brand you disparage is the hero of your commercial. So the danger is not merely wasted attention but transferred credit. He notes the practice was illegal in Germany and encouraged by the United States government as consumer information, which is a regulatory position of 1983. His enthusiasm for demonstration itself is undiminished — he wants demonstrations, and insists they need not be dull.
confounders: concluding he opposes comparative demonstration in general; his business chapter recommends comparison
reading the risk as legal rather than perceptual
assuming the finding is about believability alone, missing the hero-transfer claim
model_answer: Ogilvy reports that comparative advertising naming the competitor doesn't generally perform better. It tends to be less credible and less persuasive, and it can confuse viewers, who may remember the competitor rather than your brand. The risk, as he sees it, is that you give the competitor free publicity and viewers may misattribute the brands. Demonstrations that knock the rival can also look unfair, invite retaliation or lawsuits, and lower consumers' view of both brands. [unsure]

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: The WCAG contrast measure has no term for hue at all. Give the reasoning W3C states for that choice, and name the one case where the source says the reasoning breaks down.
answer: The stated reasoning has three steps. For people with colour vision deficiency who cannot distinguish certain shades, hue and saturation have minimal or no effect on legibility as assessed by reading performance; and the inability to distinguish shades does not itself damage light-dark contrast perception. Colour deficiencies are too diverse for prescribing effective general-use colour pairs from quantitative data to be feasible. Requiring luminance contrast instead accommodates the whole population with one number, because most of the luminance contribution comes from the mid and long wave receptors, which largely overlap in their spectral responses. The stated exception is predominantly long-wavelength colours against darker colours — generally appearing black — for readers with protanopia, and the source responds with an advisory technique on avoiding red on black rather than with a requirement. So a red-on-black pair can pass the normative test while the source's own note counsels against it.
confounders: assuming hue is ignored because it does not matter perceptually, rather than because it cannot be generalised over
assuming a luminance-passing pair is therefore safe for all colour vision — the source names protanopia and red on black as an exception
confusing this with SC 1.4.1, which is about colour carrying meaning, not about contrast computation
model_answer: The contrast ratio uses relative luminance only because luminance contrast is what matters for legibility and is perceived by nearly everyone, including people with colour-vision deficiencies. Hue differences may be invisible to people with colour blindness, so they cannot be relied on. The source notes the reasoning breaks down for red with protanopia. People with protan deficiency perceive red as much darker than its computed luminance suggests, so red on dark (or red-dependent) combinations can have less effective contrast than the formula reports. [unsure]
missed: Deficiencies too diverse to generalise; M/L receptor overlap reasoning

source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
question: What study are the 30% and 17% figures attributed to, and which of the three pages tells you the sample size?
answer: All three attribute them to a Google/Kantar study called "The Short & the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness", global, dated April 2021 — but only the Google for Business resources article gives a sample, "n=11,000 ads". Google Ads Help cites the same study, publisher, scope and month with no sample size. Think with Google cites it as "Google/Kantar Link AI, Global, The Short and the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness, 2021", naming Kantar's Link AI, dropping the month and giving no sample size. The study itself is not linked or published on any of the pages.
confounders: attributing the sample size to the Google Ads Help page, which is the page most often cited but does not give it
assuming n=11,000 refers to people surveyed rather than ads
conflating this Kantar study with the separate Ipsos collaboration described on Think with Google, which has no stated sample
model_answer: The 30% and 17% figures (ads following ABCDs show 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and 17% lift in long-term brand contribution) come from a Google/Ipsos (with Kantar?) study, 'ABCD MMM analysis' 2022. The Think with Google page gives the sample size (e.g. analysis of thousands of ads). [unsure]
missed: Google/Kantar April 2021; only Business resources gives n=11,000 ads

source_title: pandey_pandeymonium
question: What does this source give as its governing communication principle, where does it come from, and what kind of statement is it?
answer: 'Whatever you say, say it with respect for the audience, say it in a context that the audience can understand, say it spontaneously, say it without fear, say it not to intimidate or frighten, but to delight.' It comes from his father improvising verse to the household each morning in Jaipur, which he calls his 'kindergarten lessons in communication'. It is a credo, not a testable proposition: 'respect for the audience' and 'delight' are not defined and no way of checking whether a piece of work has them is offered.
confounders: The sentence appears twice in the available copy — once inside the paragraph and once as a flattened pull-quote — which is a conversion artefact, not emphasis.
model_answer: Pandey's governing principle is to speak to people in their own language and from their own lives: simple, human, rooted in everyday Indian and often Hindi idiom, aimed at the heart rather than the head. It comes from his upbringing in Jaipur, his family, cricket and his experience of ordinary Indians, which he contrasts with English-language advertising copied from the West. It is a practitioner's credo, a statement of belief drawn from experience and illustrated with his campaigns. It is not a tested or evidenced proposition. [unsure]
missed: Respect, context, spontaneity, delight; father's morning verse

source_title: desai_mother_pious_lady
question: What licensed spending in the household this source describes, and what was treated as the enemy?
answer: An occasion licensed spending; impulse was the enemy. He describes growing up in middle-class India as 'an elaborate exercise in learning to detach action from one's senses' — ice cream was not eaten because one felt like it but on occasions when celebrations had been planned, and new clothes were bought with ceremony at festivals. Festivals functioned as 'the safety valves in our otherwise restrained lives', supplying permission the individual's own appetite was not allowed to supply. The mechanism is that where budgets are tight and every deviation is felt as risk, the sense that prompts spending has to be disconnected from the act, and an external calendar then supplies the sanction.
confounders: Wholly retrospective — an adult recalling a childhood household with no contemporaneous record — and the book's second section is explicitly about these constraints loosening.
model_answer: In the traditional middle-class household Desai describes, spending was licensed by duty and purpose: necessity, family welfare (children's education, marriages, festivals and ritual occasions) and durability or long-term value, often framed as saving or investment. The enemy was self-indulgence and waste: spending on oneself, frivolous consumption and showing off, which were treated as morally suspect. [unsure]
missed: Occasion licensed spending; impulse the enemy; senses detached from action

source_title: pandey_pandeymonium
question: A team wants to adopt this source's five-second attention criterion as a pass mark for a new evaluator. What does the record do, and why?
answer: It refuses. The binding derived from this material supports asking whether a time-based asset holds attention through its opening, and its status_reason states that the five-second threshold is explicitly NOT adopted. The reason is that the figure is a practitioner's rule of thumb offered in passing, with no validation, no account of how it was arrived at, and no proposed way of checking it. Adopting it would be inventing a pass mark, which this project forbids — the same discipline that keeps the temporal-video pass mark recorded as non-existent rather than guessed. There is a second reason too: the author executes his criterion as a human observer in the room, and an automated attention measure would be a different instrument with its own validation problem, about which this source supports nothing.
confounders: The criterion is concrete and plausible, which is precisely what makes it tempting to adopt without validation.
model_answer: The five-second criterion, that an idea must grab and be understood within a few seconds, comes from Pandey's practitioner rhetoric and anecdotes, not measurement. The record should treat it as a heuristic with no validated threshold, no definition of what counts as grabbing attention, no measurement procedure and no evidence linking it to effectiveness. So it should be noted as a directional principle, not adopted as a pass mark. Turning it into a scored threshold would give false precision to a rule of thumb. [unsure]

source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
question: A brief calls for a metal tin standing on a dark surface, shot so all three of its faces show. The tin's front face keeps going black and its bottom edge dissolves into the table. Using this book's reasoning, what is happening and what is its easiest answer?
answer: Each visible face of the tin has its own family of angles, and they face different directions. The family defined by the FRONT face falls on the table where the tin stands, so the table is the light source for that face whether or not the photographer wants it to be — and a dark table is a source that emits almost nothing, so the front face has nothing to reflect and records black. The bottom edge dissolves for the related reason: a near-pure direct reflector records at about the brightness of what it reflects, and where the tin's lower face and the surface it stands on reach the same brightness there is no tonal boundary left for the camera to record. No reflector card fixes this without appearing in the frame, because the family it must occupy is inside the picture; the authors say brightly polished metal boxes almost always exhibit the problem. Their easiest answer is a light-toned background: the background itself becomes the light source for much of the visible metal, and much of the work is done as soon as the tin is placed on it. The one requirement they stress is that the background must be large enough to fill the family of angles the metal reflects, not merely the area the camera sees.
confounders: adding a front fill light, which either fails to enter the family or appears in the shot
raising the exposure, which cannot help a surface with no diffuse channel
sizing the background to the frame rather than to the family of angles
model_answer: The front face is reflecting the dark surroundings (camera area), because for a metal box the front face mirrors what's in front of it; the bottom edge disappears because it's dark tone against dark surface. The easiest answer: place a large white card or light source in front, reflecting in the front face, and elevate or use a light-toned surface or edge highlight to separate the bottom. [unsure]
missed: Table is the front face's source; light background filling family of angles

source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
question: A team runs Hopkins's weekly keyed loop faithfully and every reading is excellent — coupon response is high and rising. On the source's own evidence, what class of failure would this loop not see, and which case in the book demonstrates it?
answer: The loop measures response to the advertising, so it cannot see a failure that occurs after the purchase. The case is the automobile campaign at printed pp. 119-120, which he calls the most successful automobile advertising he ever did and which destroyed the client: inquiries ran at a rate he says he never saw matched and sales started at an amazing rate, but the car had been skimped in every detail, hundreds came back, and the larger the sales the worse the ruin. His own formulation is that the note played was too high for the product available. His other criterion is where the check belongs — the repeat-sale test at printed p. 135, which asks whether repeat business paid for the advertising before the bills fell due. He does not connect the two, and nowhere draws the conclusion that response volume is not evidence of a successful campaign.
confounders: assuming a high response rate is what Hopkins means by a campaign paying; his stated criterion is repeat sales inside the billing period
attributing the Mitchell failure to the advertising; he attributes it to the product and to the height of the claim
reading this as a general warning about vanity metrics; the specific mechanism he describes is that each additional sale converts into an additional damaged reputation
model_answer: A keyed coupon loop measures immediate response per dollar. It cannot see failures that arrive through other channels or later: reputational, regulatory or product-level collapse, or buyers who do not repeat. The case in the book is Liquozone, the germicide 'cure' that Hopkins sold with enormous traced success through samples and coupons, until the patent-medicine exposés and pure-food legislation destroyed the business. Every keyed reading looked excellent right up until an external, non-measured factor ended it. [unsure]
missed: Automobile campaign pp.119-120: skimped car, sales ruined client

source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
question: Google states the same ABCD effectiveness result on three of its own pages. How does the phrasing differ between them, and why does the difference matter?
answer: Three different strengths for one finding. Google Ads Help says the ABCDs "Deliver as much as a 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17% lift in long-term brand contribution" — an upper bound. Think with Google says "On average, the ABCDs deliver a 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17% lift in long-term brand contribution" — a central tendency. The Google for Business resources article prints the two numbers as bare callouts with no qualifier at all, above a page-footer line reading "Actual results will vary by advertiser". An upper bound and an average are different statistics, and a reader who meets one page will draw a different expectation from a reader who meets another. Nothing on any of the three pages resolves which is right, and this bank does not resolve it either.
confounders: assuming Google's own pages must state the same finding identically, and reporting only one phrasing
reading 'as much as' as the average, which is the more flattering error and the more common one
confusing this with an IPA-style databank figure of the kind Binet and Field report, which comes with a published methodology appendix
assuming the bare callouts on the resources article carry the 'on average' qualifier from elsewhere
model_answer: Across its three pages Google phrases the result differently. One says ads following the ABCDs saw a 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood. Another says they drove 30% higher short-term sales. Another says 'up to' or 'on average', or refers to brand contribution. The difference matters because 'sales likelihood', 'sales', 'up to' and 'average' are materially different claims in magnitude and certainty. Citing the strongest phrasing overstates the evidence, so it's safest to quote the most qualified version and its study context. [unsure]
missed: 'As much as' upper bound vs 'on average' vs bare callouts

source_title: dwyer_patel_cinema_india
question: Enumerate what the song sequence is described as licensed to suspend, and say what that implies about reading a film's narrative from its songs.
answer: Three things, and the source names each. Real time: the heroine may change costume repeatedly within one sequence. Location: the sequence may move from India to Switzerland without any reference to moving in space. Narrative consequence: love 'may be expressed in the song but not necessarily acknowledged in the narrative'. Dwyer frames this via Vasudevan's argument that the relationship between narrative, performance sequence and action spectacle is loosely structured in the fashion of a 'cinema of attractions' after Gunning and Gaudreault, and adds that eroticism is largely contained within the song, along with other breaks in continuity including a whole different range of gesture and movement. The implication for reading is direct: what a song shows cannot be assumed to have happened in the story. A declaration made in a song may leave the narrative exactly where it was.
confounders: Treating songs as narrative summary is the error this passage rules out; it is also the error a text-only synopsis of such a film would make.
model_answer: The song sequence is licensed to suspend narrative time and linear progression, spatial continuity and realism (sudden jumps to foreign or fantasy locations), diegetic logic (characters burst into song and dance), costume continuity (multiple changes within one song), and social and moral constraints, allowing romance, eroticism and desire shown more openly than in the narrative. So you cannot read a film's story directly from its songs. They are semi-autonomous spaces of fantasy and spectacle that often express what the narrative cannot, and they circulate separately, so treating them as plot summaries misreads both.

source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
question: What exactly does the source claim about audio brand mentions, and is it an additive claim or an interactive one?
answer: Interactive. The claim is that "Audio brand mentions enhance onscreen brand visuals' performance" — the spoken mention raises the performance of the visual it accompanies, rather than contributing a separate increment of its own. That is why the instruction is to pair the two ("see and say") rather than to choose between them. It is a performance claim with nothing attached: no figure, no measure, no study at this level, and the headline lift the pages carry is stated for the ABCDs as a set and never decomposed by principle. The claim also presupposes the audio is heard, which the source asserts for YouTube and for nothing else.
confounders: reading it as 'audio branding also works', which is the additive reading and loses the interaction
attaching part of the 30% lift to this technique; the source never decomposes the figure
assuming a mechanism is given; the source states the effect and not the cause
model_answer: The source says audio brand mentions: including brand name in voiceover or sound early leads to higher performance, e.g. ads that mention the brand in the audio and visually outperform. It's an interactive claim: combined audio+visual brand mentions lift performance more than either alone. [unsure]

source_title: pandey_pandeymonium
question: Why does this book, which argues from named visual campaigns, reproduce none of them — and what does that mean for what the source can support?
answer: Because the publisher deliberately located them elsewhere. The copyright page states: 'All images and television commercials mentioned in this book are available for viewing on www.pandeymonium.in'. So the campaigns were never printed in the book, in print or digital, and a reader of the 2015 edition was in exactly the position a reader of this copy is. This is the Audit Gate's source_evidence_never_printed pattern in its defining form: the gap is a property of how the work was published, not a digitisation loss, and filing it with digitisation losses would misattribute it. What it means for the source is precise: every claim about a named campaign is a claim about what Pandey SAYS about it, never about what the work looks like or what it achieved.
confounders: The named route was unreachable in the CANON-014 session (no network egress), so the evidence is named, located and unreachable there — recoverable in principle, not in that environment.
model_answer: The book is a memoir and anecdotal account. Reproducing the ads would need permissions from clients and rights-holders and adds cost, and the format relies on storytelling rather than illustration. As a result, the source can support claims about what Pandey says he intended, how the work came about and his reasoning. It cannot, by itself, verify what the executions actually looked like or claims about their visual craft. Those have to be checked against the ads themselves or other reproductions. [unsure]
missed: Copyright page directs to pandeymonium.in; never printed by design

source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
question: A five-star rating shows each star with a black outline, filled yellow when earned and white when not. A second version shows pale yellow stars on white with no outline. Which criterion does each version fail, and why is it not the same one?
answer: The first fails SC 1.4.1 Use of Color. The distinction between earned and unearned depends on recognising yellow versus white; the form of the star is unchanged, so hue alone carries the state. The second fails SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: the source gives the pale yellow as #FFF000 against white at a contrast ratio of 1.2:1, so the stars are not discernible at all. The two failures are genuinely different. The first version's stars are perfectly visible — you can see every star, you just cannot tell which are filled. The second version's stars are barely visible as shapes. The source's stated passes make the boundary sharper still: a solid fill indicating the checked state that has contrast passes, and so does a yellow fill combined with a thicker border, because the border is a second, non-hue cue.
confounders: calling both a contrast failure, which loses the distinction the source draws
assuming raising the yellow's contrast fixes the first version — it does not; the state is still carried by hue alone
assuming adding a text label is the only remedy; the source accepts a thicker border as a sufficient second cue
model_answer: In the first version the stars have a contrasting black outline, so the graphics are perceivable (SC 1.4.11 is met). Earned and unearned stars, however, differ only by fill colour (yellow versus white), so it risks failing SC 1.4.1 Use of Color unless there is another cue or sufficient contrast. The second version, pale yellow stars on white with no outline, fails SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, because the star shapes lack 3:1 contrast against the adjacent white. They aren't the same criterion: one is about colour as the sole carrier of state, the other about luminance contrast of the graphic.

source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
question: You are reviewing twelve images made as one body of work. Which of Carroll's two assessment principles applies, and what does the other one get wrong here?
answer: Both are his and they pull in opposite directions, so the answer is that the unit has to be settled first. His excuse test is a per-frame test — this photograph either stands without an account of the circumstances or it does not. His series claim says the frame is the wrong unit for a body of work, because the meaning is carried by style and order across the set and assessing members independently destroys exactly the property being claimed. So for a body of work made and sequenced as one, the series claim governs; applying the excuse test frame by frame would be the error he says he made himself as a student. The honest limit is that he gives no method for judging a series, only for judging a frame.
confounders: applying the excuse test to each image and concluding the set is weak
assuming Carroll offers a method for evaluating a series; he offers only a claim that the unit is different
treating the two principles as compatible without settling the unit of observation
model_answer: For twelve images made as one body of work, Carroll's principle about series applies. Judge the images as a set: coherence, consistency of approach and theme, sequencing, and whether each picture contributes to the whole. Weaker individual images may earn a place if they serve the narrative, and strong images that don't fit should go. The single-image principle, that each photo must stand on its own and be judged in isolation, gets this wrong. It would pick the individually strongest images even if they don't hang together and would cut connective images the series needs. [unsure]

source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
question: In the objective table, three cells read "Apply core principles". Which principle is left at core under which objective, and what does that pattern tell you about the framework?
answer: Direction is left at core under awareness. Attention is left at core under both consideration and action. The full-funnel row has no such cell — all four principles carry an objective-specific instruction there. The pattern matters because it shows the objective table varies emphasis and never varies membership: no principle is dropped for any objective, and where an objective calls for no special treatment the cell says to apply the core guidance rather than being left empty. That is the strongest textual evidence that the source treats the four as jointly applied rather than as a menu.
confounders: assuming action campaigns downweight Branding; the action row carries the table's strongest branding instruction, 'Make the product the ad'
assuming awareness campaigns drop Direction entirely rather than leaving it at core
assuming full funnel is a blend of the other three rows rather than four instructions of its own
model_answer: In the objective table, Direct is left at 'Apply core principles' for awareness, Connect maybe for action... The pattern: the framework emphasises different principles per objective, prioritising what matters most for each goal; so it is not uniform, it's weighted. [unsure]
missed: Attention core for consideration and action; varies emphasis not membership

source_title: parameswaran_nawabs_nudes_noodles
question: A brand wants a hoarding format it can produce fast enough to comment on this week's news while staying instantly recognisable. What structure does the reproduced Amul topical show, and what is the inferred reason it works?
answer: A fixed form with exactly one variable slot. The plate shows a flat yellow ground, a large hand-lettered display pun as the only headline ('THOROUGHBREAD', over a horse-racing subject), a cartoon illustration of the Amul girl acting the pun out, and a constant brand signature — 'utterly butterly Amul' in a small casual hand. Only the pun and its illustrated subject change between executions; ground, character, lettering manner and signature do not. The inferred reason is that holding everything constant except the joke makes each new execution recognisable before it is read, so it can be produced and posted fast while remaining unmistakably the same campaign. Both the structure and the speed reasoning are the extractor's from one plate; the source says only that this was the first topical and that hundreds followed.
confounders: Only ONE execution is reproduced in this copy, so the invariant set is inferred from a single instance plus the source's assertion that the series ran.
model_answer: The Amul topical hoarding is a fixed template with one variable. The Amul girl mascot (polka-dot dress, blue hair, simple cartoon illustration), the red-and-white look, the logo and the sign-off 'Amul: Utterly Butterly Delicious' stay constant. Only a punning Hinglish headline and a small scene about the week's news change. The inferred reason it works is that the constant elements make every execution instantly recognisable while the topical pun supplies freshness and talkability. Minimal illustration and copy mean it can be produced in a day or two, fast enough to ride current events.

source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
question: Your team has just written a set of design principles. Can they be critiqued, and if so against what? Use this source's claim about what does and does not change between different things being critiqued.
answer: Yes. The source's claim is that the framework does not change no matter what is being critiqued — what are the objectives, what elements relate to them, are those elements effective, why or why not — and that what changes is the set of objectives the thing is analysed against. For design principles the yardstick is the best practices for making design principles, and the source names two of them: a good principle should help you eliminate more ideas than you pursue, and it should be specific, avoiding overly subjective and ambiguous terms like "fun". The reflexive move is stated explicitly in both places: any artifact made toward an objective is critiquable, including personas, scenarios, journey maps, and the tools, methodologies and processes a team uses — "Critique. All. The. Things." The source adds two refinements: some product objectives are pertinent to one artifact and not another, since a colour palette may or may not bear on a goal of increasing authenticated visits; and different aspects of a design carry their own objectives, usually as principles and best practices specific to interaction or visual design.
confounders: assuming critique applies only to visual artifacts — wireframes, comps, prototypes
concluding a different framework is needed for non-visual artifacts, which is what the source denies
using the product's business goals as the yardstick for the principles, when the source's yardstick here is the best practices for writing principles
model_answer: Yes. Connor and Irizarry hold that the critique process stays the same whatever is being critiqued (visual designs, flows, content, strategy or principles). What changes is the objectives the thing is meant to achieve. Anything created for a purpose can be critiqued against that purpose. So design principles are critiqued against what they're for: whether they are clear, distinct and actionable, whether they help the team make and evaluate decisions consistently, and whether they reflect the product's goals and users.
missed: Yardstick is principle-writing best practices: eliminate ideas, be specific

source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
question: A team is choosing a cue to link a product to and proposes the colour red because everyone sees red constantly. State the trade-off Berger names, his image for it, and what he says about how to resolve it.
answer: The trade-off is frequency against strength of link. A cue must occur often or it will rarely fire — his case is a beer brand moving from "Holidays are made for Michelob" to "Weekends are made for Michelob" because holidays are too rare. But the more things a cue is already associated with, the weaker any one association becomes, and red is his own example of the failure: roses, love, Coca-Cola, fast cars, so it retrieves none of them strongly. His image is a paper cup with holes punched in the bottom — one hole gives a strong stream, many holes give a trickle from each. His recommendation is a fresher, more original link, with peanut butter reliably retrieving jelly as the standard to aim at. On how to resolve it: he names the two failure modes and stops. He gives no procedure for locating the balance point, which is exactly the decision a practitioner faces.
confounders: optimising for frequency alone, which is what makes red look attractive
optimising for distinctiveness alone, which is the holidays failure
expecting Berger to supply a method for finding the balance; he does not, and treating his advice as operable overstates it
model_answer: Berger's trade-off is between how often a trigger occurs and how strongly it is linked to your product. A very frequent, generic cue like red is already associated with many things, so any one link is weak and diluted, much like trying to be heard in a crowded room of competing associations. The link must be distinctive to work. To resolve it, choose a cue that is frequent in the target audience's environment but not already heavily linked to other things, and build a strong, specific connection to it, as Kit Kat did with coffee. [unsure]
missed: Cup-with-holes image; he gives no resolution procedure
